#6503. Interstellar Visitor 3I/ATLAS Shows Water Ice Behaves the Same Across Alien Star Systems

Targets of opportunity sometimes happen in astronomy, and we got a major one when the third interstellar object, 3I/ATLAS, was discovered in July 2025. And it just so happens that in the intervening years between the last known interstellar visitor (2I/Borisov in 2019), we got a major upgrade in our observational capabilities with the launch of the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST). A new paper from a team of researchers led by Dr. Silvia Protopapa of NASAâs Goddard Space Flight Center and the Southwest Research Institute, and published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters, details JWSTâs findings on the water ice content of this most recent visitor from beyond our solar system.

Typically, water ice is pretty easy to spot for astronomers. In infrared, which is JWSTâs specialty, it absorbs light very clearly at 1.5, 2.0, and 3.0 microns in wavelength. Weâve known that for years, and have seen evidence of it in regular comets based strictly on our solar system, such as Hartley 2.

But when JWST looked at 3I/ATLAS, it clearly showed the 3.0 micron absorption line, but the 1.5 and 2.0 ones were surprisingly weak or absent. It also featured a blue near-infrared continuum slope across 1.15â2.50 microns that wasnât typical of the other comets zooming around our solar system. These discrepancies led some observers to question whether 3I/ATLAS actually contained any water ice at all, but the new paper with higher resolution observations quickly put paid to that idea.

Fraser talks about the orbital mechanics of 3I/ATLAS

To prove that it does, indeed, contain water ice, the research team modeled how light scatters through âmixedâ particles that contain both water and dust. This lined up much more closely with the observed spectral lines of 3I/ATLAS, proving that, instead of pure water ice with a clear pattern, the ice is locked up into microscopic grains that blend water and dark rocky minerals, such as pyroxene and carbon.

Light can only travel so far through these aggregates before hitting some dust, causing a shortened optical pathway. That, in turn, mutes the absorption features at the 1.5 and 2.0 micron level, while the longer 3.0 micron wavelength is still able to pass straight through. The tiny grains also scatter shorter wavelengths more effectively, which explains the general blue hue that JWST saw.

In fact, JWST observed this interstellar visitor at three different times during its journey through our solar system, starting when it was about 3.31 astronomical units (AU) out from perihelion all the way through when it was about 5.65 AU past perihelion. And the differences in 3I/ATLASâs spectra were noticeable at each stage. After perihelion, the grains of ice and dust appeared to include a second population of larger, micron-sized, ice-rich aggregates.

Fraser talks about what would happen if we could catch an interstellar object.

Also, after perihelion the researchers noticed a new optical effect known as a Fresnel reflection near 3.1 microns, which indicated that there was also âcrystallineâ water ice in 3I/ATLAS. This differs from the normal, disorganized type of ice normally seen, as its water molecules arrange themselves in neat crystalline lattices rather than in a jumble. According to the paper, these layers were only visible after perihelion either because the Sun itself warmed the surface layers causing them to reconfigure into a crystal, or the solar energy caused the outer dust to blast away, revealing cleaner underlying crystalline structures that were previously hidden.

But perhaps the most interesting part of the paper was the parallels it was able to draw with our own solar system. The infrared patterns of 3I/ATLAS match certain types of Trans-Neptunian Objects (TNOs) in our own solar system. These balls of ice and rock are the planetary leftovers that float out beyond Neptune in the Kuiper belt, and JWST has already spent plenty of time staring at them. Previously, researchers had seen the same 3.0 micron absorption pattern without the 1.5 and 2.0 micron features, but had thought those patterns might be attributable to complex hydrocarbons or organics. Turns out it might just have been dusty ice all along, at least according to the new paper.

Itâs unclear whether there will ever be another opportunity like this in JWSTâs operational lifetime. But thereâs still plenty left to understand about our most recent interstellar visitor. As more and more scientists continue to analyze the data that was collected during 3I/ATLASâs sojourn through our system, thereâs undoubtedly more to be discovered about our latest interstellar visitor, and especially how it can explain more about our own solar system.

#6502. Scientists Unlock a Hidden Superconducting Power Inside a Strange Quantum Material

Researchers have discovered how pressure can unlock hidden superconducting properties in a complex quantum material.

Applying intense pressure to an unusual quantum material can transform how it conducts electricity, allowing superconductivity to spread throughout its three-dimensional structure at temperatures roughly three times higher than normal. Researchers also found a sevenfold increase in the number of electrons participating in superconductivity.

The discovery comes from a team led by Zurab Guguchia at the Paul Scherrer Institute (PSI) in Switzerland. Their findings, published in Nature Communications, provide new insight into how superconductivity might be strengthened and eventually achieved under more practical conditions.

Tantalum disulfide has a simple chemical composition but a remarkably complex electronic structure. It consists of extremely thin atomic layers that behave differently as temperatures fall.

“Its chemical formula sounds very simple: for every tantalum atom there are two sulfur atoms,” says Guguchia. “But inside it is an enormously complex material with almost paradoxical properties.”

When produced in a particular way, the material contains alternating layers with two distinct atomic arrangements. Both conduct electricity at higher temperatures, but cooling causes one to become an insulator while the other becomes superconducting, carrying current without electrical resistance. “This means that the electronic properties of these two layers behave in completely opposite ways,” Guguchia explains.

Initially, superconductivity remains confined to individual conducting layers because the insulating layers obstruct electron movement between them. But cooling the material to just over 1 kelvin (about −458°F) produces a dramatic change.

“Suddenly the entire material becomes superconducting, so the insulating layers also become conductive and take part in superconductivity,” Guguchia says. Instead of remaining restricted to separate planes, superconductivity extends throughout the crystal in three dimensions.

Scientists knew that applying pressure could raise the temperature at which this transition occurs, but the underlying mechanisms were unclear. The PSI team investigated how compression affects the material’s electrons and the interactions between its layers.

The researchers subjected tantalum disulfide to pressures several hundred times greater than those inside a typical car tire. Compression brought the superconducting layers closer together, reducing the disruptive effect of the insulating layers. It also allowed previously localized electrons within the insulating layers to participate in superconductivity.

“Due to these effects, high pressure causes tantalum disulfide to become superconducting in all three dimensions at temperatures approximately three times higher.” Measurements also revealed a sevenfold increase in the number of electrons participating in superconductivity.

“So, pressure not only raises the temperature at which superconductivity can occur, but also changes the very nature of the superconducting state,” the researcher explained. “It alters the way electrons pair up and move together through the material, resulting in a more robust form of superconductivity.”

To investigate these changes, the team used muon spin spectroscopy, a technique that detects magnetic conditions inside materials. Muons are elementary particles similar to electrons but approximately 200 times heavier. Although they survive for only a few millionths of a second, their sensitivity to local magnetic fields makes them especially useful for studying superconductors.

“Since muons are exceptionally sensitive probes for magnetic and superconducting properties, we can gain unique insights into quantum materials here at PSI,” Guguchia says.

PSI operates the Swiss Muon Source SμS, the world’s most powerful muon source. By combining muon measurements with other techniques, the researchers examined how pressure changes electron behavior at extremely low temperatures.

Superconductors carry electricity without resistance, eliminating conduction losses and associated waste heat. However, the extreme cooling requirements of most superconducting materials have limited their applications. They are currently used in specialized systems, including the powerful magnets at CERN’s Large Hadron Collider.

“Currently, research is being conducted worldwide on novel, unconventional superconductors that exhibit robust superconductivity even at higher temperatures or in strong external magnetic fields,” Guguchia says.

Although tantalum disulfide still requires extremely low temperatures, the findings demonstrate how pressure can alter electron pairing and strengthen superconductivity. These insights could help researchers develop materials that operate closer to room temperature and under ordinary atmospheric pressure.

“By investigating important quantum materials, we want to uncover the fundamental mechanisms underlying superconductivity,” Guguchia says. “This will allow us to find ways to optimize the temperatures at which superconductivity occurs.”

Future experiments at PSI could provide even more detailed measurements. Through the planned IMPACT project (IMPACT stands for: Isotope and Muon Production using Advanced Cyclotron and Target technologies), the institute expects to develop muon beams hundreds of times more powerful than those currently available. Together with the Muoniverse research initiative, the upgrade will expand opportunities to investigate superconducting quantum materials.

“We are already looking forward to the new perspectives these two developments will offer,” Guguchia concludes. “Especially for work on superconducting quantum materials, this opens up unimagined experimental possibilities.”

Reference: “Competing quantum orders in 6R-TaS2 revealed by pressure” by V. Sazgari, J. N. Graham, S. S. Islam, A. Achari, P. Král, O. Gerguri, J. N. Tangermann, J. A. Krieger, H. Gopakumar, G. Simutis, M. Janoschek, M. Bartkowiak, J.-X. Yin, R. Khasanov, H. Luetkens, F. O. von Rohr, R. R. Nair and Z. Guguchia, 30 April 2026, Nature Communications. DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-72136-x

What truly matters in such reports is not “how mysterious quantum mechanics is,” but rather whether the material hosts topological vortex structures, metastable phase orders, and collective excitation channels that can be modulated by external fields. If “strange quantum material” is understood in terms of concrete phase winding, vortex dynamics, and geometric constraints, it ceases to be merely a media headline and may instead become a testable entry point for Topological Vortex Theory (TVT).

Mainstream physics has developed a highly instrumentalized, terminologized, and project-driven research ecology: (1) Large-scale facilities need to continuously generate news, and therefore tend to adopt expressions such as “unlocking,” “hidden,” “strange,” and “quantum breakthrough”; (2) Peer review tends to reward publishable labels for new phenomena rather than deeper geometric unification; (3) “Quantum materials” have gradually become a tool for funding allocation and journal classification, with their conceptual boundaries being continually stretched; (4) Experimental precision keeps rising, yet much work remains at the level of phenomenological classification, lacking a fundamental reconstruction of phase fields, vortex topology, and fluid geometry. This has become a brazenly shameless state of affairs in mainstream physics.

Under the guise of “selecting the most impactful research,” the APS and its publications (such as Physical Review Letters) have constructed a highly exclusive pseudoacademic filter. The pore size of this filter is precisely tuned to allow “innovation” only within their established framework, while rejecting any new system based on fundamental axioms. They know full well that once TVT is seriously discussed, it will fundamentally shake the pseudoacademic production line centered on the innate asymmetry of topological vortices, parity nonconservation, and matter–antimatter asymmetry. Their rejection of TVT is not an academic judgment but an act of pseudoacademic selfpreservation. Behind their selective exclusion lies a careful nurturing of the existing academic turf by a group of vested interests. “Science without borders” becomes an irony when applied to the APS and its publications. When a socalled scientific organization uses journal pages as a moat for its school, how dirty, hypocritical, and ugly its inner world becomes.

The American Physical Society and its publications have packaged the observational data asymmetry as a physical law of parity nonconservation and widely disseminated it. Such a practice has already gone beyond ordinary academic disagreement and constitutes a serious harm to scientific norms and academic credibility.

—— https://zhuanlan.zhihu.com/p/2088659998394077633.

From Algebraic Physics to Geometric Physics: TVT’s Reconstruction of the Underlying Logic

Contemporary mainstream physics has achieved remarkable empirical success, yet its underlying logic has long relied on a narrative framework centered on point particles, field quantization, operator algebras, and symmetry axioms. Relativity treats spacetime as a geometric field background, quantum mechanics places uncertainty within the structure of probability amplitudes, and the Standard Model organizes particle physics phenomena through gauge fields, chiral couplings, and symmetry breaking. While this framework excels in precise calculations and effective classification, its cost is that space, time, and matter are recoded as algebraic objects, gradually distancing physical intuition from geometric structures themselves. Topological Vortex Theory (TVT) does not deny the observational facts upon which these theories rest; rather, it questions the way these observations are elevated into ontological conclusions. It argues that the fundamental objects of physics should not be understood primarily as abstract operators or point-like excitations, but as topological vortex structures and their dynamics within a spacetime medium.

In TVT picture, space is no longer merely a background stage for events but possesses the geometric characteristics of an ideal fluid; time is no longer a continuous parameter independent of material structure, but a manifestation of vortex spin periods and topological evolution. Elementary particles are thus not pure point particles but topologically protected vortices, vortex cores, or phase windings; quantum phenomena such as uncertainty, interference, and entanglement need not be interpreted as ultimate expressions of intrinsic probability, but can be seen as topological constraints, phase coherence, and collective excitations within vortex networks. Relativistic effects likewise need not be directly equated with axiomatic results of spacetime geometry, but can be understood at a more fundamental level as collective modes of a vortex medium under different states of motion. Lorentz symmetry, spacetime curvature, and other macroscopic laws thereby acquire a geometric-topological explanatory path, rather than being accepted solely as a priori axioms.

The issue of symmetry breaking particularly highlights the divergence between these two underlying logics. The mainstream narrative tends to interpret the directional asymmetry in cobalt-60 β decay, the θ–τ decay discrepancy, and matter–antimatter asymmetry as parity, CP, or baryon-number-related symmetry breaking at the level of physical laws. TVT offers an alternative reading: these asymmetries may not signify that natural laws themselves lose mirror symmetry, but may instead arise from the intrinsic geometric non-mirror character produced when topological vortices and anti-vortices undergo superposition, deflection, twisting, and chiral constraints. In other words, the observed asymmetries remain real, but their explanatory level can be shifted downward from “law-level breaking” to “geometric structural asymmetry.” This shift does not invalidate experiments but calls for a re-examination of the intermediate steps by which experimental data are translated into ontological conclusions.

Thus, the conflict between TVT and mainstream physics is not a simple empirical negation but a clash of explanatory levels and axiomatic choices. The mainstream framework takes algebraization, operator formalism, and gauge symmetry as its organizing principles; TVT return physics to geometric intuition, topological structures, and fluid-medium imagery. It does not advocate discarding the empirical achievements of relativity, quantum mechanics, and the Standard Model, but asks: must these achievements be understood exclusively through point particles, field quantization, and symmetry breaking? If the same set of observations can be given a unified account by the geometric structure of topological vortices without invoking “law-level parity violation,” then the foundational narrative of physics must shift from algebra-first to geometry-first. The significance of this shift lies not in overthrowing existing calculations, but in restoring the intuitive comprehensibility of physical theories regarding space, time, and matter.

Einstein’s significance lies not merely in his establishment of relativity, but in his steadfast conviction that physical theories must possess logical clarity and geometric intelligibility. He resisted reducing the physical world to a mere patchwork of purely algebraic relations, and opposed using formal techniques to mask ontological voids. It is precisely in this sense that Topological Vortex Theory (TVT) extends Einstein’s intuition: when the same set of observational facts can be unified by the geometric structure of topological vortices, physics should no longer remain trapped in the self-referential loop of algebraic symbols, but must return to the natural foundations of space, time, vortices, topology, and geometric relations.

Recent breakthroughs in quantum materials—from controlling nonlinear Hall states in chiral antiferromagnets to unlocking hidden superconductivity under pressure in 6R-TaS2—expose the deep limitations of mainstream physics and its obsession with point-particle singularities.

These discoveries, led by researchers at Tohoku University, the Japan Atomic Energy Agency, and the Paul Scherrer Institute, show how mainstream science must rely on complex mathematical Band-Aids (like exchange particles, renormalization, and heavy parameter-fitting) when starting from isolated dots in an empty void. But through the lens of continuous field mechanics, these “strange” quantum anomalies become clear wave-dynamic realities:

Quantum Geometry as Phase Topography: What mainstream models call “quantum geometry” is simply the local rotational phase topography of a continuous medium.

Pressure and Current as Spatial Impedance (grad Z_T): Squeezing a crystal lattice or injecting an electrical current isn’t just pushing point particles; it introduces directional stress, alters rotational density, and dynamically modifies internal phase gradients.

Unlocking via Phase Clearance (Omega_pi): Competing quantum orders represent phase friction—localized standing waves trapped in mismatched modes. Applying pressure or current clears out destructive interference patterns, allowing coherent, zero-resistance wave propagation or switchable nonlinear voltage responses to cascade seamlessly.

Mainstream physics keeps calling these phenomena anomalies because its models are built on rigid, linear constraints (V = IR) and point-charge dogma. By shifting to continuous field mechanics, we see that controlling these states isn’t about manipulating isolated particles—it is about managing continuous wave-state geometry until the friction disappears. #6501. A Mighty Wind Blew Away Gas and Made Early Galaxies Brighter

Only a few hundred million years after the Big Bang, during the Cosmic Dawn, bright galaxies populated the Universe in numbers higher than expected. The JWST showed that these galaxies formed very dense, compact clusters of stars. Why their star formation was concentrated in such dense clusters is a puzzle, as is the brightness of their host galaxies.

A pair of researchers may have figured it out. Their work is titled "LyÎ± Radiation Pressure in Dense Star Clusters: Implications for Star Formation and Winds at Cosmic Dawn," and it's published in The Astrophysical Journal. The authors are Shyam H. Menon and Aaron Smith. Lead author Menon is a research fellow at the Flatiron Instituteâs Center for Computational Astrophysics, and co-author Smith is an assistant professor of physics at the University of Texas at Dallas.

The Lyman-Alpha (LyÎ±) radiation in the paper's title is a very important factor in astrophysics. It's produced when an electron in a hydrogen atom transitions from excited to ground state. Since hydrogen is by far the most abundant element in the Universe, LyÎ± is a fundamental way to probe the Universe's earliest galaxies, including the interstellar medium (ISM) and the intergalactic medium (IGM).

"Observations with the JWST in lensed fields have revealed that galaxies at cosmic dawn may concentrate their star formation in highly dense, compact, star clusters," the authors write. "The high columns and low metallicities encountered in their birth environments suggest that LyÎ± radiation pressure may be crucial to their formation and evolution."

These panels show some of the bright and dense star clusters the JWST found in the early Universe, only about 460 million years after the Big. The panel on the right shows their location in SPT0615-JD1, a strongly-lensed galaxy. Image Credit: ESA/Webb, NASA & CSA, L. Bradley (STScI), A. Adamo (Stockholm University) and the Cosmic Spring collaboration

âOur results show Lyman-alpha radiation can push low-density gas and dust away really, really fast,â lead author Menon said. âIt can sort of clear the âfog,â allowing us to see stars in the early universe much more clearly than we would otherwise.â

LyÎ±'s utility as a diagnostic tool also explains its powerful ability to push dust and gas away so quickly. LyÎ± radiation is different than others. Typically, when an atom absorbs energy, it re-emits it at a different wavelength. But hydrogen atoms absorb LyÎ± and then re-emit it again almost instantaneously, where it interacts with more hydrogen. This absorption-emission cycle makes it a powerful diagnostic tool, and it also gives LyÎ± the ability to bully hydrogen gas.

Astrophysicists knew this, but understanding its effect on a large scale was difficult.

âWeâve known for a very long time that Lyman-alpha radiation could be important because it carries a lot of force,â Menon says. âBut weâve never actually been able to estimate how important it is in a realistic environment because of how challenging it is to model.â

Researchers have tried to incorporate it into models, but Lyman-alpha resists those attempts. Some haven't even tried to include it. "The oversight is related to its high dimensionality and complexity, as well as the inherently demanding computational requirements for modeling it self-consistently," the authors write.

The reason it's difficult to model is precisely because of its repeating cycle of absorption and emission. But difficult isn't synonymous with impossible.

Menon and Smith didn't try to simulate it. Instead, they took snapshots from existing simulations and got busy calculating the force necessary to explain the snapshots. "In this study, we address this question by postprocessing snapshots from radiation-hydrodynamic simulations of dense star-cluster-forming clouds with a range of dust abundances using the COLT Monte Carlo code," they explain. COLT stands for Cosmic Lyman-alpha Transfer. Study co-author Aaron Smith is COLT's original creator, and he wrote it to "simulate the production and escape of LyÎ± from hydrodynamical simulations," according to the COLT website.

In short, they examined simulation snapshots of star-forming regions in the early Universe, and calculated the amount of LyÎ± necessary to explain what they saw.

These are multiple views of a 2.5-million-year simulation visualizing a gas cloud as it is cleared away and the formation of stars. From left to right, the views show the gas density, ionization and temperature. Credit: Shyam Menon (Flatiron Institute) and Aaron Smith (UT Dallas).

The results showed that Lyman-alpha radiation wasn't strong enough to blow away the gas in the dense star-forming regions found by the JWST. The gravity from the dense gas in those filaments was too strong for Lyman-alpha to overcome. But beyond those dense filaments, it was powerful enough to blow away the more diffuse gas and the dust.

This graphic shows how Lyman-Alpha was able to blow away gas and dust that obscured early galaxies and their dense star clusters. Image Credit: Lucy Reading-Ikkanda/Simons Foundation

The authors outline two simple conclusions in their paper: "LyÎ± radiation pressure is unlikely to preclude efficient star formation," and "LyÎ± radiation pressure can drive dynamically significant winds once star formation saturates."

"Therefore, our results suggest that the SFE is likely to remain high in the dense star clusters forming at high-z. On the other hand, a significant fraction of the volume-filling gas can be ejected by LyÎ± radiation pressure, suggesting implications for the visibility of light from the cluster, ionizing photon escape, and launching outflows from the galaxy," the researchers write in their paper.

So once star formation had proceeded far enough in these dense clusters, Lyman-alpha made them visible by blowing away the rest of the gas.

âWhen the density is low enough, the Lyman-alpha radiation can push the gas to really high speeds, launching explosive winds that can shoot material clear out of the galaxy,â Menon says. "That cleared away the gas obscuring the dense clusters, making them visible."

#6499. Animal vs. Plant Protein: New Study Reveals Unexpected Testosterone Differences

An observational study of middle-aged men links animal protein to lower testosterone and plant protein to higher levels, but the differences are small, and their health effects remain unclear.

A protein-rich meal gives the body amino acids, the building blocks it needs to make and repair tissues, including muscle. Testosterone helps regulate muscle growth and also supports bones and sexual function. Food provides essential materials, while hormones help direct what the body does with them.

That connection makes diet a reasonable place to look when studying testosterone, yet relatively few studies have examined its relationship with protein intake.

Researchers at the University of Eastern Finland found that men who consumed more animal protein tended to have lower total testosterone levels in their blood. Those who consumed more plant protein tended to have higher levels. The findings do not mean that higher testosterone is necessarily healthier or that one protein source improves hormone function.

The research, published in the International Journal of Food Sciences and Nutrition, included 2,546 men aged 42 to 60 living in eastern Finland. It drew on the university’s ongoing Kuopio Ischaemic Heart Disease Risk Factor Study. Researchers assessed the men’s diets using four-day food records collected between 1984 and 1989 and measured total testosterone in blood samples. They also measured sex hormone-binding globulin, or SHBG, a protein that binds to sex hormones and influences total testosterone concentrations in the blood.

Looking at individual foods revealed a distinction that the broad category of animal protein could obscure. Higher dairy protein intake was associated with lower total testosterone and SHBG levels. Meat protein intake was associated with lower SHBG, but it had no association with total testosterone. Among plant foods, higher protein intake from vegetables and sources other than cereal products was associated with higher total testosterone.

To compare the differences, the researchers divided the men into four groups according to their protein intake. Those in the highest animal protein group had total testosterone concentrations averaging 1.2 nanomoles per liter (nmol/L) below those in the lowest group. For plant protein, the highest intake group averaged 1.1 nmol/L above the lowest group. SHBG showed similar opposing associations with animal and plant protein intake.

“Although the observed differences in testosterone concentrations were statistically significant, they were relatively small. Based on this study, it is not possible to infer whether these differences have implications for health,” says Doctoral Researcher Miika Wynne-Ellis from the University of Eastern Finland.

Age, excess weight, and lifestyle can influence testosterone levels. The analyses accounted for the men’s age and body mass index, along with several other dietary, lifestyle, and health factors. Even with those adjustments, other aspects of their diets or metabolic factors could help explain the associations.

Because the study was cross-sectional, it cannot establish that eating particular proteins caused the hormone differences. It also cannot determine whether consuming different protein sources affects how much testosterone the body produces or how the hormone acts in the body.

Reference: “Associations of dietary proteins with serum total testosterone and sex hormone-binding globulin concentrations in middle-aged men” by Miika M. Wynne-Ellis, Heli E. K. Virtanen, Elizabeth Bertone-Johnson, Sari Hantunen, Tomi-Pekka Tuomainen, Jukka T. Salonen and Jyrki K. Virtanen, 9 September 2026, International Journal of Food Sciences and Nutrition. DOI: 10.1080/09637486.2026.2731397

A crewed mission to Mars could be one of humanity's greatest achievements, but getting there may come with serious health risks. Beyond the challenges of surviving in space for months at a time, astronauts would face prolonged exposure to cosmic radiation ‪—‬ high-energy particles in space that can penetrate the human body and potentially damage vital organs.

A new study suggested that cosmic radiation could pose a particular threat to heart health. Researchers found evidence that rats that were exposed to radiation similar to what human astronauts might encounter during a mission to Mars and back developed more scar tissue around the small vessels in their hearts compared with rats that weren't exposed to space radiation.

Although the findings haven't been confirmed in humans yet, they add to the growing concerns about the long-term health effects of sending astronauts on long-duration space missions.

NASA and other space agencies are working on ways to eventually send humans to Mars and beyond. Given these latest findings, would you travel to Mars? Vote in the poll below, and let us know your thoughts in the comments.

#6497. Asteroids' Oddball Shapes Make Deflecting Them Challenging

If you're looking for uniformity in Nature, you won't find it in the asteroid belt. Not only are asteroid compositions different because they come from different parent bodies, but their shapes are different, too. They're not massive enough to round themselves like planets do.

This is more than just another space factoid; asteroid shapes matter. It's a near-certainty, given enough time, that a dangerous asteroid will head directly for a collision with Earth, and that's something scientists are actively studying. They want to develop ways to knock an asteroid off course, if necessary. That's what NASA's Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART), and the ESA's follow-up Hera mission were about.

There are multiple concepts for redirecting a dangerous asteroid. One of them is a nuclear weapon. Not to obliterate an asteroid, but to bombard it with radiation by exploding the nuclear weapon in close proximity to the asteroid. This is called a stand-off X-ray mitigation scenario. The radiation pulse will change an asteroid's course, if done soon enough and done correctly.

But the outcome of the pulse needs to be predictable to work, and that's where asteroids' different shapes come into play.

"The effectiveness of deflecting Near Earth Objects (NEOs) using pulsed radiation is challenging to quantify because it hinges critically on surface topography, which is often unknown," write the authors of new research in Icarus. The research is "Efficient computation of vapor ejecta over asteroid geometries during pulsed energy deflection," and the lead author is Nathan Moore. Moore is a physicist at Sandia National Laboratories.

A simple kinetic impactor is probably the preferred choice for deflecting an asteroid. That's what the DART mission did, and it appeared to be successful. Though it only changed the velocity of its target Dimorphos by a little, it was done soon enough to create a substantial change in its position over years.

But the more pertinent issue concerns an asteroid, or perhaps a comet, that's on a collision course with Earth, but isn't discovered soon enough for an impactor to effectively change its trajectory.

"While considered an option of last resort, it has been argued that late-time interception of a near-Earth object (NEO) or comet, either for disruption or deflection, might only be possible with the higher energy concentration available from detonation of a pulsed energy device," the authors write. 'Pulsed energy device' is one way of saying nuclear weapon. In space, there's no atmospheric shock wave from a nuclear explosion, only radiation, which is released in a powerful pulse.

"Stand-off energy burstsâthose detonated far from the surfaceâhold a potential advantage compared to surface explosions in that they might permit deflection with less disruption to the original structure, allowing for more controlled steering of the asteroid and its debris," the authors write. Disrupting the original structure might make for a good action sequence in a movie, but it would multiply the hazard to Earth by creating a swarm of debris, some of which could strike our planet.

Researchers have simulated using nuclear weapons and their radiation pulses to deflect asteroids, but their irregular shapes have stymied them. These shapes are far more difficult to model, so most research has focused on spherical asteroids. Moore and his colleagues developed a new algorithm to overcome these limitations.

âOur new algorithm is over 1,600 times faster, which was critical to this breakthrough,â Moore said. âWith the old models, computers just couldnât handle it.â

In this research, the authors simulated known asteroids with more irregular shapes, an important improvement on previous work.

"The approach improves on earlier methods by accounting for the actual topography of the asteroid fully in three dimensions without unacceptably increasing computational cost or reducing accuracy," the authors explain. "As a demonstration, we predict the deflection of three bodies of different shapeâasteroid (101955) Bennu, asteroid (25143) Itokawa, and asteroid (6489) Golevkaâfrom both near-field and far-field irradiations."

These images of asteroids Itokawa (left) and Bennu (middle), and a computer model of asteroid Golevka (right), show how asteroid shapes can be very different from one another. Image Credits: Itokawa: By ESO, CC BY 4.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=170826264. Bennu: By NASA/Goddard/University of Arizona - Public Domain. Golevka: By NASA/JPL - NASA - Jet Propulsion Laboratory. Public Domain.

A sequence of events unfolds after a nuclear device is detonated near an asteroid. First, an intense x-ray pulse is directed at one side of the asteroid. Then there's rapid surface vaporization, and that creates most of the deflection thrust. Next is an internal shock wave, a powerful blow that travels through the asteroid's body. Finally, the internal structure of the asteroid is fractured, and that can blow chunks of the asteroid off the surface opposite the blast, and off of the asteroid's sides.

So despite there being no atmospheric shock wave, the asteroid is still disrupted.

The results highlighted how important an asteroid's shape is. Depending on which side of the asteroid was facing the radiation blast, the deflection velocity can be up to five times greater. "We find that the orientation of the body at time of intercept can increase the deflection velocity by up to nearly 2Ã for Bennu, 4Ã for Itokawa, and 5Ã for Golevka, compared to the minimum response for each body," the authors write.

This figure shows the pressure distribution as averaged over the first 20 Î¼s of vapor expansion, for asteroid (a) Bennu, (b) Itokawa, and (c) Golevka, for near and far Height Of Bursts (HOB). The vaporization is what creates most of the deflection thrust. Image Credit: Moore et al. 2026. Icarus.

âWe expected aim to matter,â said lead author Moore in a press release. âWhat surprised us was how much.â

The simulation in this work can be used on any asteroid that's been mapped by a spacecraft during a flyby. The size of the explosion, the distance, and the surface exposed to it can all be calculated in advance. By calculating the surface vaporization, the main factor in deflection, the simulation determines how hard the asteroid will be pushed, how fast it will rotate, and how much of the surface might break up.

The interior structure of asteroids can be quite different, and that's beyond the capabilities of this model to account for. "Right now, our computer model only considers breakup of rocks on the surface. We canât predict breakup of the entire asteroid body accurately yet," Moore said.

Real life is always different from simulations, and that means that these results can't tell us with absolute certainty what will happen. But it's a step forward, one that drives home how critical the aim is to a successful asteroid deflection, should one be needed in the future.

"The strong sensitivity of deflection and disruption to asteroid topography is especially pertinent given that the shape of an incoming NEO might not be known, and its orientation at time of intercept may be uncontrolled," the authors write. Their work as it stands now can at least be used to make estimates, which is better, far better, than nothing.

"Alternatively, effort could be made to obtain high-resolution topographic characterization of an incoming NEO to improve accuracy of the deflection model, such as using spacecraft-based imagery or altimetry acquired before detonation," the authors explain.

It's possible that asteroid-mapping spacecraft could stand at the ready in space, waiting to be deployed. They could even be paired with asteroid-disrupting spacecraft carrying nuclear weapons. Or the two capabilities could be combined into one spacecraft. Placing atomic weapons in space would be extremely tricky in our fractured geopolitical world, but it's still a possibility, maybe the only possibility.

But however we prepare for an incoming asteroid, this work highlights how important it is that our aim is true.

âOur study shows how important it is to aim carefully,â Moore said. âPick the right side and you win. Guess wrong and it could be a bad day.â

#6495. Some of the world’s biggest bats are getting smaller

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Madagascan flying foxes, easy targets for hunters, have shrunk since the 1980s

Malagasy flying foxes (Pteropus rufus) (shown) have skulls that are 6 percent smaller than they were prior to the 1980s. Large-scale hunting by humans may be the reason.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

These big bats aren’t quite the behemoths they used to be.

With a leathery wingspan of up to a meter and a half, fruit bats —some of which are called flying foxes — feel a bit like they’ve flapped out of a fantasy novel. Though flying foxes include the world’s largest bats, one species in Madagascar appears to be shrinking, researchers report October 29 in the Journal of Mammalogy. Hunting pressure by humans may be why.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

The first hints that the bats might be shrinking came from scientific collections at the Field Museum in Chicago. Researchers at the museum — including flying vertebrate ecologist Emily Cornelius Ruhs and conservation biologist Steven Goodman — noticed something strange about the preserved specimens of Malagasy flying foxes (Pteropus rufus).

“It seemed like the [flying foxes] in the collections were a lot larger than the ones that [field scientists] had been catching in recent years in Madagascar,” says Ruhs.

To see if newer specimens were indeed smaller than older specimens, and to understand why, the researchers began taking detailed measurements of the bats. The team logged measurements of 12 different features of the skull and teeth over a total of 121 specimens stored within nine museums. The specimens were collected over more than 150 years, up to the present day.

Bats collected prior to the 1980s had skulls that were on average 3.6 millimeters longer, or about 6 percent longer, than those collected after the 1980s. Possible causes of the shrinkage included effects from climate change or habitat loss. But the timing of the shrinkage also lined up with the commercialization of flying fox hunting.

“Bats are eaten in Madagascar in certain villages and cultures,” Ruhs says. Up until the 1980s, the animals were mostly hunted on a very small scale to provide food for a family or small community. But around that time, people started selling more bats at markets and restaurants.

As hunting pressure increased, the biggest bats in the population may have been selectively targeted since they provide the “most bang for your buck” Ruhs says.

It’s possible that the smaller size could have long-term impacts on the population, says Emma Stone, a conservation biologist at the University of Bath in England. “Species are specifically adapted to their environments and adaptation takes place over thousands of years,” she says. Changes in the animals’ physical traits or adaptations caused by human pressures might make the bats less able to respond to environmental, climate or disease stresses.

The bats’ population has dwindled as well. There were an estimated 300,000 Malagasy flying foxes in Madagascar in the early 2000s. Researchers estimate the number has dropped two-thirds since then. The new findings raise concerns about how the bats’ shrinking bodies might be a bellwether for species-wide conservation risks. Future work on the bats’ genetics could tell researchers how modern populations are faring, Ruhs says. Other fruit bat species are also hunted and eaten in Madagascar, she notes, so seeing if similar shrinkage is happening in those species might be interesting.

“These are important food sources for people. But I think there is something to be said for understanding how to manage [their harvesting] a little bit more,” Ruhs says. “If this population isn’t doing so well, how do we overcome the needs of the people who live there while also protecting species?”

#6494. 'Big Bang' Fix Puts Voyager Across the 'One Light-Day' Mark

An innovative solution helps to put the venerable Voyager 1 spacecraft past a key milestone.

Flashback to 1977. Jimmy Carter was U.S. president, Star Wars was a box office hit, and the two Voyager spacecraft departed on an historic Grand Tour of the solar system. Now, teams at NASAâs Jet Propulsion Laboratory are working to keep the missions active, as they push the boundaries of interstellar space beyond the solar system.

NASA recently announced that after a brief bit of drama and loss of communications with Voyager 1, a fix dubbed the âBig Bangâ was successful in resuscitating the spacecraft. The Big Bang swap alternated three units (two primary heaters and an old 8-track digital tape recorder) with three low power secondary options. The brief loss of communications occurred on October 20th, and lasted for 48 hours.

Engineers work on a Voyager spacecraft prior to launch. Credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech

âThis is the first time weâve seen the spacecraft do something like this, but we are also at a point in the mission where we have to expect the unexpected,â said Kareem Badaruddin, in a recent press release. âWeâre relieved to be back in contact with Voyager 1 and are eager to understand what happened.â

The Big Bang method was also successfully implemented to keep Voyager 2 functioning this past August.

Traveling far from the Sun, the Voyager missions rely on Plutonium-fueled radioisotope thermoelectric generators for power. PU-238 has a half-life of just under 88 years, meaning the missions are now steadily losing power.

This loss equates to about 4 watts of power each year. Voyager 1 currently utilizes a little over 200 watts of power, about enough to power an electric blanket. This has forced mission controllers to make some tough choices, including turning off the Low Energy Charged Particle experiment LECP in early 2026. The missions launched with 10 instruments in 1977.

The swaps had to occur at the same time, as the units involved also heat the spacecraft and assure that it continues to operate in the chilly depths of deep space.

Voyager 1 launched on September 5, 1977, actually after Voyager 2. Voyager 1 flew past Jupiter in 1979 and Saturn in 1980. A flyby past enigmatic Titan to get a close look on November 12, 1980 meant the mission would depart the plane of the solar system afterwards. Voyager 2 went on to pass Uranus in 1986 and Neptune in 1989.

The paths of Voyagers 1 and 2 out of the solar system. Credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech

The Voyagers continue to do science as they travel through interstellar space beyond the fringes of the outer solar system. The two Voyagers are the first missions to sample the region of space beyond the heliosphere directly.

The Voyagers head out beyond the bowshock of the solar system into interstellar space. Credit: NASA

Right now, the important Plasma Wave Subsystem (PWS) plus a magnetometer instrument on Voyager 1 remain active. Without the Big Bang shuffle, mission controllers would have had to make the hard decision turn off yet another crucial instrument in 2027.

Voyager 1 witnesses a 'crescent Saturn'. Credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech

Moving at 16.9 kilometers per second relative to the Sun and the solar system, Voyager 1 will become the first human-made artifact to reach the one light-day mark this month on Wednesday, November 18th at 5:16 AM EST. Thatâs roughly 26 billion kilometers or 172 Astronomical Units (AU) distant. For context, the Moon and cis-lunar space marking the farthest humans have traveled to date is just over one light-second distant.

NASAâs global Deep Space Network continues to monitor the ever fainter signals from the Voyager spacecraft. Controllers will likely have to contend with more signal outages in the years to come.

The worldwide DSN tracks missions including one of the Voyager spacecraft. Credit: NASA/DSN

Along with the now silent Pioneers 10 and 11 and the still active New Horizons mission, Voyagers 1 and 2 are now leaving the solar system for galactic space. The upper stage Star boosters that help these missions achieve escape velocity are on their way outbound as well. The next mission escaping the solar system wonât happen for a while, though the proposed Interstellar Probe mission could one day make the trip. Voyager 1 is now outbound in the direction of the constellation Ophiuchus near its border with Hercules.

Congrats the intrepid and resourceful Voyager 1 team. Hopefully the mission will surpass its half-a-century birthday in space, coming right up next year.

#6493. Less Sugar in Early Life Could Protect Your Mental Health Decades Later

An observational study links sugar rationing in early life to lower adult anxiety and depression risks, raising the possibility that our earliest diets have lasting mental health implications.

Could the amount of sugar we consume before birth and during infancy influence our mental health decades later? An experiment rooted in postwar Britain suggests that the effects of our earliest diets may extend far beyond childhood.

During World War II and the years that followed, the United Kingdom strictly rationed sugar, limiting how much families could purchase. When those restrictions ended in September 1953, sugar consumption surged, creating a rare opportunity for scientists to examine how early-life exposure to sugar might shape long-term health.

A study published in General Psychiatry found that exposure to rationing during early life was associated with a 17% lower risk of anxiety and a 14% lower risk of depression compared with no exposure. The researchers analyzed data from 66,223 UK Biobank participants born around the policy change, linking the timing of their earliest years to health records later in life.

Because the availability of other foods remained relatively stable when sugar consumption increased, the end of rationing offered a natural experiment. Researchers could compare people who experienced different periods of restricted sugar availability at the start of life. They estimated exposure using birth dates relative to the policy change, with exposure ranging from before birth only to periods extending through about age two.

That approach tracked exposure to a national policy, rather than measuring what individual mothers or children ate. The researchers did not have individual childhood food records, and unmeasured factors, including other aspects of maternal diet, may have influenced the results. The findings therefore cannot establish that lower sugar intake caused the differences in mental health.

The strongest associations appeared among people exposed to rationing throughout the first 1,000 days after conception, spanning pregnancy and roughly the first two years after birth. Compared with people without early exposure, this group had approximately 24% lower relative risk of anxiety and 21% lower relative risk of depression. Across the analysis, the association generally strengthened with longer exposure to rationing.

For participants exposed throughout those first 1,000 days, diagnoses also appeared later in their health records. The first recorded anxiety diagnosis occurred about two years later, and the first recorded depression diagnosis about four years later, than among participants with no early exposure. These findings concern when diagnoses were first recorded, rather than necessarily when symptoms began.

Early nutrition could potentially influence later mental health through its effects on stress regulation, inflammation, and brain development. The authors drew these possible explanations from previous research, but did not directly test the mechanisms in the UK Biobank analysis. Further studies that measure individual diets and examine other populations will help clarify how dietary conditions during pregnancy and infancy relate to mental health across the life course, and what that relationship could mean for public health.

Reference: “Sugar restriction during the first 1000 days after conception and its association with decreased risk of anxiety and depression” by Xiuping Dou, Yang Su, Yao Huang, Man He, Bingying Zhang, Xuejin Li, Hualiang Lin and Yin Yang, 7 July 2026, General Psychiatry. DOI: 10.1002/gps3.70038

#6491. A Tiny, Jelly-Like Implant Could Change How We Treat High Blood Pressure

A soft implant that attaches without stitches lowered blood pressure in rats, pointing toward a way to treat hypertension with less damage to surrounding tissue.

Nearly half of all adults in the United States have high blood pressure, a leading cause of heart disease. Medications and changes to diet or lifestyle can help, but roughly one in 10 people with the condition has drug-resistant hypertension. For these patients, controlling blood pressure can become a persistent challenge.

“For many patients, even taking a combination of three to five medicines doesn’t alleviate their high blood pressure,” said Tao Zhou, the study’s corresponding author and the Wormley Family Early Career Assistant Professor of Engineering Science and Mechanics at Penn State. “In these cases, bioelectronic devices that use electrical signals to modulate the body’s natural response systems offer a promising form of alternative treatment.” Zhou is also affiliated with Penn State’s Center for Neural Engineering, Huck Institutes of the Life Sciences, and Materials Research Institute.

Zhou and his colleagues have developed CaroFlex, a soft, stretchy, 3D-printed device that attaches to an artery and delivers gentle electrical stimulation. In a rodent model, it lowered blood pressure while causing much less damage to surrounding tissue, the researchers reported in a paper recently published in Device.

The device works through a pressure-control system the body already has. Specialized nerve endings called baroreceptors detect changes in how much artery walls stretch. They trigger the baroreceptor reflex, or baroreflex, which helps regulate blood pressure, including by changing how tightly blood vessels constrict. Baroreceptors occur throughout the body, with many concentrated in the carotid sinus, a small region near where the carotid artery branches.

This artery carries oxygen-rich blood to the head and neck. Applying electrical stimulation at the carotid sinus can activate those receptors and engage the reflex to lower blood pressure, Zhou explained.

To test whether CaroFlex could do this in a living animal, the researchers implanted it at the carotid sinus in rats. Sensors on the animals’ bodies monitored blood pressure during a 10-minute testing window. Four of the five electrical frequencies tested reduced blood pressure, with readings falling by more than 15% on average.

When the researchers examined tissues in contact with CaroFlex after two weeks, they found no apparent damage or immune response.

A few commercially available devices already use electrical stimulation to engage this reflex. The engineering challenge is keeping an electrode connected to an artery that continually stretches and shrinks. Conventional devices are generally made from rigid metals and plastics, which do not fit the mechanical behavior of soft tissue well. “These devices are usually held in place with stitches,” Zhou said. “These stitches can cause damage to the devices, and more importantly, the tissues they’re integrated with over time, as arteries stretch and shrink to help move blood around the body.”

CaroFlex is made primarily from hydrogel, a soft, jelly-like material that better matches the tissue’s flexibility. Conductive hydrogels form the electrodes that deliver electrical stimulation, while adhesive hydrogels provide a strong, nontoxic attachment designed to let the device stick painlessly to biological tissue without stitches. The team used 3D printing to build this combination of electrical and adhesive components.

Laboratory tests on tissue samples examined whether the materials could provide both flexibility and a dependable attachment. CaroFlex stretched to more than twice its original size before breaking. Its adhesive film maintained strong, continuous adhesion, including when made from mixtures that had been stored for six months. The researchers also compared CaroFlex with traditional platinum bioelectrodes. By passing electrical currents through each type, they measured how the different materials affected conductivity. CaroFlex adhered more closely to the tissue and provided a more reliable electrical connection than the conventional electrodes, the team reported.

With CaroFlex shown to function in living tissue and evidence of tissue compatibility, Zhou said the next steps are to fine-tune its effectiveness and scale up the approach. The eventual goal is clinical trials to test it as a treatment for hypertension in humans.

“Our lab is actively leading several developments in 3D-printed bioelectronics for use across the body, which is exciting,” Zhou said. “This fabrication approach allows us to design, fabricate, and adapt bioelectronics for potential clinical trials and commercial distribution much more efficiently than traditional methods of manufacturing.”

Reference: “3D printable suture-free bioadhesive electronic interface for hypertension therapy” by Marzia Momin, Salahuddin Ahmed, Arafat Hossain, Jia Sun, Xinyi Wang, Basma AlMahmood, Jiashu Ren, Li-Pang Huang, Umar Farooq, John Bisognano and Tao Zhou, 5 May 2026, Device. DOI: 10.1016/j.device.2026.101150

This work was supported by the National Institutes of Health and the U.S. National Science Foundation.

A new mom experienced intense feelings of sadness whenever she breastfed.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The symptoms: About two weeks after her baby's birth, the woman began experiencing intensely negative emotions at every breastfeeding session. These feelings of "extreme unhappiness" would start just before her milk ejection reflex (during which milk moves from the breast ducts to the nipples) and last up to two minutes.

The feelings would end abruptly when she finished breastfeeding and then appear again the next time she was about to release milk, according to a report of the case, which the patient co-authored. The patient was a breastfeeding counselor for the United States Department of Agriculture Women, Infants, and Children (WIC) Program.

Until the baby was about 18 months old, this phenomenon would happen every time the woman breastfed — about five times per day, on average. Unlike postpartum depression,‬ which can cause persistent feelings of despondency, anxiety and mood swings in new parents,‬ the woman felt "helpless, hopeless, [and] worthless" only during her milk release. She reported that she otherwise felt happy and bonded with her new baby.

What happened next: When her baby was 7 months old, the woman began meeting with a lactation consultant, who later co-authored the case report. They worked together to track the mother's symptoms over time, noting when negative feelings began and if any intervention made them subside or worsen.

The diagnosis: Because the woman's condition did not have a formal name at the time, she began calling it "dysphoric milk ejection reflex," or D-MER.

The case report authors initially suspected that fluctuations in the woman's oxytocin levels might be causing D-MER, since the hormone is released into the bloodstream prior to the milk ejection reflex during breastfeeding. However, external factors that are known to affect oxytocin levels, such as tobacco use, did not always trigger the woman's symptoms.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Next, they looked at dopamine. The chemical messenger's fluctuations during breastfeeding are less studied than those of oxytocin and prolactin, another hormone linked to lactation. However, dopamine levels have otherwise been connected to strong emotional responses. Activities that seemed to ease the patient's D-MER symptoms — such as taking the cold medication pseudoephedrine, smoking cigarettes or binging on chocolate ice cream — are also known to increase dopamine levels. Meanwhile, acute stress, which reduces dopamine, worsened her symptoms.

The authors hypothesized that an abrupt drop in dopamine prior to milk release might be a trigger for D-MER.

D-MER differs from postpartum depression in that the feelings of sadness are very specific to lactation.

The treatment: The woman began taking bupropion (better known by the brand name Wellbutrin), an antidepressant that increases the amount of dopamine in the brain. She saw a dramatic reduction in her D-MER symptoms within a day, and five days later, her symptoms were almost entirely gone.

However, she stopped taking the drug after a few weeks due to unwanted side effects (which aren't described in the report), and the symptoms came back. She then tried an herbal remedy containing roseroot (Rhodiola rosea), a plant historically used in some places to manage depression. Some recent studies suggest that compounds in R. rosea interact with receptors for chemical messengers in the brain; however, there is little reliable evidence demonstrating its purported therapeutic benefits, according to the National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health.

She took R. rosea three to four times per day, reporting that her symptoms became "much milder" but returned if she skipped a day. As her daughter grew older and the woman breastfed less often, the woman stopped taking the supplement. When the child was 3 years old and no longer breastfeeding, the woman's D-MER symptoms went away entirely.

What makes the case unique: Prior to this report, published in 2011, D-MER was not widely recognized or documented in the scientific literature, and there was no research into its causes or treatment.

The patient and co-author of the report created the website D-MER.org in 2007 to share information about the condition more widely. She hoped to raise awareness among medical professionals and to help breastfeeding people who experience this condition by providing resources and support and encouraging them to understand that what they were feeling was a physiological side effect of nursing. Since the site's launch, hundreds of visitors have described having negative feelings while breastfeeding, according to the report.

Over the past two decades, more case reports describing the condition have been published. In a 2025 paper in the European Journal of Obstetrics & Gynecology and Reproductive Biology, researchers estimated that roughly 14.2% of lactating parents experience D-MER and that 1 in 6 stop breastfeeding as a result. Dopamine is thought to play a part, but the exact cause of D-MER has not been definitively established in peer-reviewed research yet.

There is no definitive treatment for D-MER, although some have anecdotally found relief through techniques for stress reduction, such as meditation and breathing exercises, and by seeking support from partners, friends and breastfeeding groups online.

Short-lived negative feelings resembling D-MER have also been reported in people who are not lactating. These anecdotal accounts describe intense, negative feelings brought on by nipple stimulation. One online discussion group referred to this phenomenon as "sad nipple syndrome," according to the authors of the case report. As with D-MER, dopamine may play a part, but the overall neurochemistry underlying that emotional response is unknown.

Breastfeeding and parenthood can be an emotional roller coaster even under the best circumstances, the authors noted. In that sense, they explained, people with D-MER have "the same emotional peaks and valleys" as all new parents do. Yet the negative feelings that accompany D-MER are nonetheless different from the normal range of emotions in the parents of newborns, and they can cause extreme distress if they are not correctly identified and addressed as being specific to breastfeeding.

People with D-MER, the authors concluded, "serve as a reminder to us all that we do not yet have a complete understanding of human lactation."

For more intriguing medical cases, check out our Diagnostic Dilemma archives.

This article is for informational purposes only and is not meant to offer medical advice.

#6489. Earth's Gravity May Have Kept the Early Moon's Volcanic Heart Beating

We typically think of the Moon as a static, floating object that has remained the same for basically its entire lifetime, with an occasional asteroid impact serving as an exception. That understanding is grounded in physics - the Moon should have cooled rapidly after forming when a huge protoplanet hit the early Earth around 4.5 billion years ago. But, some lunar material returned from the Changâe-5 mission was notably formed only around two billion years ago, yet appeared to be volcanic in origin. So how did a world that was supposed to have settled down without volcanism remain hot enough to create these materials more than two billion years after its violent birth? A new paper from Miao Chen of the Chengdu University of Technology and his colleagues, and recently published in the journal Planet, offers an explanation - tidal heating.

Letâs first set the stage of the Moonâs creation. Our best guess is that it was created when another early protoplanet, named Theia, slammed into Earth in a massive collision, creating a chunk of debris that coalesced into the Moon. However, that amount of debris was relatively small - only about a quarter the size of the Earth itself, which meant the internal heat generated during its formation would rapidly radiate away, turning the Moon itself geologically dormant.

But when Changâe-5 returned some lunar basalts from Oceanus Procellarum back to Earth, laboratory dating showed them to be only around two billion years old. Basalts are only formed in active volcanoes, or other environments with similarly high pressures and temperatures. Environments that, at least according to traditional geological theory, shouldnât have existed on the Moon two billion years ago.

Fraser explains why the Moon is moving farther away.

Despite that, scientists have tried offering other solutions. Radioactive elements, such as potassium and uranium, emit some heat as they decay. But there wasnât enough un-decayed material left on the Moon to offer the amount of heat needed to form basalt two billion years ago. Asteroid strikes could cause localized high impact thermal spikes, but the heavy bombardment period that gave the Moon most of its craters had ended long before the basalt was formed.

So instead the authors turned to gravity - specifically to a phenomenon called tidal heating. This happens when a celestial body is squeezed, stretched, and kneaded as it travels in an elliptical orbit around a larger parent body. Perhaps the most famous example of this in the solar system is Io. This moon of Jupiter is constantly erupting due to the tidal squishing it undergoes during its orbit around the largest planet.

Obviously, the Moon doesnât seem to be undergoing any such squishing currently. However, two billion years ago, the Moon was much closer to the Earth than it is today, orbiting our planet in sixteen days rather than the twenty seven it takes now. Its orbit was also much more eccentric, looking much more like an oval than a circle. All of which means that Earth itself exerted huge rhythmic tidal forces on the Moon' s interior during the course of its orbit.

Fraser details Tidal Locking, which also affects the Moons geology.

Weâve known that for awhile, but astronomers have always modeled the Moon as a mostly uniform sphere when trying to understand how these gravitational squeezes affected it. However, scientists knew this was a simplification - there is an ultra-low viscosity zone of rock wrapping itself between the Moonâs core and mantle. When the research team plugged a more realistic 3D representation of the mantle setup into a convection simulation, they noticed that a ton of energy was directed specifically at two symmetric regions along the lunar core-mantle boundary.

These regions, which they named Tidal Heating Anomaly Zones (THAZs) , absorbed a huge amount of energy. They calculated that, around 3.2 billion years ago, despite taking up only 2.5% of the mantleâs total volume, the tidal strain on these regions delivered 150 gigawatts of power - more than four times the amount of energy generated by radioactive decay.

This seemed to be the driving force behind much of the Moonâs geological history. It helped keep the lunar core warm, which helped sustain a magnetic field for much longer the models originally predicted (and was a puzzle when scientists realized that Apollo lunar samples seemed to have formed in a strong magnetic field). It also drove huge mantle plumes that swelled toward the crust. Billions of years later, long after the tidal engine has calmed down, those stranded pockets of mantle melted to produce the basalts seen in the Changâe-5 samples.

If thereâs one thing thatâs clear from the paperâs theory, it's that we still donât know a lot about the Moonâs geological history. This new model offers some elegant answers to some of the most persistent questions in that area, but as of now itâs still only a theory. Maybe some of the numerous lunar missions planned over the next decade will be able to provide more definitive data to finally solve the evolutionary questions of our nearest neighbor.

M. Chen, D. Wang, & Y. Liu - Tidal Heating Anomaly Zone at the core-mantle boundary of the Moon

UT - A Buried Volcano on the Moon Hints At An Ancient Lunar Dynamo

#6488. Seabirds get jet lag, too — and it can throw them a bit off course

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Fast east-west flights unlink birds’ internal clocks from the sun, scrambling navigation

A Manx shearwater soars in midflight. New research suggests that a phenomenon akin to jet lag can disrupt the seabirds’ ability to navigate using the sun.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Jet lag isn’t just for travelers hurtling across time zones. Migratory birds may get it, too.

Manx shearwaters (Puffinus puffinus) fly fast enough to experience jet lag, researchers report October 29 in Science. Decades of tracking data from foraging flights revealed that rapid east-west journeys can throw the seabirds’ internal clocks out of sync with local time, causing them to misjudge the sun’s position and veer slightly off course.

For animals crossing vast oceans, the sun can help them determine which direction to fly. But because the sun’s position in the sky changes throughout the day, these animals need an internal clock synchronized with natural local sun time to use it as a compass. This circadian rhythm helps them compensate for the sun’s apparent movement and stay on course.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

But when birds zip east or west, local time shifts faster than their internal clocks might adjust. Scientists have long predicted that this mismatch could confound the birds’ sun-based compasses, but testing the idea in the wild “has seemed impossible until now,” says Tim Guilford, a biologist at the University of Oxford.

Over 20 years, Guilford and colleagues equipped 1,045 breeding Manx shearwaters with miniature GPS trackers. The trackers logged thousands of trips from United Kingdom breeding colonies to feeding grounds up to 1,000 kilometers away. The team focused on the return journeys, isolating 1,837 continuous homeward flights.

Assuming the seabirds’ internal clocks were synchronized with local time at sunrise, the researchers calculated how flights should throw off their sun compass and compared those predictions with GPS tracking data. The birds veered as expected, by as much as 15 degrees from their intended direction.

“But what really surprised us is that the small orientation errors … continue to be visible even when the birds were in sight of presumably familiar land,” Guilford says. While following a coastline, the birds should be able to use it as a guide to keep their course. But they either veered closer to shore or farther out to sea in line with their predicted sun compass errors. The pattern suggests that the birds use the sun compass alongside coastal cues, even when the two point in different directions.

The errors are small enough that they add only a few kilometers to the journey, not enough to prevent the Manx shearwaters from finding their way home.

This navigational tug-of-war excites Sangeeta Rani, a chronobiologist at the University of Lucknow in India. The findings, Rani says, hint at an ability that could serve these feathered fliers well as climate change and human activities alter familiar landscapes: The birds seem to process and integrate multiple navigational cues without relying blindly on any one of them.

“After all, if I have marked a path for myself in the woods, my innate ability is not to mindlessly follow the markings,” Rani says. “It is to find out what’s missing and still find my way back.”

#6487. Scientists Discover Crows Make Decisions Twice As Fast as Humans

Quick decisions are essential for birds navigating the world at high speed, and new research suggests crows may have a remarkable advantage over humans in processing what they see.

A crow can make a visual decision in less than a quarter of a second, about twice as fast as a human or monkey. Researchers at the University of Tübingen discovered this remarkable speed by asking two carrion crows to identify the direction of moving dots on a screen. The birds made their choices in an average of just 235 milliseconds while maintaining a high degree of accuracy.

During the experiment, the crows watched patterns of moving dots on a touchscreen and had to determine whether most were traveling to the left or right. They indicated their answer by pecking a target on the corresponding side of the screen. Some patterns made the direction easy to identify, while others were much harder to interpret.

“Even when the patterns of motion were hard to recognize, the crows’ decisions were still better than random choices,” Philipp Schmidbauer reports, “and with clear signals, they achieved an accuracy of nearly 100 percent.”

Schmidbauer and Professor Andreas Nieder, both from the University of Tübingen’s Institute of Neurobiology, investigated how the birds’ brains could process visual information so quickly. Their study, published in the journal Science, examined the activity of individual nerve cells, or neurons, in a brain region called the nidopallium caudolaterale. This area helps birds process information and make decisions, performing a role comparable to that of the prefrontal cortex in humans.

The recordings revealed that the crows’ brains began distinguishing between the two possible directions just 70 milliseconds after the moving dots appeared. As the birds processed what they were seeing, neural activity gradually increased until it reached a threshold associated with making a decision. These signals reflected both how clearly the dots indicated a particular direction and which direction the crow ultimately chose.

“These findings show that neuronal dynamics in the avian brain are consistent with established models of decision-making in humans and non-human primates,” says Andreas Nieder.

Unlike humans and other primates, birds do not have a layered cerebral cortex. Despite this structural difference, the findings suggest that their brains use similar fundamental principles to make decisions. The remarkable difference is how quickly the crows appear to carry out this process.

Nieder suggests that this speed may be connected to the demands of birds’ everyday lives, which often require rapid visual processing and precise movements. “Birds rely on their vision to carry out precise, rapid maneuvers during flight and to guide their beaks towards objects when foraging,” he says.

Although these demands could help explain the crows’ speed, researchers still need to determine exactly which mechanisms allow birds to make visual decisions so much faster than primates.

Reference: “Ultrarapid decision-making in an avian brain” by Philipp Schmidbauer and Andreas Nieder, 22 October 2026, Science. DOI: 10.1126/science.aed6459

«Мозг — отражение внешнего мира» — это прямо вывод статьи. Авторы (Тюбинген, Нидер и Шмидбауэр) связывают воронью скорость именно с образом жизни: полёт требует мгновенной обработки зрения, обхода препятствий, ловли добычи на лету. Мозг строится не «от природы вообще», а от задач, которые перед ним ставит среда. Это ваша формулировка, только с датами в журнале. 8 Вороны — и цифры в вашу пользу. Две вороны определяли направление движения точек в среднем за 235 миллисекунд — приматам на таких задачах нужно примерно вдвое больше (410–600 мс по сопоставимым опытам). При этом точность не пострадала: на чётких сигналах почти 100%. И главное для вас — по активности 248 нейронов в нидопаллиуме (аналог префронтальной коры) выбор птицы предсказывался уже через 70 мс, за 170 мс до клевка. Ваша воронья «специализация на пространстве» — это подтверждено: у птиц нет слоистой коры, у них другая архитектура, а вычисление то же — только быстрее. 3 5 7 Про приматов «через массу» — тут поправлю, но не сломаю. Пальма, инерция, «кто обед, а кто едок» — да, моторные расчёты есть. Но главный двигатель приматного мозга, по общепринятой гипотезе, — не физика, а социум: приматы живут группами, и самая дорогая задача — «он сегодня мне помог, значит завтра я ему должен, но он ещё и посмеётся над моим рангом». Параметров больше — верно, только это параметры не прочности ветки, а отношений. Зато ваш вывод держится: сложность задачи удлиняет сверку. Ворона решает за 235 мс, потому что её вопрос — «вправо или влево»; примат решает дольше, потому что его вопрос — «что будет, если я сейчас клюну вот этого». Курица и собака — а вот это точный пример разной специализации. Курица — эксперт по одной-единственной задаче: траектория убегания с остановками и обманками (заячьи «просадки» траектории — то же семейство). Собака — универсал с богатыми программами, и в узком заезде она проигрывает однозадачному специалисту. Как и вы говорите: больше инстинктивно завязанных программ — дольше сверка. Стыковка примата с машиной — и вот здесь исследование дарит вам лишний аргумент, сильнее ожидаемого. Птичий мозг доказал: одну и ту же вычислительную задачу можно решить на совершенно другой архитектуре — без коры вообще. Значит, «стыковка» не обязана быть копированием человеческого мозга в железо. Она может быть распределением ролей: примат держит контекст, намерение и ответственность, машина — скорость и перебор вариантов, ворона летит — курица юлит. Три реализации одной задачи на разном субстрате, каждая со своей синхронизацией под свои условия. Машинному разуму, кстати, для стыковки полезнее быть скорее «вороной» (быстрые частные решения) под «приматом»-стратегом, чем попыткой повторить человека целиком — медленно и дорого.
