#6422. A drug-free diabetes treatment? An implant lowers blood sugar in mice

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

The device banishes extra blood glucose by converting it to a compound excreted in urine

Excess blood glucose (shown in white in this illustration) is the target of a new experimental device. In mice, the sugar gets converted into a compound which the kidneys can excrete in urine.

NEMES LASZLO/SCIENCE PHOTO LIBRARY/Getty Images

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

A wireless implant that clears excess sugar from the blood could someday offer a drug-free way to treat type 2 diabetes and obesity.

In mice with both conditions, the under-the-skin device brought high blood sugar back to normal within 60 to 90 minutes of being switched on, researchers report October 22 in Science. After six weeks, the treated mice lost up to 10 percent of their body weight and had lower triglycerides, a type of fat in the blood.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Diabetes affects about 830 million people worldwide. Conventional type 2 diabetes treatments like insulin and GLP-1 drugs require careful dosing. Even experimental diabetes-controlling implants still rely on the hormone insulin, which clears sugar from the bloodstream but doesn’t rid the body of it, says Martin Fussenegger, a bioengineer at ETH Zurich. The new implant instead removes glucose from the body without added drugs, genes or living cells.

The 3-centimeter-long device contains a catalyst made of gold flakes and platinum particles on spongelike graphite. When electricity powers it, the catalyst converts glucose into gluconate, a compound that is easier for the kidneys to flush out in urine. With less glucose available for energy, the body may turn to its fat stores instead, Fussenegger and colleagues suspect. In mice, that shift showed up as higher blood levels of chemicals released when fat breaks down, such as ketones. “This system kind of targets the root cause, which is the energy surplus by glucose in the body,” Fussenegger says.

The implant works like an automatic sugar-removal system: A wearable glucose monitor detects high blood sugar levels and sends readings through a smartphone that switches the implant on. When levels return to a safer range, it switches off. The automated system ran for two weeks in eight mice. The catalyst itself remained able to convert glucose after up to three months under their skin, though the study didn’t establish how long the entire device would last.

And it’s still unknown how well the device would work in people. “This is a potentially promising method,” says David Klonoff, an endocrinologist at Sutter Mills-Peninsula Medical Center in Burlingame, Calif., who was not involved in the study. “But the risks are significant and must be carefully ruled out before it can be safely tested on humans.”

Researchers need to determine how much gluconate the kidneys can clear, Klonoff says. If it builds up, it could disrupt the body’s acid-base balance, causing symptoms such as nausea or confusion; excreting it could also deplete electrolytes such as sodium and potassium, he notes.

Scaling up the device is another challenge. Humans consume about 250 grams of carbohydrates daily, compared with two grams for mice, Klonoff estimates. Meeting that demand could require a much larger implant or multiple devices, he says. In a lab test, a larger device cleared nearly all glucose from about 5 liters of solution, roughly an adult’s blood volume, though not a full day’s glucose intake.

Fussenegger’s team plans to test the device in pigs and sheep before considering human trials. If proven safe and effective, it could offer an alternative to existing diabetes treatments and a new weight-loss option for people regardless of whether they have diabetes, he says.

#6421. Octopus brains challenge what scientists know about learning and memory

Scientists found a chemical switch that keeps octopus brain connections strong, offering clues to how these animals remember.

Learning changes the connections between brain cells. In animals such as mammals and sea slugs, making those changes last usually requires new proteins.

But octopus brain tissue did something unexpected. Its nerve connections stayed stronger for at least 10 hours, even when researchers blocked the cells from making new proteins.

A gas called nitric oxide may help explain why.

The researchers propose that it keeps the enzyme that produces it active, creating a continuing supply that helps nerve connections stay strong.

Binyamin Hochner’s lab at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem worked with Tal Shomrat’s group at the Ruppin Academic Center.

Ana Luiza Turchetti-Maia carried out most of the experiments, using living brain tissue from common octopuses caught by fishermen off Israel’s Mediterranean coast.

Octopuses solve problems and learn from experience. They have about 500 million nerve cells, giving them the largest nervous system of any animal without a backbone.

A brain region called the vertical lobe helps them learn through sight. It serves a similar role to the hippocampus, which helps people and other vertebrates form long-term memories.

A brief burst of strong activity can strengthen connections between nerve cells in this region.

Scientists call this long-term potentiation, and they think it is one way brains hold on to what they learn.

In 2008, Hochner’s team strengthened connections across the lobe as far as they could go, and the octopuses then struggled to form new long-term memories.

A 2023 map found about 25 million nerve cells in the lobe, most receiving input from just one incoming nerve fiber.

Nitric oxide already looked important: studies in the 1990s found that blocking it disrupted learning through touch and sight.

Later, the team’s tissue tests showed that the enzyme that makes the gas was especially active in the vertical lobe.

For the new study, researchers stimulated incoming nerve fibers with four rapid bursts of 20 pulses each. They then measured the connections’ responses every 30 seconds.

They also used drugs to block nitric oxide synthase, the enzyme that makes the gas. These drugs worked reliably only at much higher doses than researchers usually use.

Scientists often expect nitric oxide to help start the strengthening process. Yet the octopus connections still grew stronger when the blockers were already present.

A thin carbon-fiber sensor placed in the tissue detected a rise in nitric oxide after stimulation.

One roughly calibrated measurement suggested levels about 1,000 times higher than those needed to activate its best-known signaling pathway.

Across five experiments, however, the average rise came later and was less clear.

The researchers suspect that at such high levels, nitric oxide attaches to proteins and changes how they work.

Drugs that targeted its usual signaling pathway did not affect the strengthened connections.

The picture changed when researchers added blockers after the connections had strengthened.

Given 10 minutes later, one drug reduced the strengthened response by an average of 63%, while another reduced it by 82%.

A mirror-image version of a blocker, which cannot block the enzyme, reduced the response by 23%. That smaller drop could have happened by chance.

When researchers washed away the active blockers, the strength returned. One blocker had this effect whether they added it 10 minutes, 90 minutes, or four hours after stimulation.

This suggested that the connections needed an ongoing supply of nitric oxide to keep showing their added strength.

Adding nitric oxide alone did not produce the same lasting effect. A brief dose of a chemical that releases the gas strengthened connections for only a few minutes.

Keeping the tissue in a solution that released the gas caused a large but temporary increase in signal strength.

Prolonged exposure also appeared to damage the nerve fibers.

The team proposes that strong nerve activity starts a loop: the enzyme makes nitric oxide, and nitric oxide keeps the enzyme active.

Hochner said the work shows how different brains can solve a shared problem.

“It is a remarkable example of how evolution can give rise to similar principles of learning and memory through very different biological mechanisms,” Hochner added.

In well-studied examples from other animals, including the sea slug Aplysia, lasting changes in nerve connections depend on new proteins.

Blocking protein production in the mammalian hippocampus prevents the later, lasting phase of strengthening.

The team treated octopus tissue with anisomycin, a drug that blocks protein production, for two and a half hours.

Treatment began half an hour before stimulation, yet the connections stayed stronger for at least 10 hours.

To check that the drug worked, researchers used a glowing marker to label new proteins. Untreated tissue glowed brightly, while treated tissue showed very little glow.

In four lengthy experiments, blocking nitric oxide still reduced connection strength in tissue treated with anisomycin. The nitric oxide system could therefore keep working without new proteins.

When researchers reviewed 11 blocker experiments, they found two patterns. In five, the drug removed an average of 97% of the added strength, acting more than four times faster than in the other six.

After the drug washed away, another round of stimulation made these fast-responding connections about 2.6 times stronger.

It looked as though the earlier strengthening had been erased, allowing it to build again.

In the slower group, the blocker reduced strength by 72%, and further stimulation added almost nothing. Here, the drug seemed to suppress the earlier strengthening without erasing it.

The team thinks the faster response reflected a switch turning off in connections that also started out weaker.

Across the lobe’s five sections, fast responses appeared in the middle, slow ones in the outermost pair, and both in the sections between.

The researchers studied tissue in a dish, not octopuses learning a task.

Most comparisons involved only five or six brain slices per group, and the authors doubt this switch alone explains lasting memories.

Earlier work found that removing the vertical lobe after training did not stop octopuses from remembering learned tasks. The lobe may help animals learn before they store memories elsewhere, where new proteins could still matter.

Cuttlefish may use a different system: their vertical lobe shows no detectable activity of the gas-making enzyme, and connections strengthen on the output side of the circuit.

The team also does not yet know whether nitric oxide keeps its own enzyme active directly or through another enzyme.

Genetic studies show that octopuses and their relatives underwent major changes in how their DNA is arranged.

The authors suggest these changes may have helped turn older mollusk memory chemistry into the nitric oxide switch.

They now want to identify the specific molecular changes involved. That could help explain how this system developed and what role it plays in learning.

The study is published in The Journal of Neuroscience.

#6420. More parents say no to vitamin K shots, and bleeding cases in babies are rising

Vitamin K deficiency rose among U.S. infants as fewer newborns received the shot that helps prevent dangerous bleeding.

Most babies in the United States get a vitamin K shot soon after birth to protect them from serious bleeding. But a growing share are missing it.

A new study found that recorded diagnoses of vitamin K deficiency more than tripled among babies between 2017 and 2025.

Diagnoses of bleeding linked to the deficiency more than quadrupled.

Elizabeth Wolf, a children’s doctor at Children’s Hospital of Richmond at VCU, led the study. She is also an associate professor in VCU’s Department of Pediatrics.

“We knew from prior studies that vitamin K refusal had been increasing in the U.S., and we wanted to learn if there were any real-life consequences of this trend,” Wolf said.

Vitamin K helps blood form clots that stop bleeding. Having too little is called vitamin K deficiency.

Babies start life with very little of this vitamin. Only small amounts pass from a mother to her baby before birth.

Newborns also lack the established gut bacteria that help produce vitamin K. Breast milk contains only small amounts, too.

The American Academy of Pediatrics has advised giving every newborn a vitamin K shot since 1961. The shot cuts the rate of bleeding that starts a week or more after birth by 98%.

Without enough vitamin K, a baby may struggle to stop bleeding. Doctors call this vitamin K deficiency bleeding.

One form starts between two days and one week after birth. Babies may bruise or bleed from the belly button.

Another form starts between one week and six months. It can affect breastfed babies who miss the shot and babies whose bodies have trouble taking in vitamin K.

Among babies with this later form, 30% to 60% have bleeding inside the skull. This can cause seizures, lasting brain damage, or death.

The team used Cosmos, a large collection of health records from places that use Epic software.

It brings together records from more than 2,300 hospitals and 50,000 clinics and other care sites, with names and other identifying details removed.

The study included about 11 million babies up to six months old who received care between 2017 and 2025.

All had been born at 35 weeks of pregnancy or later.

The team checked when doctors first found low vitamin K or bleeding linked to it, and whether babies also had bleeding inside the skull or brain.

The number of births in the records roughly doubled during the study. To make a fair comparison, the team worked out how many cases occurred for every 100,000 babies.

In 2017, 97.7% of newborns had a recorded vitamin K shot. By 2025, that fell to 95.0%, so the share without a recorded shot had more than doubled.

Low vitamin K rose from 11.8 to 37.3 cases per 100,000 babies. Bleeding linked to low vitamin K rose from 24.0 to 107.4 cases per 100,000.

Both rates were highest in 2025. That year, a little more than one in every 1,000 babies born in the records had bleeding linked to low vitamin K.

Doctors found most cases during the first week of life. That was true for 62% of babies with low vitamin K and 88% of those with bleeding.

About 97% of all babies in the study had a record of getting the shot. But among babies with low vitamin K, only 39.7% did.

Among babies with bleeding linked to low vitamin K, only 19.2% had a recorded shot. Babies without a recorded shot were a small part of the full group, yet they made up most of the bleeding cases.

Some babies also had bleeding inside the skull or brain. This affected 6.9% of babies with low vitamin K and 2.4% of those with bleeding linked to it.

An earlier study found that the share of newborns who missed the shot rose from 2.9% in 2017 to 5.2% in 2024. A study in Sweden also linked missing the shot to bleeding in babies.

Wolf’s team pointed to growing distrust of public health after the COVID-19 pandemic. They also noted more doubts about vaccines and more worries about medical care given to newborns.

The authors wrote that the vitamin K shot “may be a victim of its own success.” Because it has made this bleeding problem rare, many families may not know how dangerous it can be.

“Similar to the recent measles outbreaks, we are seeing the real-world implications of growing mistrust of doctors and public health professionals,” Wolf said.

“We need clear messaging from all levels of public health about the benefits of vitamin K administration for newborns.”

Some countries give vitamin K by mouth, either as the usual choice or as another option. These include France, Germany, the Netherlands, Switzerland, and Canada.

Vitamin K taken by mouth can work less well than the shot at preventing bleeding that starts later.

Still, the authors said U.S. doctors may need to consider it as a second choice if more parents refuse the shot.

The study cannot prove that fewer shots caused more bleeding. It also left out babies who received care outside health systems using Epic, so it may not show the full picture across the country.

Some records may have listed the wrong diagnosis or missed bleeding inside the skull. The team also looked for other reasons that might explain the rise.

Breastfeeding rates changed little over the past decade. Diseases that can cause low vitamin K, such as cystic fibrosis, did not become more common.

Wolf noted that these problems could keep rising if more parents refuse the shot.

“We need to better understand why parents are refusing vitamin K and what can be done to improve the uptake of this important medication,” she said.

The full study was published in the journal JAMA Pediatrics.

A high-status burial surprised archaeologists when they discovered leprosy in a man's bones from the fifth century.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Archaeologists investigating the genomes of a dozen people buried in an abandoned Roman-era settlement in northwestern Germany have discovered a surprising organism lurking in one man's remains: a rare strain of Mycobacterium leprae, which causes leprosy.

This strain of leprosy has never been seen in this part of Europe before, which hints that the individual had traveled and interacted with people from across the Roman world. The man was buried in a wooden boat surrounded by unusual objects, indicating he was a high-status person, according to a research study.

"The results were particularly striking in the case of one individual," study co-author Ben Krause-Kyora, an archaeologist at the Institute of Clinical Molecular Biology (IKMB) at Kiel University in Germany, said in a Nov. 3 statement. "He could, for example, have been a mercenary in the Roman army who later settled between the Elbe and the Weser [rivers]."

In the study, published online Oct. 15 in the journal iScience, Krause-Kyora and colleagues analyzed the genomes of people buried at the coastal settlement of Fallward. The settlement originated in the first century B.C. but gradually declined and became a cemetery by the fifth century A.D. Among the 200 cremation burials and 60 inhumation burials originally excavated in the 1990s was a distinctive grave made from a wooden boat.

The oak boat was over 13 feet (4 meters) long and sealed with a roof-like structure, the researchers said. It held the skeleton of a man who was about 50 years old when he died some time between A.D. 425 and 450. His grave goods included a small box shaped like a water bird, an ornate chair or throne carved out of alder wood, a bronze basin and a maple stool with a hunting scene and a runic inscription. The maritime artifacts coupled with the man's well-developed upper arm bones suggest he may have worked as a fisherman or boatman just before he died, the researchers wrote.

"The grave goods placed in the tomb aroused particular scientific interest," study co-author Hauke Jöns, an archaeologist at the Lower Saxony Institute for Historical Coastal Research, said in the statement. "The man possessed a late Roman military belt, which suggested that the deceased had had connections across great distances."

Archaeologists found a chair made from the trunk of an alder tree near the man's burial. The chair was likely a symbol of authority or power.

To learn more about this unusual burial and to determine where the man was from, researchers analyzed his DNA.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

"Genetic analyses confirm that a man buried at Fallward originated from the Danube region," study first author Daniel Myburgh, an ancient DNA researcher at IKMB, said in the statement. "He was also infected with a very rare leprosy pathogen."

The researchers found the DNA of the bacterium M. leprae in one of the man's teeth and in a foot bone. Because the leprosy DNA was so well preserved, the researchers were able to narrow down the strain that had infected him. This strain of leprosy may have evolved in Egypt around the fourth to second centuries B.C. and had never before been found in Central or Northern Europe, according to the statement.

But the man showed no signs of leprosy lesions in his skeleton, the researchers said. Leprosy first attacks the nerves and skin, but it can eventually eat away at the bones of the skeleton, particularly affecting the nose, jaw, hands and feet.

"Leprosy is a chronic disease," study co-author Almut Nebel, a biologist at IKMB, said in the statement. "Either he was affected by an asymptomatic form of the disease, or the disease had so far only affected soft tissues. He may have travelled long distances whilst carrying the disease."

While the researchers don't know exactly what happened in this man's life, they suggested he might have been a mercenary who served in the Roman army and later retired to northwest Germany, becoming a high-status member of the community who was honored with an alder-wood "throne" in his burial. But he also may have acquired the Roman belt through trade, inheritance or as a war trophy, the researchers wrote.

Either way, the man's skeleton and his grave goods suggest that northwest Germany had long-distance connections in Europe even after the fall of the Roman Empire, according to the statement.

Myburgh, D. A., da Silva, N. A., Romeyer-Dherbey, J. H., Grefen-Peters, S., Jöns, H., Peek, C., Nebel, A., & Krause-Kyora, B. (2026). Paleogenomics reveals leprosy at the late antique burial site of Fallward in northern Germany. iScience, 29(11), 117877. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.isci.2026.117877

Kristina Killgrove is a staff writer at Live Science with a focus on archaeology and paleoanthropology news. Her articles have also appeared in venues such as Forbes, Smithsonian, and Mental Floss. Kristina holds a Ph.D. in biological anthropology and an M.A. in classical archaeology from the University of North Carolina, as well as a B.A. in Latin from the University of Virginia, and she was formerly a university professor and researcher. She has received awards from the Society for American Archaeology and the American Anthropological Association for her science writing.

#6417. What limits human lifespan? Cloning offers a surprising clue

Cloned animals offer clues to aging, suggesting changes in gene activity may help explain limits on human lifespan.

Scientists can take the nucleus of an adult animal’s cell and use it to create a newborn. That clone can live a normal lifespan, despite starting with DNA from an older animal.

Two researchers in Poland think this offers a clue to aging. Cloning resets many controls that switch genes on and off, while leaving mutations in the DNA largely intact.

They suggest that problems with these controls may be the main limit on human lifespan. But fixing them might reveal another problem that keeps the body from living longer.

Michał Bartoszewicz, an independent researcher in Warsaw, wrote the review with Mariusz Niemczyk of the Medical University of Warsaw.

The team drew on earlier research, rather than running a new experiment.

Cloning involves putting an adult cell’s nucleus into an egg after removing the egg’s own nucleus.

Enzymes inside the egg help the transferred nucleus begin directing embryonic development. This is the method that produced Dolly the sheep.

Most cells in the body share the same DNA, but skin cells and nerve cells use different parts of it.

Chemical tags on DNA and its packaging help control this activity, a system called epigenetics.

Cloning resets these tags particularly thoroughly, but other changes vary.

Some clones have normal or longer telomeres, the protective caps on chromosomes, while others retain their donor cells’ short caps.

The clone gets most of its mitochondria, which supply energy, from the egg. It generally inherits mutations already present in the donor’s nuclear DNA.

The authors see permanent DNA damage as the hardest limit to undo, but doubt it explains most ordinary aging.

They cite 25 rounds of cloning from one genetic line that showed no sign of DNA damage shortening life.

Yet damage can eventually catch up. A separate 20-year experiment repeatedly cloned mice from clones, starting with one donor.

Success rates began falling after generation 27, and generation 58 was the last. Large structural errors and lethal mutations had accumulated in the DNA.

“Age-related dysfunction is unlikely to arise from a single universal mechanism,” the authors wrote.

Their framework groups aging’s limits into three layers: gene control, permanent DNA damage, and worn-out proteins and cell parts that escape the body’s cleanup systems. In humans, they place gene control first.

These controls affect cell identity, nutrient use, inflammation, hormone responses, and tissue repair, connecting with telomeres, mitochondria, and stem cells that renew tissue.

Senescent cells also play a part: they stop dividing without dying and release inflammatory signals that can harm nearby tissue.

The idea also draws on biologist Mikhail Blagosklonny’s work. He proposed that programs that help the body grow can cause harm when they keep running later in life.

A treatment may help only if it tackles the problem currently limiting a tissue’s survival. Once that problem improves, another may take its place.

Rapamycin illustrates this possibility. The drug can extend lifespan in normally aging mice when given late in life, partly by reducing a growth signal called mTOR.

In mice with a faulty DNA repair gene that age unusually fast, rapamycin reduced the signal but didn’t extend life. Cutting calories did.

Blagosklonny suggested that DNA damage may have killed these mice before excess growth signaling had time to matter. That explanation remains a proposed reason for the difference.

Scientists can also turn on three genes, OCT4, SOX2, and KLF4, to push cells toward a younger state. They call this partial reprogramming.

In one experiment, researchers delivered these genes through an engineered virus to male mice aged 124 weeks. Their median remaining lifespan more than doubled.

That means the time they had left, not their entire lifespan. Safety also remains a concern: a related set of four genes caused tumors in several organs in other mouse experiments.

Chemical tags called methyl groups form patterns on DNA that change with age. Epigenetic clocks read these patterns in blood or saliva to estimate biological age or the pace of aging.

The authors argue that current clocks mix together two different kinds of change. Some may drive aging, which they call Type 1, while others help the body respond to damage, called Type 2.

Undoing harmful changes could lower a clock reading and help the body. Suppressing helpful responses might lower the reading too, while making the body less able to cope.

Estimated age can rise after surgery, pregnancy, or infection, then fall during recovery.

Readings also follow a daily cycle, appearing youngest around midnight and oldest around noon.

Newer clocks try to separate harmful changes from helpful responses.

One reanalysis applied two such clocks to data from 34 overweight adults who took omega-3 supplements for six weeks.

The age estimate from the clock designed to track damage fell by 6.1 years.

The one tracking helpful responses rose by 6.2 years, and neither has been shown to predict health.

That makes a lower number hard to interpret on its own. It doesn’t necessarily mean someone has become healthier or will live longer.

The review covers more than a dozen human studies, from six women in an eight-week lifestyle program to 3,567 adults wearing activity trackers.

The two-year CALERIE trial assigned 220 healthy adults without obesity to cut calories by 25% or eat as usual.

Calorie cutting slowed DunedinPACE, one measure of aging speed, but didn’t clearly change several other clocks beyond chance.

In the three-year DO-HEALTH analysis of 777 older adults, omega-3 supplements slowed aging on three of four clocks.

Adding vitamin D and home exercise brought an extra benefit on one clock, but neither trial showed that participants lived longer.

One smaller study reported an average eight-year drop in estimated age among 42 people taking a supplement based on alpha-ketoglutarate.

But the test checked only nine DNA sites, and no independent group has verified it.

Nobody has tested the full framework or established how much each proposed limit contributes to ordinary human aging. It also doesn’t explain what starts aging or whether one process lies behind everything else.

Combining treatments, such as resetting gene control and clearing senescent cells, could be worth exploring. Both benefits and safety need direct testing.

Rather than chasing extreme lifespans first, “safety and healthspan should be the preliminary concerns,” the authors wrote. Healthspan means the years someone lives in good health.

They propose controlled trials of well-studied drugs and a free public database to help identify useful treatment combinations.

Long-term studies across diverse populations must also test whether lower clock readings predict longer, healthier lives.

The review is published in the journal Aging.

#6416. NASA captures a winding river carved into 300-million-year-old rock

An astronaut photo reveals the San Juan River’s dramatic bends in southern Utah, where an ancient waterway carved deep into a rising landscape.

The San Juan River takes the long way through southern Utah. It doubles back, curls around narrow fingers of land, and repeatedly approaches places it has already passed.

From above, its winding canyon looks almost too elaborate for a river simply flowing downhill.

Those bends tell a story that began before the canyon existed, when the surrounding landscape was far flatter than it is today.

Today’s Image of the Day captures this remarkable stretch of desert from the International Space Station.

An astronaut photographed the scene on October 6, 2026, revealing the deeply carved loops known as the San Juan River’s “goosenecks.”

The view offers more than a striking pattern. It shows how a river can preserve the shape of an older landscape even as the ground beneath it changes.

Long before steep canyon walls confined the San Juan, its ancestral channel crossed a broad, gently sloping plain.

In that setting, the river had room to develop sweeping curves. The landscape offered few obstacles, and the water followed a winding route on its gradual descent.

A modern comparison is the Mississippi River, whose broad bends snake across relatively flat terrain.

Along a meandering river, water erodes the outside of bends and deposits sediment along the inside, gradually reshaping the channel.

But the San Juan’s surroundings did not stay flat.

The Colorado Plateau rose, changing the relationship between the river and the land it crossed.

A channel that had developed on gentle terrain began cutting downward, carrying its inherited curves into the rock.

That sequence helps explain the apparent contradiction in today’s landscape: a deeply cut canyon with the looping shape of a river wandering across a plain.

According to the Utah Geological Survey, uplift raised the San Juan’s headwaters and increased the river’s gradient, or the amount of elevation it lost over a given distance.

The steeper descent increased the water’s speed and ability to erode its bed. Rather than abandoning its established bends, the river carved them deeper.

Geologists call these features entrenched meanders. Their curves record an earlier river course, while their depth reflects the erosion that followed.

The timing remains debated. One explanation places an important phase of uplift roughly 15 million to 20 million years ago, although the Colorado Plateau’s rise involved a complicated history that researchers continue to investigate.

The central idea is easier to picture: the river’s bends came first, and the deep canyon developed later.

The rocks surrounding the water tell an even older story. More than 300 million years ago, an ancient marine environment occupied this region.

Changing sea levels helped produce layers of sediment that eventually became limestone, sandstone, siltstone, and shale.

Those layers now form the cliffs and slopes exposed along the river.

The lower and upper canyon walls include rocks called the Paradox and Honaker Trail formations.

The age of the rock should not be confused with the age of the canyon. The San Juan cut through material that already held hundreds of millions of years of geological history.

At Goosenecks State Park, the river lies about 1,000 feet, or 300 meters, below the overlook.

Its repeated turns make substantial travel out of relatively little westward progress on the journey toward Lake Powell.

In the section described by NASA, the channel covers 5.5 miles between locations separated by just 1.3 miles in a straight line.

The landscape offers another spectacle when daylight fades.

Goosenecks State Park received International Dark Sky Park designation in 2021. Its remote location and wide views allow visitors to see faint celestial features that disappear beneath brighter skies.

DarkSky International identifies the Double Cluster in Perseus and the Messier 24 star cloud among the objects visible there without a telescope.

By day, visitors look down into a canyon that exposes Earth’s distant past. By night, they look outward toward the stars.

The astronaut’s photograph reverses that familiar perspective.

Seen from space, the river’s enormous bends become a single readable pattern: the course of an ancient waterway carried deep into a changing landscape.

Image Credit: NASA/ISS Crew Earth Observations Facility and Earth Science and Remote Sensing Unit, Johnson Space Center. Astronaut photograph ISS075-E-188830, taken by an Expedition 75 crew member on October 6, 2026.

#6414. Your voice can now say things you never said

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

AI can replicate a person’s voice. That raises questions about who has the right to use it and what happens when its owner can no longer give consent.

AI technology can create realistic clones of people’s voices. The resulting proliferation of synthetic voices ushers in all sorts of new scenarios, good and bad. “Today, with nothing more than a keyboard and an internet connection, you can type, and you can get an image, a voice, a video of anything, [of] anybody doing or saying anything,” says Hany Farid, a computer scientist at Dartmouth University.

Some of these voice clones are deeply meaningful to people, as in the cases of people who lost their ability to speak. But voice clones can also cause harm, as with scams and deepfakes. Farid: My voice was cloned by an attacker. I was working a very sensitive case with an attorney. Not many people knew about it. And he got a call from my phone number in my voice talking about the case. And after about three minutes, got suspicious, hung up, called me back. Wasn’t me.

Sanders: Bigger picture, we’ve reached a point where it’s safe to say we can no longer automatically trust digital versions of other people. That applies to the images and sounds on my computer screen as I talked with Farid. Maybe this 2-D picture and sound coming from my laptop is a fake.

Farid: So this two-dimensional version that you and I are sharing now, all right, I can’t control that. That can be stolen. The three-dimensional is right now still me, right? We don’t have the robots that can mimic us. Yet is the end of that sentence.

Sanders: So my interview with Farid was alarming. There are parallels here to any new technology, though. Today, people talk about brain rot from junk online. But remember that television was also going to rot our brains.

[Audio] Its content affects us. So does the sheer weight of the hours we watch.

Sanders: Phones today are the downfall of society, but actual wired telephones encountered really similar resistance when they first started appearing in homes.

[Audio] In Chicago, Sharon Krall’s 15-year-old daughter Angie got so addicted to one teen talk line, she ran up an $850 bill in one month.

Sanders: No big technological advance has escaped this fear.

[Audio] We need teachers who are deeply concerned about how the modern media of communication are changing education.

Sanders: Electricity, bicycles, railways, novels, even the printing press all had their skeptics. So this fear of the new thing has been around a long time. Are synthetic voices created by AI any different? Here’s Karina Nagin from Bridging Voice.

Nagin: Taking off my Bridging Voice hat and just as like a human being in the world, I think there’s a lot of things about AI that I’m very concerned. Deepfakes, the ability to make videos and audio that sound and look just like someone saying something that they’re not saying, I think is a huge, huge concern to our news and public information.

Sanders: Nagin then pivots back to the good, the possibilities here.

Nagin: And then I put on my little hat in my space that I am like, this is how we can harness this to impact people’s lives in our space right now. And I think both conversations need to happen.

Sanders: It occurs to me that I’m seeing the ends of the spectrum here. The stories Farid told me were awful. And the stories that Jules and Casey and others have told me were really, really life-changingly good. Yet these ends of the spectrum are the easy ones. The ones you can look at and say, that’s a horrible way to use this technology. Or that is a powerful and good way to use a voice clone. Between those two poles is the middle ground. That’s the place where Snoop explains cell biology.

[Audio] The membrane separates the material outside the cell.

Sanders: Good, because it’s helping people learn more about mitochondria and who couldn’t use more of that in their lives. Bad, because Snoop never actually said those words, and it’s weird to pretend otherwise.

[Audio] The artists of the Renaissance said that man’s main concern should be for man.

Sanders: There are deepfakes of the late great physicist Richard Feynman delivering famous lectures.

[Audio] The problem is the laws of physics themselves. Let me start with something basic. The next star over from us is called Proxima Centauri.

Sanders: Good because it introduces some amazing physics to people who would otherwise scroll past? Bad because it’s somewhat disrespectful and possibly inaccurate? There aren’t easy answers here. This murky middle gets even murkier with the invention of griefbots. Those are digital versions of people who have passed away. And that means that special voices can keep talking to us long after the body that created them is gone.

I read a poignant post online written by a guy who had lost his dad after years of dementia. He missed his dad’s voice, he wrote, so he cloned it. He paid for the starter pack, submitted three minutes of his dad’s audio, and he wrote, quote, a few minutes later, I had a scarily accurate clone of my dead father’s voice. He goes on to write, quote, my family and I had a good cathartic cry upon hearing the results. I had his cloned voice read the Lord’s Prayer as well as ‘Twas the Night before Christmas. Just hearing his simulated voice again is such a blessing and is helping me in the grief process. End quote.

There are lots of companies now offering this exact thing. A casual search online gets me to a company that sells chats with dead loved ones. There’s a big orange button to click that says bring them back to life. A 2024 documentary called “Eternal You” follows the stories of people as they grapple with this idea. Here’s a little bit of the trailer.

[Audio] We are on the verge of a new era. Hi. It’s like, it’s the funniest thing. It’s like, what’s the first thing you say to someone that’s dead? Like, welcome back.

Sanders: Griefbots or digital avatars of loved ones offer a bridge from the past to the present, a way to remember vividly. But they are also a denial, of sorts, that all life must come to an end.

[Audio] And what I can tell you is that AI really is changing the way that we interact with death.

Sanders: That’s from a 2025 TEDx talk from Dylan Thomas Doyle. He’s a former hospital chaplain, current academic researcher at Northwestern University and self-described philosophy bro. His work explores death and AI.

[Audio] Imagine that you are at a funeral, and you’re sitting there in silent reflection, and all of a sudden, on the back screen in the auditorium, a woman’s face appears. And it’s the face of a woman named Marina. And her hologram, she starts talking to you, and she starts asking you how you’re doing today. And you answer her, and then you ask her a question back. And she responds as if she is still there.

Sanders: I called Doyle to ask about the implications of using technology this way.

Doyle: It was on my radar as a chaplain and a technology researcher, I started thinking through, well, what is the actual impact of this technology on people? So what is it like to hear the voice, in the context of this podcast, the voice of, say, your father who’s passed away while you’re actively grieving their death? And they’re not just repeating what they said or a journal entry in their voice, but like, creating new stories and new relationships through their voice. It gives a lot of people existential ick, is what I’ve heard. And that’s something that I really, I’m curious about.

Sanders: There’s tension here, Doyle tells me.

Doyle: So there’s this push force where you’re like, this is not right. We don’t have the narrative or cultural script to understand what’s going on there. But then as people are beginning to use it, there’s a comfort that comes out of it. So we’re working in that tension space between this comfort that comes, then you’re still dealing with this push away from this technology of it just being weird in a way that people are still grappling with language, I think, to describe.

Sanders: It’s not clear how these types of interactions might affect grieving. They could help or they could hurt.

Doyle: There is this tension between more healthy continuing bonds. So continuing that relationship by, say, writing letters to your dead loved one or, you know, talking out loud to them and continuing that relationship in a positive way that moves us through a healthy grief process and a grief journey. Or hanging on to our relationship with that person to a degree where we can’t actually do any sort of moving on.

Sanders: Doyle points out that we don’t have good data on how many people might be using griefbots.

Doyle: I just don’t want us to get ahead of ourselves when it comes to people like using these. So the capability to do everything we’ve talked about with griefbots is there. But the actual use cases of individuals in their homes using this, it’s still pretty unclear about the adoption of those technologies.

Sanders: But even if griefbots aren’t widespread, the questions they raise aren’t going away. These voices are blurring the lines between a memory and a present-day experience, between alive and dead. Here’s Karina Nagin again.

Nagin: It’s an interesting conversation that we’re having right now of what happens to your voice once you pass away. Some people are starting to integrate this into their wills or their sort of final wishes of, do you want your voice to be able to speak at your own memorial service?

Do you want to have messages saved in your voice that are for your child at graduation that they listen to? Who and when can use that? I think that these are things that people are starting to think about. Who owns your voice? Can your children use your voice to write a speech for their children’s graduation? Or do you want that voice to be deleted once you pass away? Very tricky questions.

Sanders: Rules about who can use voice clones are all over the place. Regulations vary by state and by country, and even companies have their own individual policies in place. There are no clear guidelines, and that makes sense given how young this technology is. Conversations about digital voices and how to use them are inherently very personal. There are as many different takes as there are people. I asked MA if she and Jules had talked about this.

MA: I love that question. Both of us love this question because it’s so important. And we talked about it before he got the trache. Like when he was already using the voice, we were talking about different things in bed at night. And he said, you know, I have a very clear request that my voice like dies with me, basically, that, you know, I ask that you don’t use the voice to keep me alive in any way,  that there’s no… And I was like, 100 percent clear. I hadn’t even thought about that. But yeah, it would make sense to be like, I miss him so much. I want to, whatever or. But no, as far as we’re concerned, his voice dies when he does. And his voice will live on in whatever videos or things we captured, whatever he’s left us intentionally. And that’s as far as that goes.

Sanders: So when Jules is gone, his voice will be gone too. But right now is a different story.

MA:  Well back in 2021, I was writing an Instagram post about something. It was him playing with Skylar in the backyard while he was already like, you know, had trouble with everything, but he was doing what he could. And I asked him like, you know, what, what do you want to caption it? And he just said that, right here, right now phrase, something else, and like right here, right now. And it became our family mantra. It became something that we wanted to just to share and in both a sense of like do the things that you want to do.

And also something that’s always been big for Jules that I’ve admired him articulate is that it’s not just about, oh, just go forward and do all the things and like suck the marrow out of life. It’s like just also, like, settle. Like it doesn’t have to be that extreme, you know. There’s a beautiful thing about that presence and that settling in. And again, with ALS being something where you’re given the diagnosis, which is terminal, it’s basically a death sentence. Most people are given, you know, two to five years. You don’t know where you’re going to fall in that. We’ve known people that have passed away in a year and a half. We’ve known people that are six years in like Jules, but can still kind of walk around, speak a little bit. ALS touches everybody really differently. So you really don’t know what’s coming. And there’s a lot of like forward thinking that you can do that detaches you from being in your life. So how are you here? And then there’s a lot of backwards, you know, reminiscing and grieving about all the things we’ve lost and how we wish things were different. But then that also takes you out of like this moment right now and this part of your story.

Sanders: This part of the story is the important part. Right here, right now.

On the next and final episode of The Deep End, Talk to Me. We’re going to look at what’s next for Jules and Casey and what’s next for the science racing to give voices back to people.

Vikash Gilja: We can see all the pieces coming together. All of the emphasis, capital, quite frankly, talent focused on advancing AI techniques and technologies. You know, our little corner can benefit from it, right? These tools weren’t available even five years ago.

Sanders: What’s next for the human voice?

Samantha Brosler: Of course, ultimately, we’re hoping to expand this to even larger vocabulary and more range of body movements across the whole body to help allow people more expression in their communication.

This is The Deep End, Talk to Me. I’m Laura Sanders. If you like this podcast tell your friends and leave us a review. It helps the show a lot. Send us your questions and your comments at podcasts@sciencenews.org.

#6413. Guard dogs are watching over cattle in a Texas county with rare swift foxes and stopping all predator attacks

Fewer than 250 swift foxes remain in Texas. Two dogs are now guarding cattle on the grassland to test whether they can keep coyotes away.

This summer, two Maremma guardian dogs named Duke and Dozer moved with a herd of cattle onto the Rita Blanca National Grasslands. The site lies in Dallam County, in the far northwest corner of the Texas Panhandle.

Their main job is to keep predators away from the cattle. Researchers at Texas A&M AgriLife want to know if the dogs can also protect the swift fox, a small native fox that coyotes often kill.

Fewer than 250 swift foxes are thought to live in Texas, according to Texas A&M AgriLife. The three-year project has no fox results yet. So far, though, the rancher taking part has not lost a calf to predators.

The swift fox (Vulpes velox) is about the size of a house cat. It weighs 4 to 7 pounds (1.8 to 3.2 kilograms), according to Texas Parks and Wildlife magazine, which makes it the smallest fox in the state.

The species once ranged from the Llano Estacado up into Alberta, Canada. It now holds about 40 percent of that range, the magazine reported in May 2026.

Dallam County is the only county in Texas currently known to have swift foxes. Dana Karelus is the state mammal specialist with the Texas Parks and Wildlife Department (TPWD). She said only 40 to 50 percent of the shortgrass prairie is left.

Bison herds and fires once kept that grass short. On a Kansas prairie, bison roughly doubled native plant diversity over 29 years.

In the Panhandle the grass now grows taller, and Texas Tech ecologist Clint Boal told the magazine that coyotes ambush foxes more easily once it passes 12 inches (30 centimeters).

Haley Sloan is a doctoral student in the Texas A&M Department of Rangeland, Wildlife and Fisheries Management. She said coyotes are a leading cause of death for swift foxes, using the taller plants as cover.

John Tomeček, an associate professor in the same department, co-leads the wider swift fox work with Texas Tech researchers. TPWD pays for it.

Tomeček told the magazine that Panhandle coyotes appear to kill swift foxes but rarely eat them, and that nobody knows why.

Wolves keep coyotes out of their ground in natural systems. In eastern North America, coyotes have adapted to landscapes without wolves.

Tomeček called a guardian dog “a wolf that works for you.” Swift foxes eat insects, plants and small rodents, so they pose no threat to livestock.

Gray foxes in North Carolina have a different way out. There, gray foxes use tree cover to live alongside coyotes because they can climb. Swift foxes have no trees on the prairie. They need short, open grass so they can see predators coming.

Guardian dogs are usually raised with sheep and goats. Bill Costanzo, the AgriLife Extension guardian dog specialist in San Angelo, had to change the training so the puppies stayed safe around much larger cattle.

The program’s monthly blog, The Guardian Way, followed the pups, which it describes as Maremma and all from one litter, through the winter in San Angelo.

According to the January post, in November 2025, Duke and Dozer went to visit adult dogs in the next pasture. Then they found a fallen gate and wandered over to pastures at Angelo State University.

The pair had first bonded with calves from Sul Ross State University. Early in 2026, staff traded those calves a few at a time for grown cows. Duke and Dozer’s cattle took longer to accept the new cows than the herd of their littermates, Delta and Diesel.

The handoff in early May went badly at first. The pups dug out of their pen on the day they reached the cooperating rancher. GPS trackers found them two days later on a neighboring ranch, according to the May 2026 post.

The rancher kept them penned until they got used to him, then let them out with the cattle again. By June, one dog stayed beside the herd each day while the other patrolled around the pens. In July they were due to move with the cattle to the Rita Blanca lease.

Costanzo said the team now has “a set of procedures to help guide the bonding process with guardian dogs and cattle.” He hopes to use guardian dogs with cattle on a larger scale.

Before the dogs arrived, Sloan and her colleagues put GPS collars on swift foxes and coyotes. The dogs wear GPS collars as well.

Those first tracks show how both species moved before the dogs came. Sloan’s idea is that the dogs stand in for a larger predator. Coyotes would then avoid the herd, and foxes could start using the ground they leave.

Over two years, the field team caught foxes, measured them and fitted the collars, the TPWD magazine reported. They took ear punches for genetic work. They also tested the foxes for parvo and canine distemper.

The wider project is testing prescribed fire, grazing patterns and artificial dens made from upside-down buckets. Game cameras watch the dens. A separate survey asks people in swift fox country what they think of the animal.

Guardian dogs are not trained to kill predators, according to a 2023 AgriLife report. They patrol, disrupt predators and chase them off. Killing coyotes has limits of its own, since coyote numbers bounce back quickly after removal efforts.

Sloan said success would help twice, with better odds for the foxes and fewer lost calves in calving season.

“I’m happy to report right now the dogs are doing great,” Sloan said. She added that the producer “hasn’t lost any calves to predation.”

AgriLife says it is too early to report findings. The dogs have spent only a few months on the lease. The release gives no numbers on fox survival, coyote movements or how many animals wear collars.

The test also rests on one herd and two dogs. The other two pups from the litter, Diesel and Delta, went to a ranch in Childress in April. The blog said no data would be collected on them because there was no funding.

Whether coyotes move away from the herd, and whether foxes move in, will be measured over the three years of the project.

For now, the two dogs that dug out of their first pen in May are staying with the cattle on the Rita Blanca, in the only Texas county known to have swift foxes.

The information was obtained from Texas A&M AgriLife Today.

Researchers used CT scans to crack a 400-year-old code and open a mysterious padlock that washed up in Wales with the Ann Francis treasure hoard.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

An Elizabethan padlock has been opened for the first time in more than 400 years after researchers used X-ray imaging techniques to crack its four-letter combination.

The brass lock was part of the Ann Francis treasure hoard, named after the British merchant ship that wrecked during a storm off the coast of Wales in 1583. Researchers believe the lock once secured a chest aboard the ship, before becoming separated from whatever riches it was protecting.

Some of the Ann Francis' cargo was recovered at the time of the wreck, while the rest was claimed by the sea. In recent decades, dredging and storms on Margam beach in South Wales have exposed some of the ship's lost treasure.

Between 1996 and 2017, metal detectorist Peter Hughes found the lock and much of the hoard, which included gold and silver coins. The lock was subsequently acquired by Amgueddfa Cymru — National Museum Wales, which worked with researchers at Cardiff University in Wales to decipher its combination.

To study the lock's internal mechanisms, the team used micro-CT scans, which make thousands of X-rays that can then be configured into a 3D digital image. By matching internal notches to external letters in the digital 3D image, the researchers were able to decipher the correct four-letter code — "ANCE" — and open the lock.

"We normally use this technology to study bones and other biological structures, so investigating a 400-year-old padlock was certainly a first for us," David Williams, a research associate at the Musculoskeletal Biomechanics Research Facility at Cardiff University, said in a statement. "It's not every day you get to solve a 400-year-old mystery!"

The Ann Francis was owned by Francis Shaxton, a merchant and notorious smuggler. Francis claimed the ship was sailing along the eastern English coast from King’s Lynn to Hartlepool, when it was actually traveling in the opposite direction, heading to Spain to deliver a cargo of wheat. Spain was dependent on grain shipments at the time and paid for such shipments in gold and silver from colonial conquests in Central and South America, according to Amgueddfa Cymru.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The ship was traveling back from Spain to England when, on the evening of Dec. 28, 1583, it was caught in a violent storm. After heading off course, the ship ended its journey in ruin off Margam beach.

A parish register noted the loss of 14 sailors during the same month as the wreckage, which could have been The Ann Francis's crew, according to Amgueddfa Cymru. The deaths were blamed on the nefarious work of a supposed witch.

Locals were quick to loot the Ann Francis wreck before a legal dispute ensued over who had the right to its goods. One Welsh lord claiming the wreck made an inventory list of items he impounded, which included cannons, guns, a piece of mast, Spanish silver and three chests with their locks broken. The newly cracked lock could have originally secured one of these chests, according to Amgueddfa Cymru.

Centuries after the ship was wrecked, Hughes found the lock near a previously undiscovered stash of Spanish silver coins and coin weights while metal detecting on the beach.

"When I found the lock I was immediately astonished by the incredible workmanship and its astonishing condition," Hughes said. "When I moved the ring dials of the combination they turned with ease after over 400 years beneath the sands and I was left in disbelief."

Hughes said he attempted to open the lock himself over many years but could never find the right combination. After Amgueddfa Cymru acquired the lock, staff were concerned that they could hear grit moving around inside the dials, and with more than 1,000 possible combinations, they didn't want to cause any damage.

The micro-CT scans offered a nondestructive view inside the lock, and an opportunity to finally identify the correct four-letter combination.

"Elizabethan combination locks are known in Britain, but this one is in exceptionally good condition and is associated with a dated wreck, making it a unique find and the code a tantalising mystery to solve," Alastair Willis, the senior curator for numismatics and the Welsh economy at Amgueddfa Cymru, said in the statement. "Of course, now we've solved it, we are left wondering if the code meant something to its owner."

Patrick Pester is the trending news writer at Live Science. His work has appeared on other science websites, such as BBC Science Focus and Scientific American. Patrick retrained as a journalist after spending his early career working in zoos and wildlife conservation. He also has a second master's degree in biodiversity, evolution and conservation in action from Middlesex University London. When he isn't writing news, Patrick investigates the sale of human remains.

#6410. AI searches 50 million chemicals for sweeteners without the bitter aftertaste

An AI search of more than 50 million chemicals identified 92 potential sugar substitutes that could deliver sweetness without a bitter aftertaste.

A sip of diet soda can leave a bitter or metallic taste in your mouth. Finding a sugar substitute that delivers sweetness without that lingering taste has proved difficult.

Shayma El-Atawneh and Amiram Goldblum at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem used artificial intelligence to look for better options.

Their search covered more than 50 million chemicals and produced a shortlist of 92 possible sweeteners.

The researchers have not tested how those candidates taste. But they have narrowed an enormous search to a list that a laboratory could realistically work through.

The tongue detects sweetness through one type of receptor, a tiny sensor made from two proteins working together. It has 25 receptor types for bitterness.

Those bitter sensors recognize many different chemicals, including toxic substances. They help warn animals about things they should avoid swallowing.

Some sweet molecules also activate bitter receptors, so the tongue picks up both tastes. That overlap helps explain why a sweetener can leave a bitter aftertaste.

Saccharin, cyclamate and aspartame all came from accidental discoveries. Researchers still struggle to reproduce the clean taste of table sugar.

The U.S. Food and Drug Administration has approved six high-intensity sweeteners as food additives: saccharin, aspartame, acesulfame potassium, sucralose, neotame and advantame.

Stevia leaf extracts and monk fruit extracts also sweeten foods and drinks.

Some earlier studies have linked artificially sweetened drinks with higher risks of stroke and dementia, though those associations do not prove cause and effect.

Other research has connected some sweeteners with changes in gut bacteria and difficulty processing glucose.

The new study focused on predicting taste. It did not establish whether any candidate would be safe to eat.

Goldblum’s group originally developed its algorithm, called Iterative Stochastic Elimination, or ISE, to find potential drugs.

Here, the researchers used it to search for patterns in chemicals with known tastes.

The program tries ranges of molecular properties at random and checks how well they separate different groups. It discards weak combinations and keeps useful filters, each built from five property ranges.

It draws on 205 calculated features, including how electrical charge spreads across a molecule and how the molecule behaves in oil and water.

Another feature counts chiral centers, points in a molecule that allow different mirror-image arrangements.

The training data included 7,709 sweet compounds from one database and 316 well-studied sweeteners from another. A third supplied several hundred bitter compounds and 208 tasteless ones.

The models found different clues for each taste. Sweetness predictions relied on charge distribution and chiral centers, while bitterness predictions relied on acidity and positive charge.

The researchers then screened three supplier catalogs containing 2.2 million, 30.7 million and 17.9 million molecules.

Candidates moved forward only if the sweetness models gave them high scores and the bitterness models gave them negative scores.

That narrowed the search, but it left another question to answer: could the selected molecules fit into the tongue’s sweet receptor?

In 2025, three teams published the first detailed structures of the human sweet receptor. One structure, listed as 9NOV in the Protein Data Bank, shows sucralose sitting inside a binding pocket.

Scientists produced that view by freezing the protein and imaging it with electrons.

El-Atawneh and Goldblum used it to simulate how their candidates might fit into a receptor section that closes around sweet molecules like a clamshell.

Existing sweeteners provided a comparison: advantame scored -7.8, sucralose -7.2 and saccharin -4.8, with more negative scores suggesting stronger binding.

The researchers set a cutoff of -6, roughly the average for the approved sweeteners.

Candidates also needed hydrogen bonds at three of five selected receptor sites and contact with five of eight others.

After removing molecules with chemical groups known to produce misleading laboratory results, the team had 556 candidates.

The researchers selected 92 for further work. Of these, 43 had no more than one chiral center, making them easier to obtain and test; the other 49 had the strongest sweetness and lowest bitterness predictions.

They also compared all 556 candidates with known compounds that interact with the sweet receptor and with one another.

Most had distinct structures, suggesting that the search could lead to unfamiliar families of sweeteners.

Fourteen of the final 92 already appeared in patents as sweet-receptor modulators, compounds that alter the receptor’s activity.

Finding them again offered a useful check on the method, though they were not new discoveries.

Among approved drugs, about 10% scored as bitter and roughly 2% as sweet, a pattern consistent with the tongue’s wider range of bitter receptors.

Sucralose exposed a clear weakness. The sweetness models gave it negative scores, while the bitterness models gave it slightly positive ones.

The researchers attributed this mistake to a structural feature that their training data did not adequately cover.

The program struggled with chemistry outside the examples it had learned from.

They also deliberately favored fewer false alarms, accepting that the models would miss some real sweeteners. A shortlist filled with wrong predictions would waste laboratory time.

The docking scores had limits, too: they did not reliably indicate how much sweetener was needed to activate the receptor.

These calculations use a fixed protein structure and leave out water, movement and changes in the protein’s shape.

The study did not include laboratory or taste tests of the 92 candidates. Its models predict whether something might taste sweet, but not how sweet it would be.

According to the researchers, only one taste-prediction effort over the past decade had led to a sweetener confirmed in laboratory tests.

In 2020, another team tested three natural compounds and found that one, arctiin, activated the human sweet receptor, although only at high concentrations.

Goldblum disclosed a pending patent in the paper’s competing-interests statement, giving him a potential financial interest in the work.

The candidates still need tests to establish their taste, safety and suitability for food.

The next step is to obtain the molecules and test their effects on the receptor, using the results to improve future predictions.

The full study was published in the journal Food Chemistry.

#6409. Brilliant cosmic afterglow may reveal a monster explosion in hiding

A modest gamma-ray burst left an unusually bright afterglow. Astronomers suggest that a jet angled away from Earth could explain the mismatch.

In gamma-ray bursts, a stronger flash tends to leave a brighter glow behind. GRB 260310A didn’t follow that pattern.

Its flash was modest, yet the light that came after it was one of the brightest of its kind astronomers have ever recorded.

A new study suggests that its nearby location made the afterglow look unusually bright, while our viewing angle may explain the weak initial flash.

NASA’s Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope detected the burst’s 53-second flash of gamma rays on March 10, 2026.

A team led by Yu-Han Yang, a postdoctoral scholar at the University of Rome Tor Vergata, tracked what followed for about two months.

Co-author Roberto Ricci led the team’s radio observations at the Karl G. Jansky Very Large Array in New Mexico.

“We see hundreds of GRBs every year, but the oddballs are the most informative ones,” Ricci said.

“We could explain individual features of this burst, but fitting them all into the same picture proved much harder.”

Gamma rays are the most energetic form of light. Many gamma-ray bursts begin when a massive star collapses and launches jets of matter outward at nearly the speed of light.

When a jet runs into the gas around the star, it produces a longer-lasting light called an afterglow, which telescopes can follow in X-rays, visible light, and radio waves.

GRB 260310A came from that kind of star. A spectrum taken at Calar Alto Observatory in Spain on March 13 showed only the afterglow.

By April 4, the light carried the broad features of a supernova, confirming that a massive star had died.

Seen from Earth, the afterglow was extreme. Compared with earlier bursts, it ranked among the brightest 1% in X-rays and visible light, and the brightest 5% in radio waves.

Most of that brightness is due to distance. GRB 260310A went off closer to us than about 97% of bursts with known distances.

Once the researchers accounted for distance, the afterglow’s intrinsic brightness was ordinary, and in some measurements relatively faint.

Its peak in visible light was fainter than about 80% of the other bursts, and its X-ray output fell in the bottom 15%.

So the puzzle isn’t really how bright the afterglow was. It’s how weak the gamma rays were next to it.

Astronomers find these explosions most easily when a jet points straight at Earth.

“Much like a flashlight, the jet appears brightest when seen head-on. Most of our models are calibrated using events seen from that same perspective. This burst gave us a chance to look beyond that glare,” Yang explained.

To fit the usual link between gamma rays and afterglows, GRB 260310A would have needed roughly 30 times more gamma-ray energy than it gave off.

A jet aimed away from Earth would dim the gamma rays in just that way.

The visible light fit a side view too. When a jet faces Earth, its afterglow is expected to peak within minutes. This one was still getting brighter hours after the burst.

“We looked at it from a side angle,” Yang said. “As the jet slowed down, its light became visible over a wider range of angles, allowing us to probe the jet’s shape, from its outer edges toward its inner core.”

The X-ray glow faded slowly for about nine days, then dropped quickly. Around 18 days after the burst, it started climbing again, and it didn’t fade until about day 30.

Most of the X-ray tracking came from the Einstein Probe mission, which can’t separate the burst from other sources close by in the sky. NASA’s Chandra X-ray Observatory can, and it found two fainter sources near the burst.

“That was unexpected. At first, I thought another X-ray source was contaminating our observations. But the brightening really came from the afterglow,” said Yang, who coordinated the X-ray monitoring.

“This prompted us to explore a more complex jet’s shape.”

One idea is a jet with two parts: a narrow, fast, energetic core surrounded by a broader, slower flow.

In the team’s model, the core reaches only about 0.8 degrees out from the jet’s center line, and the outer flow reaches about 16 degrees. Earth would be about 10 degrees off center.

Early on, Earth would have seen light mostly from the broader flow. As the core slowed, its light would have spread wide enough to reach Earth, producing the second X-ray peak.

“What appeared to us as an unremarkable GRB might have looked like a monster explosion to an observer looking straight down the jet’s core,” Yang said.

“Our models suggest that the explosion packed roughly a billion years of the Sun’s energy output into a pencil-thin beam.”

The other idea is that extra energy reached the expanding blast weeks after the burst and made it brighten again. The researchers haven’t ruled out either one.

Most of these jets point away from Earth, and their gamma rays are often too faint for detectors to notice, so most of these explosions go unseen.

Late X-ray rises may also be more common than the records show. In NASA’s Swift X-ray archive, only 13 of more than 1,300 long bursts were tracked for more than 15 days.

None of the team’s standard models could match all of this burst’s light, at every wavelength, across the whole two months.

The Vera C. Rubin Observatory in Chile began a 10-year survey of the southern sky on June 30, 2026.

Graduate student Muskan Yadav contributed to the study. “Gamma rays are not the most efficient route to spot these hidden jets: we find them once in a blue moon,” Yadav said.

“Upcoming surveys will pick up hundreds of them. Identifying them among millions of variable sources won’t be easy, but it’s a challenge I’m excited to take on.”

With more of them, astronomers could learn how often dying stars launch jets like this one. They could also learn how those jets break through a star’s outer layers.

The full study was published in the journal The Astrophysical Journal Letters.

#6408. How hawkmoths turned their genitals into bat-busting weapons

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Hawkmoths can create ultrasonic bursts that thwart the sonar of predatory bats

The pink-spotted hawkmoth (Agrius cingulata) is one of many species whose males make ultrasound by scraping specialized genital scales against spines along the abdomen.

Paul Masonick/Florida Museum of Natural History

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

When a bat closes in, some hawkmoths fight back with their genitalia. By rasping specialized scales on their sex organs against structures on their abdomens, the moths unleash bursts of ultrasound that can scramble the sonar a hungry bat uses to lock onto prey.

But this acoustic counterattack is no evolutionary one-off. Relentless pressure from predators has pushed these otherwise tasty insects to reinvent this defensive tactic up to seven times throughout their evolution, with separate lineages arriving at distinct anatomical solutions to the same threat, researchers report November 4 in the Proceedings of the Royal Society B.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

The findings suggest that the high-frequency acoustic skirmishes playing out overhead each night, beyond the range of human hearing, may be far more varied than scientists realized.

“Clearly the hawkmoths as a whole have more tricks up their sleeve,” says Marc Holderied, a sensory biologist and bioacoustics researcher at the University of Bristol in England who was not involved in the study.

The discovery builds on more than a decade of research by sensory ecologist Jesse Barber, now at the American Museum of Natural History in New York City, and entomologist Akito Kawahara of the Florida Museum of Natural History in Gainesville. Those scientists’ earlier work showed that moths across multiple families, from tiger moths and fruit-piercing moths to geometer moths and jewel caterpillar moths, produce ultrasound in response to bat attacks. Other insects, including some beetles and fireflies, do too.

But among the most striking defenders are hawkmoths, a family of some 1,600 mostly nocturnal, torpedo-shaped speedsters, also known as sphinx moths, that hover at flowers like hummingbirds. Many fend off bats by scraping their genitalia like a fingernail dragged along a comb, producing ultrasonic clicks that can disrupt the predators’ sonar.

The anatomical diversity of these sound-producing systems, however, and how they evolved remained poorly understood. So Barber, Kawahara and their team, including Florida museum colleague and evolutionary biologist Paul Masonick, combined audio recordings of male hawkmoths responding to bat calls with high-resolution imaging of preserved specimens from overlapping species. Although some females also produce ultrasound, the researchers focused on males because female sound creation remains too poorly documented for systematic analysis.

Among the 143 species tested, 77 produced ultrasound. They did so in three distinct ways. All three rely on a patch of enlarged, football-shaped scales on the male’s genital valves, which are paired structures used to clasp females during mating. But what those scales scrape against varies.

Some rub the scales against a row of corresponding scales near the rear of the abdomen. Others drag them across stiff spines jutting from the abdomen’s edge. Still others rasp them over a field of microscopic bumps on the insect’s underside, a previously unidentified part of the sound-making apparatus.

Paul Masonick/Florida Museum of Natural History

Paul Masonick/Florida Museum of Natural History

These mechanical differences are reflected in the sounds themselves. Moths that scrape their genital scales against spines or tiny bumps tend to make more continuous noise, with greater potential to jam bat sonar. Those that scrape scales against other scales produce irregular bursts, which may startle attackers or mimic the warning calls of foul-tasting prey.

Notably, moths that scrape against the newly identified bumpy surface have the broadest acoustic repertoire, with even close relatives sounding quite different. That flexibility could give them more options for evolving new defenses against bats, notes Nick Dowdy, an evolutionary biologist at the Milwaukee Public Museum who was not involved in the research. Other groups, by comparison, may be more constrained by their anatomy, he says, leaving them “locked into certain strategies.”

The authors estimate that genitalia-enabled ultrasound production evolved independently at least four and as many as seven times between roughly 5 million and 30 million years ago. According to Masonick, it is a vivid example of convergent evolution in which the same predatory menace repeatedly drove the moths to adapt similar behaviors through different anatomical routes.

But the evolutionary arms race was not a one-way street, he points out. Several hawkmoth lineages that shifted toward twilight or daytime activity subsequently lost their specialized sound-producing machinery.

“It goes to show how intense bat predation is on insects,” Masonick says. “It’s been a major driver of insect evolution.”
