#6406. Engineers created a new tattoo ink that disappears and reappears when you shine different lights on it

Engineers built tattoo inks that switch on under UV light and fade indoors, and the inventor has worn the color-changing tattoo for two years.

A tattoo is forever. That is the whole appeal and the whole problem. About a quarter of people with body art end up unhappy with a permanent mark.

Now there is an ink that stays colorless under the skin until ultraviolet light hits it. Then it turns blue, magenta or yellow in a few seconds, and fades again under ordinary room light.

Engineers at the University of Colorado Boulder built the inks from color-changing dyes sealed inside tiny plastic beads. They tattooed the inks into silicone and pig skin and showed that the three colors can be written, erased and rewritten with light alone.

One person has carried the inks in living skin for more than two years. He is the lead author.

The tattoo itself doesn’t go anywhere. Only the color does.

Carson Bruns of the ATLAS Institute and the Paul M. Rady Department of Mechanical Engineering at CU Boulder led the work, with Mollie Stockton, Emily Gardner and Hyejin Kwon.

The multicolor images were made only in skin models, and the inks have not been through safety testing for people.

In an interview with Earth.com, Bruns put the first caveat in plain words. “First, a PhotoTat is still a permanent tattoo. The pigment stays in the skin indefinitely, exactly like conventional tattoo ink.

What is rewritable is the color, not the tattoo,” he said. “Rewritable does not mean removable.”

Each ink is water carrying beads of PMMA, the clear plastic in plexiglass, bone cement and some dermal fillers.

The beads are a few hundred nanometers across, about the size of ordinary tattoo ink particles. Each one is loaded with a dye that flips between a colorless form and a colored one when light hits it.

The team chose PMMA for a second reason. It bends light almost the way skin does, so the beads scatter very little of it and are hard to see when the dye is switched off.

Three dyes give three primary colors. Mixed in different ratios, they produced a range of shades in a 16-patch test array.

To write a full-color picture, the team switched all three on at once, then erased each color selectively with the red, green and blue light of a laser projector.

“PhotoTat is like a switch. You turn the tattoo on with UV light, but you can turn it off again when you go to grandma’s house,” Bruns said.

Switching the tattoo on takes two to three seconds under a small 365-nanometer UV lamp. That dose of UV is roughly what six to 10 seconds of average sunlight delivers, the team calculated, far below what it takes to redden even the most sensitive skin.

How fast the color fades depends on how bright the room is. Under typical indoor lighting it lasts for hours, but it can persist for days. A bright white keychain lamp pressed against the skin erases it in seconds.

Bruns told Earth.com that mismatch is what makes the system usable. “That asymmetry is what lets skin behave like a display without any power source in the body,” he said.

Sunlight complicates things, because it carries enough UV to switch the ink partly on, even on an overcast day. The team found that SPF 30 sunscreen over the tattoo switched it off completely outdoors in every skin model they tested.

Bruns had a set of black fish-scale outlines tattooed on his shin and thigh. Between January 2024 and January 2025 he filled them with the color-changing inks, more than 30 small tattoos in all. The inks for that pilot came pre-mixed from HYPRSKN Inc., a company he co-founded.

When he assessed the tattoos, 1.4 to 2.2 years after they went in, all three colors still switched on under UV and off under white light.

In one scale he drew a smiley face with a UV pen and erased it. Then he wrote a heart through a printed mask, erased that, and wrote a musical note through a stencil.

Asked by Earth.com what surprised him, he named that durability. “I was surprised by how well the PhotoTats held up in my skin,” he said.

Color-changing compounds are known to wear out with repeated switching, he explained, and skin clears and shuffles pigment over time. So whether the inks would last for years in living tissue was an open question.

One person’s leg is not a study of people. Bruns has fair skin, and the authors wrote that a single-subject pilot can’t be generalized to anyone else.

In the lab, the blue dye wore out after 10 to 100 switching cycles and left behind a permanent purple tint that stayed visible in the off state. The authors call that burn-in a critical flaw, because an ink that is supposed to disappear can’t disappear.

Magenta and yellow held up far better over the same number of cycles.

Bruns said his own blue tattoos have so far shown negligible fading or purple discoloration after years of switching. This is different from the lab result that he raised himself.

Two other gaps are built into the chemistry. There is no white channel, so the system can’t make a patch lighter than the surrounding skin. And the blue reads as blue rather than a true cyan, which narrows the range of colors.

The color change also weakens as skin gets darker, for the same optical reason that colored tattoos show less contrast on brown skin, Bruns said. That limit comes from melanin, not from the ink.

Bruns is co-founder and president of MGC INK CORP, which sells a single-color version of this technology as Magic Ink. He is also co-founder and chief scientific officer of its parent company, HYPRSKN Inc.

Two co-authors hold financial interests in both companies, and Bruns is a co-inventor on a related patent assigned to the University of Colorado.

The single-color ink has been through a pilot clinical study of 11 people, published separately in the Journal of Nanobiotechnology.

No adverse events were reported, and the color switching still worked after at least a year. That study validates one formulation, not the three-color system, he said.

Beyond body art, the team sees medical uses. Many people getting radiation therapy are tattooed with small permanent dots so doctors can line up the beam, and most of them report being unhappy with the marks.

“They’re not beautiful, and they become a permanent reminder of a traumatic experience,” Bruns said.

“With PhotoTat, we could turn an involuntary medical tattoo into something that’s only visible to the doctor when you go in the clinic, and then it can be invisible the rest of the time.”

The three-color inks have not been through safety testing in people. Each color has to pass toxicity, sterility and purity testing on its own, Bruns said, and that work is still ahead.

The team also did not look at where the nanoparticles end up in tissue. Their statement that the beads stay in the dermis rests on what is already known about ordinary tattoo pigments, not on biopsies of their own samples. They list that check as a next step.

Clinical studies of the platform in more than one person are underway, the authors wrote. Finding a sturdier blue dye is the chemistry problem that has to be solved first.

Until then, the color-changing tattoo is a laboratory result, one man’s leg, and a single-color product with a different formula.

The full study was published in the journal Matter & Light.

Seeds found in an ancient grave and chemical compounds discovered in mummy hair have revealed people got high on marijuana 2,800 years ago.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Archaeologists have unearthed the oldest evidence of cannabis use from a 2,800-year-old monumental tomb in Siberia. The presence of plant seeds in the grave and chemical traces of the drug in mummy hair suggest people practiced a funeral ritual that may have involved a grim practice: calming human sacrifice victims with cannabis.

In a study published Thursday (Nov. 5) in the journal Science, researchers investigated the contents of a "royal mound" burial at the Tunnug archaeological site in the Uyuk valley of southern Siberia. Archaeologists discovered four wooden structures containing several log coffins in the middle of the mound. On top of the wooden burial structures were the skeletons of horses that once formed a "spectral cavalcade," a Scythian funeral tradition that involved sacrificing horses and humans. And inside the burial structures, the archaeologists discovered piles of tiny seeds from the plant Cannabis ruderalis, a wild type of cannabis or marijuana.

Cannabis likely originated in Asia and was cultivated thousands of years ago for various purposes, including for ropes and textiles, and 6,000 years ago as an oilseed crop, according to the study. But it's unclear when people learned about the psychoactive properties of the plant. In the fifth century B.C., the ancient Greek historian Herodotus wrote that the Scythian nomads inhaled the fumes from burning hemp seeds. And evidence of cannabis use was previously discovered in a cemetery in China dated to about 500 B.C. The new study, however, pushes back this date by three centuries.

Archaeologists found evidence of cannabis use in a burial mound in southern Siberia.

Researchers discovered more than 1,000 whole cannabis seeds and around 500 partial seeds in the Tunnug burial mound, and they carbon-dated them to between 800 and 760 B.C. They also recovered several human hair samples from the grave. An analysis of the hair revealed signals matching cannabinol and THC (tetrahydrocannabinol), psychoactive chemical compounds found in cannabis. The tests could not determine how much of the drug people consumed, however.

"The molecular traces in the hair and the cannabis seeds come from the same grave and suggest that cannabis was used for its intoxicating properties," study first author Gino Caspari, an archaeologist at the Max Planck Institute of Geoanthropology in Jena, Germany, said in a statement.

But given the burial context of the discovery, the use of cannabis may have had a darker purpose.

"In this princely tomb, the burials were accompanied by extensive horse sacrifices and, most likely, human sacrifices as well," Caspari said. The tradition of human sacrifice, in particular, "would have potentially made the plant a useful agent to calm individuals who were to be included in the rituals," the researchers wrote in the study.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The new study confirms the ancient use of cannabis in funerals in Central Asia and extends the date back to 2,800 years ago, the researchers noted. Future work is planned but will focus on other aspects of ancient cannabis.

"We have already begun sequencing some of the plant samples," Caspari said. "This will help us learn more about the history of the domestication and spread of the crop soon."

Caspari, G., Sadykov, T., Formicheva, D., Blochin, J., Armbruster, D., Happel, O., Ryabogina, N., Boxleitner, K., Spengler, R. (2026). Direct evidence for psychoactive cannabis use 2800 years ago. Science. http://dx.doi.org/10.1126/science.aeg3800

She has received awards from the Society for American Archaeology and the American Anthropological Association for her science writing.

#6404. A man using a metal detector in Germany found the biggest stash of Roman silver coins from Emperor Hadrian ever discovered

A metal detectorist discovered 934 Roman silver coins near Cologne, Germany, uncovering the country's largest known hoard from Hadrian's reign.

Oliver Riedl had already dug up 15 Roman silver coins in a field near Wesseling, south of Cologne, when his metal detector kept signaling. He immediately notified the regional heritage office.

The excavation that followed recovered 934 Roman silver denarii, about 6.8 pounds (3.1 kilograms) of silver. It is the largest coin hoard from the reign of Emperor Hadrian ever found in Germany.

The LVR Office for Archaeological Heritage Management in the Rhineland (LVR-ABR) announced the find on September 22, 2026.

Riedl, an amateur metal detectorist, was searching the field with official permission.

“For me it was clear that something bigger was lying in the ground here,” Riedl said. “So I notified the office immediately.”

The LVR-ABR‘s branch in Nideggen responded immediately and excavated the site. To study the find more closely, archaeologists lifted it in a block of soil and X-rayed it at the LVR-LandesMuseum Bonn‘s restoration workshop.

Dr. Erich Claßen is the state archaeologist and head of the LVR-ABR.

“This makes it the largest coin hoard from this period in Germany, and worldwide it is the fifth largest,” Claßen explained.

The latest coin in the hoard was minted in AD 124 or 125. The archaeologists think the coins were buried in the second quarter of the second century, under Hadrian, who ruled from AD 117 to 138.

Most of the coins date to the Flavian emperors, who ruled from AD 69 to 96. Among them is a denarius of Domitian, the last emperor of that dynasty.

The oldest coin was struck in 148 BC, during the Roman Republic. It was more than 270 years old when it went into the ground.

The fortune was probably assembled around AD 100 and buried on purpose decades later.

In that period, the Rhine formed the frontier of the Roman province of Lower Germany. Its defenses, the Lower German Limes, ran about 250 miles (400 kilometers) from south of Bonn to the North Sea, according to UNESCO.

From the late first century BC, that frontier protected the Roman Empire for more than 450 years. Its remains include legionary fortresses, forts, watchtowers, roads and towns.

Dr. Rahel Otte, a research associate at the LVR-ABR, studied the coins.

“At that time, an ordinary soldier in the legion earned 300 denarii a year,” Otte noted.

About half of that pay was withheld for food and equipment. To save 934 denarii, a legionary would have had to set aside all of his available money for about six years, Otte calculated.

Who amassed this considerable fortune remains unclear. The owner may have lived on one of the Roman country estates in the surrounding area.

“We can of course only speculate about the motives, but very probably someone wanted to keep this money safe. After all, there were no banks back then,” Claßen observed.

Why the silver stayed in the ground is also unknown. The owner may have died without passing on what they knew about the coins.

The soil block also held fragments of a buried clay pot and remains of straw.

“The coins were probably originally buried in a pot padded with straw,” Otte explained.

Years of farming had destroyed the pot and scattered the coins through the topsoil.

“But in our investigations we were able to find and recover all of the coins,” Otte stressed.

“Mr. Riedl really behaved in an exemplary way,” Claßen remarked. “Thanks to his care, we were able to recover the hoard properly and completely,” he added.

Under the monument protection law of North Rhine-Westphalia, the hoard now belongs to the state. Because Riedl acted lawfully, the state ministry responsible for heritage will give him a reward.

Metal detecting in the Rhineland requires a permit from the heritage authorities and the landowner’s consent, whatever a person is searching for.

Applicants first attend an information session run by the LVR-ABR and mark the areas they want to search on a map. Detectors are allowed only on arable fields, not on meadows or in forests.

Simon Matzerath chairs the West and South German Association for Archaeological Research. About 300 archaeologists from across Germany saw the hoard at the association’s annual conference in Bonn.

“The private use of metal detectors can be an incredible support for science if everyone follows the rules, but unfortunately we also often have to deal with so-called illegal digs,” Matzerath said.

The hoard will go on public display for the first time at the LVR-LandesMuseum Bonn.

The information was obtained from the LVR Office for Archaeological Heritage Management in the Rhineland.

#6403. Archaeologists Found 120,000-Year-Old Human Footprints Where They Shouldn’t Be

They might just rewrite the story of human migration—as a tale of who failed, not who survived.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Between roughly 112,000 and 121,000 years ago, a handful of people walked along the muddy shore of a lake in what is now Saudi Arabia’s Nefud Desert. Elephants and camels had churned up the ground, and the humans left seven footprints among hundreds of animal tracks before sediment sealed the whole scene for eternity. When researchers described the site, called Alathar (Arabic for “the trace”), in a 2020 paper in Science Advances, we called the prints “the oldest-ever human footprints on the Arabian Peninsula” and marveled that they had survived at all. As the researchers noted, an experimental study of modern footprints in mud flats “found that fine details were lost within two days and prints were rendered unrecognizable within four.”

Six years later, the original interpretation still holds. “The age estimate remains about 120,000 years ago based on scientific dating,” Michael Petraglia, an archaeologist at Griffith University in Australia who studies human evolution and dispersal, tells Popular Mechanics. “The size and shape of the footprints are consistent with Homo sapiens.” What has changed is the record around them. Petraglia says sites dated since 2020 suggest that people entered Arabia when wetter weather filled the peninsula with lakes. During these “Green Arabia” periods, people could find drinking water in places that are now desert. When the water disappeared, some of those populations may have disappeared with it, possibly including the people who left the Alathar tracks.

Arabia went through this cycle many times. For a 2021 study in Nature, Huw Groucutt, Petraglia, and their colleagues dated ancient lake deposits in the Nefud that contained stone tools and animal fossils. They found that human ancestors moved into the Arabian interior at least five times between about 400,000 and 55,000 years ago, each time during a wetter spell, and each phase had its own style of stone tools. “This looks like different populations, and indeed species, moving into the area at different times,” says Groucutt, an archaeologist and senior lecturer at the University of Malta who studies human prehistory and environmental change. Once the rains stopped, he says, there probably wasn’t enough water for anyone to stay.

Even in the good years, people probably kept moving. Groucutt pictures groups traveling among scattered small lakes and other water sources in a landscape that was still highly seasonal, with very hot summers. Alathar fits that picture. The researchers found no stone tools or butchered bones at the site and concluded that the lake “was only briefly visited by people,” most likely for drinking water. For Petraglia, that brevity is what makes the tracks valuable. “Footprints capture a moment in time, illustrating that people walked along lakeshores at the same time as animals,” he says.

These walkers may have no living descendants

If the Alathar walkers were Homo sapiens, Groucutt thinks they belonged to a branch of humanity that didn’t make it. “The dominant view from genetics is that people living outside Africa today descend from people spreading into Asia around 50 to 80,000 years ago, so earlier people died out,” he says. By that reasoning, the footprints are “probably an example of an earlier, failed, migration.” That kind of failed migration is also known from other sites, including Skhul Cave on Mount Carmel, where fossils of early Homo sapiens were found. Reaching Arabia, then, came with no guarantee of surviving there. The people who left these tracks may have died out, and a much later migration brought the ancestors of most people living outside Africa today. Petraglia describes the same pattern of shifting fortunes: “Migrations were repeated movements, with groups expanding, contracting, and possibly disappearing from parts of the peninsula as conditions changed.”

As Arabia dried, Groucutt thinks, people may have retreated south, following the water into the wetter parts of the peninsula. Differences in stone tools suggest that these southern populations developed their own ways of doing things as they lost contact with people farther north. But the south eventually dried up too. Groucutt reads gaps in the archaeological record as a sign that the remaining groups became too small and isolated to make it through the worst dry spells. The same lakes that drew people into Arabia could leave them stranded, crowded around whatever water remained and with fewer and fewer places to go. The Alathar tracks date to a dry spell during the last interglacial, which puts their makers in exactly this kind of shrinking landscape.

The proof is hard to find in a hot desert

Settling the question will take evidence that a desert doesn’t give up easily. Groucutt would welcome hominin fossils, though he doubts they would be the “smoking gun” people sometimes imagine, since bones can be hard to date and hard to assign to a species. Ancient DNA could do more, but in low latitudes it “just doesn’t go that far back,” he says, because “hot places are bad for preservation.” Petraglia is hunting for something more specific. “A securely dated human fossil or a long, stratified sequence showing human occupations across both wet and dry periods would be transformative,” he says. Working with Saudi colleagues who help choose sites and reach them, his team is searching around former water sources for evidence of people who stayed as the climate changed.

Until that evidence turns up, the Alathar footprints remain one of the few direct records of these early travelers. If they left no descendants, the site’s name may best describe what survives of them: a trace.

#6402. Nov. 5, 2006: Mars Global Surveyor goes quiet

Designed to study Mars in a comprehensive way, examining its atmosphere, its interior, and its surface, the Mars Global Surveyor (MGS) launched Nov. 7, 1996. By Sept. 12, 1997, it would reach Mars and slip into orbit around the Red Planet. Over the next nine years, it revealed an evolving world of ongoing geological dynamism, analyzed the history of water on Mars, tracked the movements of ice at its poles, and analyzed its topography and weather. With nearly 200,000 photos captured, MGS supplied more images of Mars than all the missions before it – combined. It also helped NASA plan for future rover missions to the Red Planet.

MGS substantially exceeded its two-year mission, but on Nov. 2, 2006, the orbiter signaled to NASA that it was experiencing difficulties with its solar panels. Two days without communication followed. On Nov. 5, more signals were sent, and then MGS went silent. The mission officially ended on Nov. 14, with NASA concluding a battery failure had caused a computer error that closed out MGS’s tour.

Elisa Neckar is senior production editor of Astronomy magazine, and the editor of the Today in the History of Astronomy feature on Astronomy.com.

#6401. A virus found in one out of ten patients in China is carried by a tick species that is spreading across the US

Researchers in China identified a new tick-borne virus, ALTNV, linked to fever and more severe illness when combined with another virus.

Researchers in China found a newly identified tick-borne virus in 10.4 percent of 3,163 patients they tested. The virus, called Asian longhorned tick nairovirus (ALTNV), also turned up in ticks collected from 15 provinces.

Patients infected with ALTNV alone recovered. Among 38 patients also infected with the virus behind severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome (SFTS), seven died.

The tick species that carried ALTNV most often, the Asian longhorned tick, has spread across parts of the United States. The Chinese study tested only patients and ticks in China, so it does not show whether the virus is present in U.S. ticks.

The work was led by researchers at the State Key Laboratory of Pathogen and Biosecurity in Beijing, with Xiao-Ai Zhang as first author. They reported it in September 2026 in a letter titled “A Zoonotic Orthonairovirus from Febrile Patients in China.”

Their starting point was a gap in diagnosis. More than 30 percent of patients clinically diagnosed with SFTS test negative for Dabie bandavirus (DBV), the virus that causes the disease.

The team screened 3,163 patients with fever and a history of tick exposure. They looked for ALTNV genetic material or IgM antibodies, which the immune system makes early in an infection.

Among patients who had tested negative for DBV, 15.1 percent tested positive for ALTNV.

ALTNV belongs to the genus Orthonairovirus in the family Nairoviridae. Its proteins share less than 80 percent of their amino acids with other species in that genus.

The researchers described 56 patients with ALTNV alone. Fatigue affected 84 percent of them, and 80 percent had gastrointestinal symptoms.

Low platelet counts, known as thrombocytopenia, appeared in 38 percent. Raised levels of the liver enzymes called aminotransferases appeared in 36 percent.

All of these patients recovered without lasting effects.

In the 38 patients carrying both ALTNV and DBV, coinfection was linked to more severe illness. Respiratory symptoms affected 61 percent of them, compared with 38 percent of patients with DBV alone.

Kidney impairment affected 84 percent of the coinfected patients, compared with 66 percent. Seven of them, or 18.4 percent, died.

The two viruses circulate in the same areas and share a tick vector. The authors call for better tests to tell these tick-borne viruses apart where SFTS is common.

The team also tested 47,428 ticks gathered across 15 Chinese provinces. ALTNV genetic material turned up in 1.29 percent of them.

The Asian longhorned tick, Haemaphysalis longicornis, carried the virus most often, at 1.75 percent.

In laboratory experiments, the species passed ALTNV to mice.

Outside Asia, this tick can reduce production in dairy cattle by 25 percent in some regions of New Zealand and Australia, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) noted in 2018.

New Jersey was the first U.S. state to report the tick, on a sheep in August 2017, according to the CDC.

A single female can reproduce without mating. As a result, hundreds or thousands of ticks can build up on one animal or in one area.

Ben Beard, Ph.D., was then deputy director of the CDC’s Division of Vector-Borne Diseases.

“The full public health and agricultural impact of this tick discovery and spread is unknown,” Beard said in 2018.

By October 2025, the U.S. Department of Agriculture had documented the tick in 21 states, with Kansas the most recent.

There, it was found on a dog in Franklin County, according to the Kansas Department of Agriculture and the Kansas Department of Health and Environment (KDHE).

The ticks have been collected from New York south to Georgia and west to Missouri. They are not competent vectors of the bacterium behind Lyme disease, the USDA’s Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service (APHIS) states.

In cattle, the species can transmit Theileria orientalis Ikeda, a parasite responsible for bovine theileriosis. U.S. ticks passed it to cattle in the laboratory, and it has been detected in ticks collected in the field.

In 2025, the Connecticut Agricultural Experiment Station (CAES) reported the first evidence in the U.S. of a longhorned tick infected with Ehrlichia chaffeensis. This bacterium causes human monocytic ehrlichiosis.

Dr. Goudarz Molaei is a research scientist and medical entomologist at the CAES and an adjunct associate professor at the Yale School of Public Health.

“A rigorous program in mitigating risks should include expanded tick surveillance programs, strict measures to inspect animals, plants, and other imported materials at ports of entry, accurate and proper identification of exotic ticks and pathogens, effective eradication and prevention measures, and the ability to test exotic ticks for both native and nonnative pathogens,” Molaei said.

In 2019, an Asian longhorned tick in Virginia was found to be infected with Bourbon virus, the Kansas agencies noted.

The study was published in the journal New England Journal of Medicine.

#6400. Food contains thousands of overlooked chemicals. This physicist is mapping them

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

By Tina Hesman Saey, Mandana Tadayon and Anna Mattson

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Computational physicist Giulia Menichetti is looking for “dark matter” in our food. In addition to known macronutrients, vitamins and minerals, the things we eat contain a whole world of natural chemicals we have no idea about. And those chemicals may affect our health.

“They have the ability to interact, to bind to human proteins, to modulate our microbiome,” says Menichetti of Harvard Medical School. “We want to leverage this to talk more and more about the role of food and nutrition in human health.”

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Menichetti leads Foodome, a project to map our food’s full chemical complexity. Her team uses AI to mine scientific papers for every chemical compound that has ever been linked to a food. She singles out ones that haven’t been tracked by epidemiological studies — the “nutritional dark matter.” So far, her team has cataloged about 140,000 molecules.

When one hears about chemicals in food, they might initially think of artificial additives. Her team addresses those, but she’s also interested in naturally occurring chemicals. Take garlic, for example. Foodome has cataloged almost 7,000 different molecules in raw garlic alone. Some of these compounds have been investigated for health effects, but some are entirely new.

Foodome is still mining the scientific literature for these molecules and building out databases. Eventually, Menichetti would like AI to be able to predict how all these food molecules interact together and in the human body.

“There is a legacy of chemical complexity that comes from organisms that are all around us,” she says. “Food is part of that. It is actually our way to interact with our environment. We need to study it better.”

#6399. Arctic winter sea ice is being overestimated by climate models

Ancient algae preserved in Arctic seafloor mud suggest climate models overestimate winter sea ice, pointing to less ice in the decades ahead.

Arctic sea ice loss usually gets told as a summer story, counting down to the first ice-free summer. Yet climate models disagree most about winter ice.

Together, they simulate nearly a million square kilometers too much March ice – about 386,000 square miles, close to Texas and New Mexico combined.

A new study used traces of algae buried in 6,000-year-old seafloor mud to grade 27 climate models.

The corrected projections show about a million square kilometers less winter ice than before, in every coming decade and under every emissions path.

Crystal Fu of the Scott Polar Research Institute led the work with Matthew Osman at the University of Cambridge, and Marco Aquino-López of CIMAT in Mexico.

The numbers are model projections re-weighted by evidence from the past, not new measurements of today’s ice.

In an interview with Earth.com, Fu compared the missing ice to a country.

“A million square kilometers is a huge amount of sea ice to go missing – that’s roughly 4x the size of the UK,” she said.

Winter ice matters because it’s a lid. Open water in the Arctic winter releases heat and moisture into the air.

That release has been linked to colder winters and heavier snow across Eurasia and North America. It has also been linked to shifts in storm tracks and extreme rain in the Mediterranean.

In March 2025, the Arctic’s annual maximum was the lowest on record.

Yet the models’ biggest disagreements and biggest errors fall in March, not September, and most of the testing has gone into summer.

Fu’s team wanted an exam the models couldn’t have been tuned to pass.

Between 5,000 and 7,000 years ago, a wobble in Earth’s orbit gave the Arctic more summer sunlight. The extra sunlight warmed the region and reduced its sea ice.

The extra heating was comparable in size to what future greenhouse gases are expected to add.

Algae that live inside sea ice leave a distinctive molecule behind, and algae that live in open water leave others.

The ratio of the two in a layer of seafloor mud records how much ice covered that spot. Fu’s team compiled 46 such records from sediment cores across the Arctic, the largest set of its kind.

“What really struck us was just how much information is preserved in tiny traces of algae buried in mud across the Arctic seafloor,” she said.

The team converted the 27 models’ ancient Arctic ice simulations into molecular ratios for comparison with the sediment records.

That let the models be compared with the cores on equal terms. Each model got a weight based on how well it matched, with related models sharing credit.

Weighted that way, the models’ average March ice for the recent past matched the satellite record. The bias of nearly a million square kilometers disappeared.

The range of disagreement shrank by about 6.3 million square kilometers (2.4 million square miles), or 85%. The remaining range was comparable to ordinary year-to-year swings.

The ancient records turned out to be the sharper test. Weighting by the mid-Holocene alone corrected the models more than weighting by 1950 to 1999 did.

The same weights applied to the models’ futures lowered the projected March ice by 4% to 6% for the 2090s, under low, middle and high emissions alike.

Fu noted that the cause of the ancient warming doesn’t change the lesson.

“It doesn’t matter if the warming is natural variation or caused by human activity: if it warms, sea ice is going to melt,” she said.

In the Barents Sea, the Greenland Sea and the Labrador Sea, the weighted maps put the winter ice edge farther north than the unweighted models do.

The shift reaches 5.5 degrees of latitude, about 380 miles (610 kilometers).

Asked by Earth.com where winter sea ice was most vulnerable, Osman pointed to the Barents Sea.

“The Barents Sea, north of Norway and Russia, is probably the place to watch most closely right now,” he said.

The Greenland and Labrador Seas, farther south, are the next places to watch, Osman said.

More ice loss there could affect marine wildlife, shipping, the Atlantic’s circulation and the stability of the Greenland ice sheet, he added.

The projections assume the ice will keep responding to warming the way it did 6,000 years ago and in the 20th century.

The weighting improved the combined projection, but it did not explain why individual models produced different amounts of ice.

Links between winter ice and weather farther south also need confirming. Under high emissions, the weighted models suggest late-winter snowfall over southeast Greenland may be underestimated by more than 30%.

Winter and spring rain in the Mediterranean may be twice what the standard models project, which would raise flood risk there.

Fu said exactly how the Arctic changes will affect Europe’s winters is still being studied.

Earlier work tied a weaker polar vortex and cold snaps to a bare Barents Sea, but those links still need verifying.

Osman said the bigger payoff lies beyond sea ice.

Decades of records of ancient climates can be paired with the right mathematics to test climate models and narrow their projections, he said.

The snowfall and rainfall estimates suggest that ancient climate records could help refine projections beyond sea ice, although those results still need further testing.

The full study was published in the journal Nature Geoscience.

#6398. Some Evidence Suggests Amelia Earhart Was Eaten by Crabs. The Twist: She Could Have Eaten Them to Survive.

The crustaceans of Nikumaroro may have been the aviator’s best source of food—and the reason almost nothing remained of her.

If there’s one thing we love at Popular Mechanics, it’s a scientific hypothesis with enough meat on its bones to nourish a deeply-rooted psychological obsession. So it’s not surprising that one of our favorite stories focuses on the question of what might have happened if Amelia Earhart and her navigator, Fred Noonan, were marooned on Nikumaroro (then known as Gardner Island), following the disappearance of their plane over the Pacific Ocean in 1937.

In particular, one prominent, longstanding theory posits that the famous aviator indeed was stranded on the island, and that she eventually perished there. But her body was never found because her remains were subsequently eaten—and her bones scattered—by the giant coconut crabs (Birgus latro) that live in great profusion on the atoll.

But that raises a question. If you’re stranded on a remote Pacific island that’s jam-packed full of thousands of crabs, wouldn’t you try to eat them, instead of the other way around? Which brings us to another question.

Well, the answer to that one is pretty simple: oh yeah, absolutely! Coconut crabs are generally quite edible—in fact, they’re considered a highly prized delicacy in many Pacific island cultures. But eating them comes with significant safety warnings.

So if you’re considering eating a coconut crab, here’s what you need to know before going through with it.

First, they’re protected by conservation laws in most places where they’re found, so don’t poach them! But the flavor is fantastic. The meat is famously sweet, and it’s often compared to a very dense, firm lobster. The fat sac (the hepatopancreas) in the crab’s abdomen is particularly prized: It’s often said to have a rich, nutty, coconut-like flavor. But that delicious coconut flavor isn’t a genetic trait—it comes from their diet. Coconut crabs are opportunistic scavengers, and the fat sac functions as a storage organ. If a wild crab has recently been surviving on a diet of, say, dead birds, rotting wood, and other crabs’ molted shells, its fat will still be rich, buttery, and oily, but it won’t taste like coconut.

That’s one of the reasons why people typically capture these crabs alive, keep them penned up, and feed them an exclusive diet of coconuts for several weeks before cooking them up. This process infuses the fat sac with that highly prized, sweet coconut flavor everybody talks about.

But even more importantly, deliberately feeding the crabs a special diet flushes out any toxins that might ordinarily have built up in their flesh. The poisonous sea mango tree (Cerbera manghas) grows in exactly the same places where you’re most likely to find coconut crabs.

Both species share the same geographic distribution from the western Indian Ocean far into the South Pacific, including Kiribati, where Earhart was theoretically marooned. Coconut crabs spend most of their adult lives foraging in the same coastal scrub forests and beach thickets where sea mangoes grow. Because this ecological overlap is so common across thousands of miles of ocean, the cultural practice of penning and “purging” coconut crabs on a safe diet before eating them evolved independently across multiple different island nations. Eating a toxic crab can cause severe cardiac problems, and even death.

The answer is most definitely yes, because without sea mango trees, the main source of potential toxicity is eliminated. Nikumaroro is in a very remote area of Kiribati called the Phoenix Islands, a chain of coral atolls that often experience severe, multi-year droughts. It’s simply too dry there for the sea mango, which loves moisture, to survive. Instead, the crabs on Nikumaroro get their food from three sources: coconut palms, which were left over from failed British colonization and plantation attempts in the late 19th and early 20th centuries; Pisonia grandis (Buka) trees that can grow up to 50 feet tall, providing rotting wood and organic matter; and native coastal scrub plants like Cordia (kanawa trees), Scaevola, and Pandanus, which provide fleshy fruits for the crabs to eat.

In short, the giant crabs on Nikumaroro enjoy a diet that undoubtedly makes them beautifully flavorful when eaten. So Nikumaroro’s giant crabs could certainly have provided an abundant, safe—and delicious—source of food for Earhart and Noonan.

However, surviving on coconut crabs would have presented them with severe practical challenges. Here’s how their coconut crab situation probably would have played out.

First, there’s the challenge of catching the crabs. Coconut crabs are enormous, heavily armored, and nocturnal. More importantly, their pincers have a crushing force comparable to the bite of a lion or a bear. Trying to catch, subdue, and kill a coconut crab without proper weapons or traps, especially while weakened by dehydration or starvation, would have been extremely difficult and dangerous. A pinch could easily break a finger or cause a severe, infection-prone laceration. Plus you really have to watch your back at night when you’re trying to sleep, so you’d probably be hunting them while very tired.

Second, you need to cook the crabs. Raw crab carries a high risk of bacterial infection and parasites, so the castaways would have been obliged to build fires to cook them. And as it turns out, there’s circumstantial evidence that they might have done just that. In the early 2000s, researchers from TIGHAR (The International Group for Historic Aircraft Recovery) performed excavations on Nikumaroro at a location called the “Seven Site.” They discovered the remains of small campfires there, and in the ashes, they found the cooked bones of birds, fish, and turtles. So there’s little doubt that someone did successfully cook local wildlife there at some point in time.

The final issue is that the most famous association between Amelia Earhart and the Nikumaroro coconut crabs isn’t that she ate them, but that they likely ate her.

TIGHAR's leading hypothesis for why Earhart's complete skeleton was never found is that after she died of starvation or exposure, the island’s massive population of coconut crabs scavenged her remains. The crabs are known to swarm dead bodies and carry bones deep into their underground burrows or into the coral rubble. The TIGHAR researchers argued that this aligns with the fact that only 13 human bones were discovered on the island in 1940, instead of a full skeleton. (The bones, alas, were subsequently lost).

So while Nikumaroro’s giant crabs could unquestionably have provided safe, high-calorie meals for a castaway with a fire and a club or spear made from local wood, the crabs were ultimately much better equipped to survive the island than Earhart was. The most likely winner of a theoretical Earhart vs. coconut crabs survival competition was, with little doubt, the crabs.

Shawn Gorman is Deputy Editor of News for Popular Mechanics. Before joining Pop Mech, he specialized in academic reading for educational testing. His diverse academic background also includes time spent as a lecturer and librarian at institutions such as the University of Kentucky, SUNY, and Harvard University. Shawn holds a Ph.D. in Modern Foreign Languages and Literatures from Boston University, an M.A. from The Ohio State University, and a B.A. in History from the University of Oregon. His favorite subjects to explore include computer science, physics, math, and biology. He lives on a medium-sized cat ranch in Easton, Pennsylvania, with his wife and two daughters.

#6397. Curiosity captures a martian dawn

The morning Sun casts a hazy glow over Mars’ Mount Sharp, lighting up distant wind-carved rock formations known as yardangs. This scene is cropped from a six-image panorama captured by the Mastcam on NASA’s Curiosity rover at 8:30 a.m. local time on Aug. 11, 2026, the mission’s 4,982nd sol (martian day). Mount Sharp, formally Aeolis Mons, stands 3.4 miles (5.5 km) tall at the center of Mars’ 96-mile-wide (154 km) Gale Crater. Since 2014, Curiosity has climbed roughly 0.6 mile (1 km) up its stratified slopes, reading each new layer like a chapter of martian geology.

The mountain’s lowest, oldest layers likely formed from sediment deposited by lakes and streams that have long since vanished. This photo is the most detailed view to date of the much younger yardang layer. Of particular interest is the fact that the color and orientation of the yardangs don’t match the surrounding material. Scientists think these features could have been built up from volcanic ash that settled after a nearby eruption, and was then carved away by the wind. Curiosity should reach the yardangs’ base in 2027, where its instruments will help uncover how the layer formed.

Brooks Mendenhall is a staff writer at Astronomy, based in Chattanooga, Tennessee, fueled by an unending curiosity about the universe. A former classroom teacher, he has a knack for breaking down complex concepts for a wide audience.

#6396. Taking cold showers is good for your health and also the environment, according to a new study

In trials with 719 adults, people who took cold showers at least 70% of the time reported 26% fewer illness days and 31% fewer days off work.

Giving up a warm shower sounds simple until it’s time to step under the water. In a Swiss study, plenty of people signed up to try it, but many stopped early.

Those who kept going reported fewer days feeling sick and fewer days off work over 12 weeks. Their showers also came with a small estimated drop in carbon emissions, although extra encouragement did little to help people keep the habit.

Lena Glaser, a psychologist and psychotherapist at the University of Basel, knows from her clinical work how hard people can find change.

For her doctoral dissertation in the Faculty of Psychology, she studied whether a habit is easier to keep when people can fit it into their day and get something out of it.

“We need a more empathetic approach if we want people to change their behavior,” Glaser said.

Cars, food, and recycling usually come up when people discuss their climate impact, Glaser said. Yet European and U.S. energy agencies put water heating at about 15% to 25% of the energy used in homes in wealthy countries, a use that gets much less attention.

“Taking a cold shower isn’t exactly pleasant, but it’s a small change to make,” she said. “After all, we shower anyway.”

Ice baths and cold plunges have made cold water a popular health topic, but the evidence remains limited. A 2025 review found 11 trials in healthy adults, only one of which tested showers.

That Dutch trial, published in PLOS ONE, asked people to finish a warm shower with up to 90 seconds of cold water. They reported 29% less sick leave than a comparison group, but no fewer days of illness.

Glaser brought together results from three trials she and her colleagues ran between late 2019 and mid-2024. In all, 719 adults took part.

To join, people had to speak German, be healthy, and be between 18 and 65, with no cold-shower habit already in place. Pregnancy ruled people out, as did conditions such as severe asthma or severe heart disease that cold might make worse.

The instructions were straightforward: turn the tap to its coldest setting and stay under the water for two to five minutes. Once a month, volunteers filled out surveys about days with cold, flu, or other symptoms and days they’d missed work because of illness.

Two of the trials asked everyone to try cold showers, which left no randomly chosen comparison group. So for this analysis, Glaser’s team put people who showered cold at least 70% of the time in one group: 459 volunteers, or about three in five.

Before the trials, volunteers reported about three days of illness and one day off work each month. Over 12 weeks, regular cold showerers reported 26% fewer illness days and 31% fewer days off work than everyone else.

The difference was modest for any one person. The team’s calculation put it at one fewer day of illness among 16 people taking cold showers for a week.

The gap stayed similar from the first month to the last. Cold showerers also scored slightly higher on a standard well-being questionnaire, but their physical well-being scores did not differ reliably.

Skin health ratings were much the same in both groups, with complaints including dry or itchy skin and a few slips in the shower. No one reported a serious problem.

The team looked more closely at quitting among 586 people in the two later trials. Only 217, or 37%, kept taking cold showers for all 12 weeks.

People were most likely to quit in the early weeks. They became less likely to stop as time went on.

“That suggests people gradually get used to it,” Glaser said.

Women were more likely to stop than men. About 32% of women reached the end, compared with about 47% of men.

In the second trial, some volunteers watched short monthly videos giving them reasons to continue, from personal benefits to climate action. None of the four versions helped people last longer than basic instructions did.

Weekly emails didn’t help either. Of the 71 volunteers who received five emails with confidence-building texts and videos in the third trial, just 10 finished the 12 weeks, the lowest completion rate of any group.

The researchers suggested that weekly messages may have made a personal choice feel like an obligation. That could weaken people’s motivation instead of helping.

“When people see a personal benefit from changing their behavior and don’t feel that they’re giving something up or missing out, they’re more motivated to stick with it,” Glaser said.

The energy calculation started with a five-minute shower using 12 gallons (45 liters) of water. Taking that water from a warm 104°F (40°C) down to 59°F (15°C) would save about 1.3 kilowatt-hours.

That worked out to an estimated 33 pounds (15 kilograms) less carbon dioxide per volunteer over the study. Using the team’s comparison, that’s about as much as a car releases on a 62-mile (100-kilometer) trip.

For someone keeping up the habit for a year, the team estimated savings of about 143 pounds (65 kilograms). That equals about 2% to 3% of an average person’s annual household carbon footprint in wealthy European countries.

The researchers didn’t put meters in people’s homes. They assumed a daily five-minute shower and used average emissions figures for German and Swiss energy, so the savings in a particular home would depend on its water heater.

The volunteers averaged about 26 years old, and roughly two-thirds were women. They also chose to take on the challenge, so they were probably more motivated than most people.

Everyone knew which group they were in, and the researchers relied on survey answers for both shower habits and illness. No medical tests confirmed whether people were sick.

There’s another complication: people who managed to keep showering cold might have differed from those who gave up. Comparing those groups cannot tell us whether cold water itself made anyone less likely to get sick.

The researchers don’t know who carried on after the 12 weeks ended. Nor did they track whether volunteers went on to use more energy elsewhere because they felt they’d already done their bit, a possibility people have also raised about recycling.

For Glaser, keeping a habit needn’t mean doing it exactly the same way every day.

“The water doesn’t have to be equally cold every day,” Glaser said. “We don’t feel equally brave every day, and that’s okay.”

One question for future studies, Glaser suggested, is whether this small change could make bigger ones feel more manageable. Would people who get used to cold showers become more willing to change what they eat or fly less?

The full study is available as a doctoral dissertation through edoc, the University of Basel’s open-access repository.

New research shows that a powerful 2021 marsquake emanating from Valles Marineris — the largest canyon in the solar system — was triggered by unexpected movement in a fault line deep below the gigantic structure, revealing that tectonic activity can still occur on geologically "dead" worlds.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Mars' supersize Valles Marineris — the largest known canyon in the solar system — is still tectonically active even though the Red Planet is geologically "dead," new research on a previously record-breaking marsquake reveals.

On Aug. 25, 2021, NASA's InSight lander, which touched down on the Red Planet in 2018, detected a powerful marsquake, designated S0976a. The Martian equivalent of an earthquake reached magnitude 4.2, which, at the time, was the most powerful quake that InSight or any other Mars lander had ever seen. (Since then, a 4.7 magnitude marsquake in May 2022 knocked it off the top spot, but S0976a remains second on this list.)

Unlike most marsquakes, which have been minor tremors triggered by meteorite impacts near InSight, S0976a was a deep rumble that originated from the opposite side of Mars as the robotic seismologist, in the western half of Valles Marineris.

In the new study, published Oct. 15 in the journal Nature Communications, researchers reanalyzed the seismic wave data of S0976a and found that the quake originated from within a fault line running below the enormous canyon. The most likely explanation, they argue, is that there was tectonic movement in this hidden crustal crack.

"Valles Marineris is one of the most spectacular geological structures anywhere in the solar system, but until now we didn't know for certain that its faults are still active," study first author Jung-Hun Song, a researcher in the Department of Earth Science and Engineering at Imperial College London, said in a statement. "What we see is that this is not just a 'dead' fossil landscape, as faults deep beneath the canyon can still slip and generate marsquakes, long after the geological processes that originally formed them have ceased."

S0976a is the second-largest marsquake ever detected by NASA's InSight lander, shown here in a NASA clean room on April 30, 2015.

Valles Marineris is an enormous set of interconnected gullies and ravines stretching up to 2,500 miles (4,000 kilometers) in length, or roughly 10 times longer than the Grand Canyon. It is also up to 20 times wider and five times deeper, meaning that if you found yourself stranded at the bottom, it could take you a couple of months to climb out again.

The enormous chasm — named after the Mariner 9 spacecraft, which helped discover it in 1971 — is clearly visible from space, like a giant scar carved into the Red Planet's face. From orbit, you would also see the nearby Tharsis region, which is home to Mars' giant volcanoes, including Olympus Mons, which is at least three times taller than Mount Everest.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

These imposing structures are proof that Mars was once geologically active, perhaps even more so than Earth. However, scientists think the Red Planet's surface has remained relatively unchanged for nearly 3 billion years, according to the European Space Agency.

Valles Marineris is almost as long as the continental U.S. is wide. (In this photo, captured by NASA's Mars Odyssey orbiter, an optical illusion known as relief inversion may make the canyon appear as if it is raised above the surface, which it is not.)

The reason for this is twofold. First, Mars is smaller than Earth, so its core and mantle have cooled much faster than our planet's and are, therefore, less dynamic. Second, Mars has no tectonic plates. Instead of giant patches of crust butting against each other, the Red Planet's outermost layer is almost completely intact and acts like a giant lid over its cooling molten innards. (Research published earlier this week throws the "dead" theory into question, hinting that magma may still lurk below dormant Martian volcanoes).

Despite this, Mars still has fault lines. But rather than being a boundary between tectonic plates, these lines are more like giant cracks in its crust, some of which are visible at the surface.

In the new study, researchers discovered proof of what they call a slip-strike marsquake, where "blocks of crust move horizontally past one another along a steep, deeply rooted fault," the team said. They believe this occurred somewhere between 12 and 25 miles (20 to 40 km) below Valles Marineris.

The researchers also simulated several other potential causes of the marsquake, including a major asteroid strike or a landslide within the canyon, but nothing else could explain the patterns they saw.

Using seismic wave data captured by InSight, researchers were able to pinpoint the epicenter of the S0976a masquake (represented as a yellow star near the top of this map).

"What makes the result compelling is that several completely different types of evidence point in the same direction," Song said.

The finding also raises hopes that similar tectonic activity could one day be detected on other worlds across the solar system.

"Our study opens up exciting possibilities for discovering ongoing seismic activity on other planetary bodies that we might otherwise consider geologically inactive," Song said.

The discovery highlights the importance of detecting and studying marsquakes, which were only officially discovered in 2019, thanks to InSight. (Scientists have since uncovered older marsquakes, using data collected by the Viking landers in the late 1970s.)

InSight sent back a final selfie to Earth on Dec. 19, 2022, showing a heavy coating of Martian dust on its solar panels. Its mission was officially ended two days later.

"S0976a has turned out to be an extraordinary event," study co-author Doyeon Kim, head of Imperial College London's Terrestrial and Planetary Seismology Lab, said in the statement. "Its waves traveled through the core and helped us investigate the deepest part of Mars, and now they are telling us what happened at the source itself. From a single marsquake, we can learn both about the center of the planet and about an active fault beneath one of its most remarkable landscapes."

Scientists have similarly used marsquake vibrations from InSight to map out Mars' interior, leading to several intriguing subsurface discoveries, including dozens of blobs left over from ancient protoplanets, the hidden cause of the planet's uneven hemispheres, a potentially active "mantle plume" and a gigantic underground water reservoir containing enough liquid to cover Mars with a mile-deep (1.6 km) ocean.

Unfortunately, in December 2022, InSight quite literally bit the dust: A thick covering of Martian powder blocked its solar panels, preventing the lander from returning signals to Earth and thus ending its mission.

This means we currently have no way of detecting new marsquakes. However, the new study proves that the lander's archived data can still lead to exciting discoveries.

Song, J., Kim, D., Kolawole, F., Davis, J. M., Parry, R., & Maguire, R. (2026). Active crustal straining and fault reactivation at Valles Marineris. Nature Communications, 17(1). https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-78193-6

#6394. Pumping hydrogen in and out of a deep fault may steady it rather than shake it loose

Computer models of a natural hydrogen deposit in Albania suggest that pumping hydrogen in and out each year could leave its fault steadier.

Pumping gas in and out of a fault deep underground sounds like a good way to make it slip. For a natural hydrogen deposit under a mine in Albania, a new modeling study suggests the opposite.

With the right injection depth, each year of filling and emptying left the fault less likely to slip than the year before.

That points to a new job for hydrogen pockets too small to be worth mining. They could become storage sites for hydrogen made somewhere else.

Lei Hou, an associate professor at the China-UK Low Carbon College of Shanghai Jiao Tong University, designed the study with his colleague Zhengxin Zhang. Fengshou Zhang of Tongji University and Derek Elsworth of Penn State were among the co-authors.

Everything they report comes from computer simulations – no hydrogen has been pumped into this fault yet.

An energy system that runs partly on hydrogen needs somewhere to keep huge amounts of it for months at a time. Tanks at the surface can’t do that at scale, so the gas has to go underground.

The usual candidates are caverns cut into thick salt, porous rock soaked with salty water, and old oil and gas fields. None of them, the authors wrote, comes with direct proof that it can store hydrogen in particular.

A natural hydrogen deposit does. If the gas has built up there over geological time, the rock has already shown it can keep hydrogen in.

Many such deposits are too weak to sell. Their natural flow typically falls at least ten times short of what commercial production needs, and the authors expect most future finds of natural hydrogen to fall short too.

Hundreds of these sites are already on record worldwide, including a mine in northern Ontario, and the list keeps growing.

The deposit the team modeled lies under the Bulqizë chromite mine. In 2024, other researchers reported in Science that the mine releases at least 220 tons (200 metric tons) of hydrogen a year, one of the largest natural flows ever recorded.

Gas sampled there is 84 percent hydrogen. The gas collects in a fault zone inside slabs of ancient ocean crust. The fault tilts at 80 degrees, almost straight down, and reaches as deep as about 3 miles (5 km). Temperatures along it run from about 104°F to 320°F (40°C to 160°C).

That heat helps. The main microbial routes that consume hydrogen underground work best below about 104°F (40°C), and the methane in the mine’s gas appears to come from rock chemistry rather than microbes.

Other teams have looked for large deposits beneath mountain ranges. Bulqizë is one of the best-studied deposits, and its steep, deep fault makes it one of the hardest places to store hydrogen safely.

Stored hydrogen can disappear in three ways. It can dissolve into underground water, microbes can consume it, or it can react with carbon in the rock to make methane.

The team gave each one generous assumptions, so real losses should be smaller. In the simulations, about 1 percent of the stored gas dissolved into water, and most of it came back out when the gas was pumped up again.

The reaction with carbon took less than 0.3 percent, and microbes took even less.

Added together, the losses stayed under 2 percent. That fits the deposit’s own history. It holds an estimated 5,500 to 55,000 tons (5,000 to 50,000 metric tons) of hydrogen and has kept releasing gas with no sign of running dry.

Underground oil and gas work has been linked to earthquakes before, so the team tested where along the fault to inject. They ran 72 combinations of depth, pumping rate, and how easily gas moves through the rock.

In the model, injecting near the top, where the fault meets the rock layer sealing it, pushed the fault toward slipping every time. Shallow and middle depths were safe only at the slowest rate, which stored too little. The very bottom caused trouble too, because gas piled up in the tight rock there.

Injecting at about 14,500 feet (4,400 meters) worked best. Under the best plans, the team estimates the fault could hold roughly 12 to 17 billion cubic feet (350 to 480 million cubic meters) of gas, depending on the rock.

That’s about as much as the fault held naturally, and in some setups more.

The team then ran ten simulated years. Hydrogen went in from April to September and came out from October to March, at about 26 million cubic feet (750,000 cubic meters) a day.

That pace held for the full decade. And the fault’s slip risk during each filling season fell further every year, because the moving gas evened out the pressure inside it.

In an interview with Earth.com, Hou said the team had started from the opposite worry, since any engineering in a fault zone calls for caution. “What surprised us was that the cycling itself helped.”

“This stabilizing effect is not automatic – it depends on choosing the right injection depth,” Hou added.

Some processes are missing from the model. It doesn’t capture how shifting stress changes the rock’s ability to pass gas, and its grid may miss fine detail near the wells.

It also leaves out rock fatigue from repeated pressure swings, which could change the fault’s behavior beyond ten years.

Hou was asked when a site like this could store hydrogen commercially. “I cannot give you a date, and I would be cautious of anyone who does,” he told Earth.com.

Field trials and engineering costs will set the timeline, he said. The appeal, in his view, is economic. An explored deposit too weak to develop currently leaves its operator two choices: suspend the project or abandon it. Storage would add a third.

What the fault would do after a decade of cycling remains an open question. Until hydrogen is pumped into a real fault in a field trial, the steadying effect exists only in simulations.

The full study was published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

#6393. ALS Stole His Voice—Then, a ‘Digital Twin’ Read His Thoughts And Started Speaking for Him

This technology could restore the art of conversation for people with paralysis, but questions remain about who is really in control.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:

Did Walter want coffee? His virtual avatar responded, but it gave an unexpected answer. Instead of nodding or signaling yes with a thumbs-up, it waved goodbye. The mistake was funny, but it illustrated a serious problem: When technology communicates on someone’s behalf, an incorrect gesture can change the meaning of an entire exchange.

Walter, who has amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, or ALS, knows how much can be lost when communication becomes difficult. He went from slightly slurred speech to being unintelligible within approximately six months. He eventually relied on emails, text-to-speech applications, and telephone relay services. ALS is a progressive neurological disease that damages the nerve cells responsible for voluntary muscle movement, gradually affecting a person’s ability to speak, swallow, move, and breathe. Although the disease weakens muscles, it does not necessarily impair thinking or understanding.

“Somehow you try to keep a communication going while compromising to focus on the most essential content,” Walter says. “That doesn’t leave space for emotions and gestures at all.”

Determined to find a more efficient way to communicate, Walter began researching brain-computer interfaces. After attending an ALS Association webinar about emerging technologies, he discovered that neurosurgeon Edward Chang, MD, at the University of California, San Francisco, was leading a study that could potentially change lives. He contacted the research team himself, undeterred by the prospect of the invasive implant it would require. With ALS shortening his life expectancy, he also saw participation as an opportunity to advance technology that might benefit future patients, even if he never lived to use a commercial version.

The team began working with Walter on the virtual avatar in early summer 2025, gradually training the system to recognize his attempted speech and movements separately before combining them. “Every step and progress was fascinating and quite unbelievable at the same time,” he recalls. But the defining moment came when the avatar successfully decoded his speech and gestures together. “What a great milestone!” he says.

The research team’s brain-computer interface (BCI) decodes attempted speech and gestures simultaneously through a single implant, translating those signals into words and movements performed by a personalized virtual avatar. Their study, published in Nature Neuroscience, offers a glimpse of technology that could eventually restore something beyond words: the expressive dimensions of human conversation.

The process of getting your own virtual avatar started with electrocorticography (ECoG), which records electrical activity from electrodes positioned over the brain’s surface. The researchers’ implant covered a broad region of the sensorimotor cortex, which is involved in controlling speech and movement. Different areas are more strongly associated with different body movements, providing clues that machine-learning models can use to distinguish attempted speech from gestures.

But the researchers encountered an unexpected complication.

“What surprised us was that models trained on speech and gestures separately didn’t work as well when participants attempted both at the same time,” Samantha Brosler, a UCSF researcher and first co-author of the study, says.

The problem involved overlapping neural activity. Some brain regions respond during both speech and gesture attempts, and their activity patterns can change when those actions occur together.

Jennifer Collinger, PhD, a neuroprosthetics researcher at the University of Pittsburgh who was not involved in the research, describes this as context-dependent neural activity. “The neural activity associated with a particular movement, such as waving, may be different depending on whether or not you are speaking at the same time,” she explains.

To address this, the UCSF team, led by neurosurgeon Edward Chang, MD, trained two parallel decoding models using recordings of participants attempting speech and gestures separately and together. A participant attempting to say “hello” while waving, for example, supplied neural activity that could train one model to recognize the phrase and another to recognize the movement. The combined training improved decoding performance.

Encouragingly, the models could recognize some speech-and-gesture combinations they had not encountered during training. That matters because teaching a system every possible combination of human words and movements would be impractical.

The study involved three participants with paralysis, although the main simultaneous speech-and-gesture experiments involved two. For a participant with ALS, the researchers tested 10 predefined phrases and 10 gestures. For one participant, the system recognized 10 conversational phrases, including “hello,” “thank you,” “nice to meet you,” and “how’s it going?,” alongside 10 gestures such as waving, nodding, shrugging, pointing, and shaking hands. The avatar could combine the two, allowing someone to say “hello” while waving or “nice to meet you” while extending a hand. Researchers tested all 100 possible phrase-and-gesture pairings, including combinations that would rarely occur in ordinary conversation, to assess how reliably the system could decode both actions together. During real-time testing, speech decoding reached 70 percent accuracy, and gesture decoding reached 66 percent. Offline testing for participants with paralysis following a brainstem stroke also produced valuable results.

Collinger considers the findings encouraging but emphasizes their experimental boundaries, in part because this study was limited to a finite set of speech and gesture actions. The system wasn’t generating spontaneous conversation. It recognized predefined phrases, displayed decoded speech as text, and triggered corresponding avatar animations when gestures were detected.

That distinction raises questions about user control. Walter’s accidental goodbye was amusing, but an incorrect gesture in another situation could misrepresent someone’s intentions. User feedback is essential to ensuring the technology communicates what someone actually intends, Collinger says.

Future versions could allow users to confirm or correct decoded outputs, potentially through eye tracking, Brosler says.

The system currently relies on a wired connection to external computers. An everyday user would need an overhaul that allows true freedom: wireless transmission, portability, and reduced communication delays. It must overcome multiple engineering challenges, Brosler says, such as miniaturizing parts, attaining reliable neural recordings, lowering power consumption, and reducing heat generation.

Walter has his own priorities: the human dimension of the technology’s development. “It’s a two-sided learning curve for the avatar and the patient,” he explains.

An ideal solution would decode a user’s neural cues, he says, adding that wireless mobility and less invasive technology could make such systems more attractive to users.

During one successful experimental dialogue, the system decoded Walter’s attempted speech and gestures together without error. He remembers being overwhelmed. “I was extremely moved by the avatar’s response to my ‘thoughts,’ I couldn’t help laughing uncontrollably with pure joy.”

Even with its limitations, Walter describes the personalized avatar as a digital twin whose movements reflect his intentions and personality.

For Collinger, experiences like Walter’s demonstrate why accuracy alone cannot define success. “Restoring the ability to communicate is not just measured in words per minute,” she says. Independence, relationships, community participation, and personal expression matter, too.

The UCSF experiment has not yet restored unrestricted, natural conversation. But it suggests that the future of brain-computer interfaces may depend on understanding communication as more than the transmission of words—and giving people greater control over everything those words cannot express.

Taayoo is an award-winning writer based in New York City. She regularly covers health topics, primarily inequity in healthcare and issues in aging. #6391. Earwax’s surprisingly slippery but sticky properties deters insects

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Earwax is anything but waxy and may help protect the ear against insect intrusions

This fire ant is struggling to walk on a clump of earwax, a substance that experts think may exist in part to help keep our ears free of insects.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

There are few things more annoying than having a bug fly into your ear. But the body is prepared to fend off these insect invasions, says David Hu, a bioengineer at Georgia Tech.

The goop inside our ears may act as a natural insect repellent, Hu’s team reports 28 October in Soft Matter. What we call earwax is not really waxy at all. Instead, the brownish substance absorbs water, a property that might help it regulate moisture in the ear and keep bugs out, the new analysis shows. “[This] familiar biological material may represent a sophisticated physical defense against small arthropods,” says Stanislav Gorb, a functional morphologist at the University of Kiel in Germany, who was not involved with the work.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Researchers have not studied earwax as much as other body fluids, such as snot, spit or even pee. “It’s a big mystery why we even have [it] in our ears,” Hu says. It can frankly seem like a nuisance. Earwax can build up, clogging earbuds and hearing aids and interfering with hearing, so understanding this substance better may help resolve those problems.

Hu and colleagues analyzed the mechanical and chemical properties of 36 earwax samples from pigs, sheep, dogs, cows, rabbits and humans. They also observed how fire ants (Solenopsis invicta) reacted to both natural and synthetic earwax.

Even though ants seem able to scale kitchen cabinets with ease to invade countertops, they flounder when they attempt to climb earwax. Hu thinks the earwax sucks moisture from the ants’ feet that helps them grip. But earwax also sticks to ants’ bodies, causing the insects to start grooming incessantly trying to get rid of it. “It’s both sticky and slippery,” Hu says.

The chemical analyses provide some clues about the origins of these properties. Dead skin cells make up 60 percent of earwax, along with a smattering of oils and moisture. The earwax contains pores that Hu believes may be shaped like ink bottles to help it absorb twice its weight in water and prevent water from sloshing around in the ear canal. Like snot, earwax has a huge range of consistencies.

Under normal conditions, earwax becomes dry and crumbly in about 10 weeks. As it dries, it’s moved outward by a layer of cells lining the ear canal that act as a cleaning conveyor belt. In this way, the ear maintains just the right thickness of earwax to keep insects at bay, Hu says. “It’s most potent when it’s thin,” he explains. “Too much, and the ants can use their tiny claws to grab hold and climb in.”

Hu admits there’s no practical way to turn earwax into a commercial insect repellent. Each person has a volume of earwax about equivalent to that of a grain of rice in each ear at any given time, says Hu, so even if you add up all the earwax on Earth, “it’s a pretty rare substance.” But, he adds, companies “are trying to come up with biodegradable and biofriendly ways to deal with insects.” And, says Gorb, perhaps earwax “could inspire a new generation of physical, nontoxic pest control surfaces,” that could provide coatings for protecting stored food, agricultural products and technology.
