#6390. North America’s oldest footprints tell a story of drought and survival

Ancient footprints at White Sands reveal how people returned for nearly 2,000 years as drought and warming transformed an ice age lake.

The last ice age can sound like a time when landscapes barely changed across generations. But ancient footprints at White Sands tell a different story.

At White Sands in New Mexico, the footprint makers watched a lake shrink into a flat, salty mudflat called a playa, and a pine forest give way to sagebrush.

A severe drought came and went within about a century. Through it all, people kept walking the same shoreline for nearly 2,000 years.

A team led by Kathleen Springer and Jeffrey Pigati of the U.S. Geological Survey dug a new trench at the footprint site. Jessica Tierney of the University of Arizona reconstructed the climate from its mud.

The layers at White Sands National Park record conditions in steps of about 50 years, roughly a human generation.

“Even though these footprints have been buried in the gypsum mud for more than 20,000 years, they look like someone walked out on the playa yesterday,” Tierney said.

“This is an incredibly rare opportunity to be able to do paleoclimate reconstruction and combine it with archeology in the same exact place.”

The original trench, dug in 2020, was 36 feet (11 meters) long. The team extended it to 82 feet (25 meters), and the number of footprint layers rose from seven to 20.

Most of the measured footprints were consistent with children’s feet.

Of the 152 measured footprints, 72 were consistent with children around six years old, and another 12 with children around 12.

Eight came from toddlers under four, and 60 from adolescents or adults.

Mammoths, ground sloths, members of the dog family and possibly bears left tracks in the same layers, beside drag marks from people hauling loads on poles.

There was no sign of a camp, so the team read the site as a place people passed through rather than settled.

The first dates for the White Sands footprints, published in 2021, came from seeds of a water plant from the lake.

Critics argued those seeds could have absorbed old carbon from the lake water and so look older than they are.

Pine pollen doesn’t have that problem, because the trees took their carbon from the air.

Earlier pollen dates had carried uncertainties of more than 2,000 years, so they couldn’t settle the question.

The USGS lab sorted up to 75,000 pollen grains out of each sample with a cell-sorting machine and measured how much modern carbon the laboratory process introduced.

The uncertainty on each pollen date dropped fivefold.

The pollen dates came out younger than seed dates from the same layers, by up to 1,330 radiocarbon years.

The corrected dates placed the footprints between 23,500 and 21,700 years ago.

The oldest mud in the trench formed under standing water between about 24,200 and 23,600 years ago.

Lake Otero covered the site, and pine, fir and spruce made up 40% of the pollen blown in from the mountains.

The team estimated air temperature from microbial fats in the mud, whose makeup changes with temperature: about 54°F (12°C), roughly 7°F (4°C) colder than the area today.

Then the lake began to shrink. From about 23,600 years ago the sediment switched from lake clay to silt and sand washed in over land, and oak and sagebrush replaced the conifer forest.

Warming sped up around 22,400 years ago, and the upper layers filled with gypsum and salt left behind by evaporation.

The White Sands warming was the opposite of the trend across the rest of the Northern Hemisphere, which kept cooling until about 18,000 years ago.

Ocean records off California show the same early warming, which the authors suggested may have been widespread across the Southwest.

Between 24,200 and 23,600 years ago the basin was wet, and hydrogen in preserved leaf wax points to winter rain off the Pacific rather than summer monsoon rain.

Then, 23,200 years ago, a severe but short drought hit.

The water turned saltier, drought-tolerant piñon and juniper spread, and the shallow lake turned permanently into a mudflat wet only in patches.

The oldest footprint layer dates to that drought, when newly exposed ground became walkable.

The same moment shows up in Greenland ice cores as a sudden warming, one of a series of abrupt climate swings during the ice age.

The White Sands footprint dates carry smaller errors than the ice core’s, so the authors wrote that their record may date that event more sharply.

“This tells us that local changes in aridity at White Sands were quite large and followed global climate shifts,” Tierney said.

Another wet spell around 22,700 years ago left clay from a short-lived pond, and the water plant’s share of the pollen rose to 60% in some wet layers.

People kept walking the shoreline through every swing. The authors read that as a sign of how much the waning lake still offered.

Springer said early humans in the region “were real-time witnesses to a rapidly changing environment discernible within a human lifetime – that is really food for thought.”

Ed Jolie, a curator at the Arizona State Museum who is Oglala Lakota and Hodulgee Muscogee, noted that the findings “humanize the deep Indigenous past of the Americas.”

He said they support Native nations’ oral traditions of having been here since time immemorial.

The footprint counts are rough. Some excavated patches are small and crowded, so the team cautioned that its estimates of how many people walked each layer can’t be used for population figures.

Ages from foot length are approximations too. A larger question concerns the connection between Greenland’s warming and drought at White Sands.

Tierney and her colleagues don’t yet know why a warming spike over Greenland would dry out a valley in New Mexico. Working out that mechanism is their next step.

The 50-year resolution of the White Sands record gives them something to test ideas against.

The full study was published in the journal Science Advances.

#6389. Monkeys that lived through a deadly outbreak showed surprising caution around food

Japanese macaques from groups hit by a deadly outbreak were more likely to avoid food on feces, even if they had never tested positive.

In the first weeks of COVID-19, many households wiped down their groceries before putting them away.

Japanese macaques that lived through a deadly outbreak of their own also showed greater caution around food.

Macaques from groups where the virus had spread refused food placed on a soiled surface far more often than those from a group it never reached.

And the virus they had survived isn’t even known to spread through food.

Stephan Kaufhold and Federico Rossano of the University of California San Diego‘s Department of Cognitive Science ran the tests at a primate sanctuary in southern Texas.

The researchers tested whether monkeys would eat a grape placed on feces.

The experiment measured food avoidance, which does not necessarily indicate disgust.

The sanctuary’s Japanese macaques descend from a troop moved from Japan to Texas in 1972. Today they live in four separate fenced enclosures.

In January 2020, the sanctuary confirmed that a virus called simian retrovirus Type II was circulating in the Japanese macaques.

A long-tailed macaque that had retired from a research laboratory had carried it in without showing symptoms.

Late in 2019, the virus had likely changed enough to spread to the Japanese macaques.

Some infected monkeys died quickly of severe bleeding.

Others carried it with no symptoms, and some later lost weight and fell ill with other infections, much as people with AIDS do.

The virus passes through blood and saliva, mostly in bites and scratches during fights, and it has never been shown to spread through feces or food.

Three of the four groups went through the outbreak. The fourth, called Kyoto, didn’t.

Between October 2022 and March 2024, the team set two baited objects on the ground inside each enclosure and filmed what happened.

One was a plain piece of wood. The other was real macaque feces, collected from healthy animals and sealed under clear epoxy so it looked fresh but had no smell and couldn’t infect anyone.

A grape was placed on each object, and every monkey was free to take both.

Monkeys from the three outbreak groups ate the grape off the feces in 47% of 117 trials. Monkeys from Kyoto ate it in 79% of 80 trials.

So a monkey that had lived through the outbreak usually took the clean grape and left the other one lying there. A monkey from Kyoto usually ate both.

Within the outbreak groups, some monkeys had tested positive for the virus and some never had.

Kaufhold’s team compared the two, and the uninfected monkeys avoided the dirty grape about as much as the infected ones did. Both avoided it far more than the Kyoto monkeys.

In an interview with Earth.com, Kaufhold said that was the result he hadn’t expected.

“What surprised us was that animals within the exposed groups that had not been infected avoided the contaminated food just as much as those that had,” he said.

Kaufhold said the team doesn’t know why some monkeys escaped infection. Their immune systems may have resisted it, or they may have stayed out of the fights that spread it.

“Either way, the shift in behavior seems to follow having lived through the outbreak, for example witnessing others getting sick and dying, rather than being infected oneself,” he told Earth.com.

Only nine monkeys in the outbreak groups are confirmed uninfected, and the team treats that comparison as preliminary.

The outbreak groups showed greater caution around feces, even though the virus is not known to spread that way.

Kaufhold said the pattern “suggests a general increase in pathogen sensitivity rather than avoidance of the specific transmission route.”

In another experiment in the same paper, the team tested macaques from seven species, one at a time, with a sliding table that held the same two objects.

Among those tested, 14 were born at the sanctuary and raised by their mothers, while 15 were former pets raised by people.

The former pets had about twice the odds of taking food off the feces that the sanctuary-born monkeys did, even after years of living in monkey groups.

Kaufhold told Earth.com that one possibility is that the former pets “missed the chance to learn these behaviors from their mothers and other macaques early in life.”

Earlier studies found that young macaques watch their mothers and older groupmates forage, and that what they see others do shapes what they eat.

There is a cost, Kaufhold said. “Pathogen avoidance is always a trade-off.”

“Being too sensitive means leaving resources like food on the table, while being too indiscriminate increases exposure to pathogens and potentially disease.”

The outbreak monkeys were paying that cost in grapes.

The researchers can’t rule out that the four groups already differed before the outbreak, because nobody tested them then.

They also can’t yet say whether each monkey learned the caution on its own or picked it up from the group.

One precedent they cite is a troop of wild baboons in Kenya. A tuberculosis outbreak in the 1980s killed the troop’s most aggressive males, and the calmer culture that followed was passed on to males who joined years later.

Kaufhold said two questions come next: how long the heightened caution lasts, and whether monkeys that join these groups later pick it up.

“If newcomers picked up the increased caution, that would suggest social transmission, which could lead to a group-specific tradition,” he said.

Kaufhold said the macaque data “does not directly speak to how human behavior changed during and after COVID-19, but there are some interesting parallels.”

Studies of people found that disgust sensitivity rose during the pandemic, including toward things that had nothing to do with how the coronavirus spread.

The authors argue that human disgust was built on an older system for avoiding disease, one that changes with experience.

The team hasn’t yet measured whether that caution will still be there in the Texas enclosures a few years from now. They hope to go back and find out.

The full study was published in the journal Royal Society Open Science.

#6387. The Sky This Week from November 6 to 13: Venus in the spotlight

Friday, November 6The waning Moon leaves us with perfect skies for deep-sky observing. Let’s kick off the week with a bright planetary nebula in Aquarius: NGC 7293, commonly known as the Helix Nebula.

Despite its impressive magnitude of 7.3, the Helix presents a challenge: It is a broad 13’ across, which spreads its light over a relatively large part of sky, lowering its overall surface brightness. That said, you can still find the Helix in large binoculars or any small scope, tucked into southeastern Aquarius, roughly 7.7° southwest of magnitude 3.3 Skat (Delta [δ] Aquarii). If you turn south around 7 P.M. local time, find Skat to the upper right of bright Fomalhaut in Piscis Austrinus, then scan to its lower right, toward 5th-magnitude 66 Aqr. That star lies about halfway between Skat and the Helix Nebula.

Once you’ve located the Helix, the more magnification you can turn on it, the better. Larger amateur scopes will start to show structure in the ring of glowing gas surrounding the central white dwarf, with the northern and southern edges glowing brighter than the eastern and western sides. That gas was once part of the central star, which puffed up and blew away its outer layers as it aged. Sunrise: 6:35 A.M. Sunset: 4:52 P.M. Moonrise: 3:56 A.M. Moonset: 3:16 P.M. Moon Phase: Waning crescent (5%)

Saturday, November 7Venus is our (morning) star of the week, capturing attention above the eastern horizon before sunrise. This morning, the Moon passes 1.1° due south of Earth’s sister planet at 7 A.M. EST.

You can easily catch the pair an hour before sunrise, some 6° high in the east and climbing as the sky begins to brighten. Magnitude –4.5 Venus blazes to the upper left of the delicate crescent Moon, whose western limb is just barely lit as the Sun sets across the lunar nearside. Look for earthshine on the already-shadowed portion of Luna’s face, as sunlight bouncing off Earth lights it up.

Near Venus is another bright light: This is Spica, Virgo’s alpha star, shining at magnitude 1.0 and also lingering in the morning twilight. This morning it lies 1.3° northeast of Venus, with the planet and star roughly side by side above the horizon. Use this view as an anchor point: By the 10th, Venus will have moved to stand due west of this star and will be located to its upper right.

Sunrise: 6:36 A.M. Sunset: 4:51 P.M. Moonrise: 5:01 A.M. Moonset: 3:40 P.M. Moon Phase: Waning crescent (1%)

Sunday, November 8Rising with the stars of western Leo shortly before midnight, bright Jupiter and its Galilean moons put on a show early this morning, better visible the farther east you’re located.

Jupiter is just under 5° northwest (to the upper right) of Regulus as they rise in the east. Fainter Mars stands roughly 3° above Jupiter. You’ll want your telescope trained on the gas giant soon after rising to catch the show, which begins at 1:29 A.M. EST as a shadow appears on the planet’s eastern limb. This is Io’s shadow — but don’t be fooled by the positions of the moons you see in your scope. The moon closest to Jupiter on the east is Callisto, while the moon just east of that is Io, whose shadow we see. Ganymede lies farthest east, while Europa is currently hidden behind the planet in an occultation. The latter appears from behind the eastern limb about 1:54 A.M. EST, not long before Callisto reaches the planet and begins a transit at 2:07 A.M. EST.

Keep an eye on Io and Europa: Io passes north of Europa at 2:23 A.M. EST, then heads into its own transit about 2:42 A.M. EST. Now the race is on, as Io approaches and then catches up with Callisto as the two moons transit, passing Callisto and moving west of it within half an hour. The two moons and Io’s shadow continue to transit until 3:45 A.M. EST, when Io’s shadow leaves the western limb, and Io takes about an hour and a quarter longer before egress. Callisto continues trundling along, finally finishing its transit about 5:51 A.M. CST, with the sky now starting to brighten with twilight in the Midwest.

Sunrise: 6:37 A.M. Sunset: 4:50 P.M. Moonrise: 6:07 A.M. Moonset: 4:08 P.M. Moon Phase: New

Monday, November 9New Moon occurs at 2:02 A.M. EST. Dark skies make tonight the perfect opportunity to try spotting Comet 161P/Hartley-IRAS, still nearly 50° above the western horizon two hours after sunset.

Glowing around 10th magnitude, the comet is currently located in far northern Aquila, near the Eagle’s border with Sagitta the Arrow. You can use Aquila’s bright luminary, Altair, to guide your way — the comet floats 7.7° north-northeast of this star. A closer but fainter guide is 4th-magnitude Alpha (α) Sagittae, just 2.3° north of the comet’s position tonight. Even a small scope will nab you the comet, but larger apertures will yield better views. Under high magnification, look at the comet’s southern side, which should be sharper as it plows into the solar wind.

Not far from Hartley-IRAS’ position is the famous Coathanger asterism, located in Vulpecula the Fox. Cataloged as Collinder 399, you’ll find it roughly 5° northwest of the comet’s position, or about 4° northwest of Alpha Sge. Visible in binoculars or any telescope (in this case, lower magnification is better), you’ll immediately see why this star pattern bears its name. It looks exactly like its namesake, with a line of stars bisected by a small curve extending to the south. At the Coathanger’s eastern edge lies the open cluster NGC 6802.

Sunrise: 6:38 A.M. Sunset: 4:49 P.M. Moonrise: 7:12 A.M. Moonset: 4:40 P.M. Moon Phase: Waxing crescent (1%)

Tuesday, November 10The waxing crescent Moon passes 0.3° south of Antares at midnight EST, although the pair is not visible at that time. You can catch our satellite setting in the west around sunset, although it will likely disappear before Antares pops out of the twilight — that will likely happen only shortly before the star itself sets as well.

Instead, challenge yourself with a different type of observation: picking up Saturn’s moon Iapetus, which tonight reaches greatest eastern elongation 9.4’ east of the ringed planet. The two-toned moon is tidally locked to its parent world, which means it rotates in time with its orbit. At eastern elongation, Iapetus’ darker hemisphere faces earthward, reducing the moon’s magnitude to nearly 12. This, combined with its distance from Saturn, makes it more of a challenge to find, but you can give it a try if you’ve got a larger scope.

Try around 9 P.M. local time when Saturn is highest, some 50° above the southern horizon. It’s the brightest point of light in this region of the sky, hanging just below Pisces and to the far upper left of Fomalhaut, the brightest star in Piscis Austrinus (much closer to the horizon). Even if you can’t locate Iapetus or don’t have a large scope, Saturn is magnificent through a telescope. Its disk spans 19” and its rings are roughly 43” across, showing off their southern side. You should definitely spot its largest and brightest moon, mid-8th-magnitude Titan, just over 2’ west of the planet. Depending on your scope and when you look, you may also spot at least three other moons: 10th-magnitude Tethys, Dione, and Rhea, closer to the planet. Tethys lies to Saturn’s west, while Rhea and Dione are to the east.

Sunrise: 6:39 A.M. Sunset: 4:48 P.M. Moonrise: 8:15 A.M. Moonset: 5:19 P.M. Moon Phase: Waxing crescent (4%)

Wednesday, November 11Venus reaches a stationary point among the stars of Virgo at 10 A.M. EST. This brings its retrograde (westward) motion to an end; after today, Venus will begin moving eastward or prograde through the sky, swinging north of Spica.

You can easily catch the bright planet in the eastern sky before dawn. Venus’ brightness has increased over just the past few days, and it now blazes at magnitude –4.7. An hour before sunrise, you’ll easily spot it alongside Spica, standing just to the star’s upper right. Both are 10° high and rising as dawn approaches. Check out Venus through a telescope: its disk shows off a crescent phase just 10% lit, but stretches an impressive 53” in the sky.

Also just becoming visible at this time is Mercury, barely 1.5° above the horizon and glowing at magnitude 1.2. See if you can locate it about 13° east (to the lower left) of Venus, although you’ll need a particularly flat horizon free of trees, buildings, and lights. Mercury, too, rises as twilight brightens, which may make the planet harder to see in the growing light. Try scanning for it with binoculars, although make sure to put them away well before sunrise from your location, which may differ from the time given below.

Sunrise: 6:41 A.M. Sunset: 4:47 P.M. Moonrise: 9:15 A.M. Moonset: 6:05 P.M. Moon Phase: Waxing crescent (8%)

Thursday, November 12The constellation Perseus is famous for its bright Double Cluster, but these two open clusters aren’t the only groups of young stars in the Hero worth viewing. Today, let’s shift our gaze to the western portion of this constellation, near its border with Andromeda, to check out M34, a mid-5th-magnitude open cluster containing about 100 stars.

Sitting 5.2° west-northwest of 2nd-magnitude Algol (Beta [β] Persei), M34 spans about half a degree, roughly the size of the Full Moon. In physical space, astronomers believe the group spans about 14 light-years and sits 1,400 light-years away. It’s best seen under lower magnifications, such as in binoculars or small amateur scopes (4 inches or so). You’ll spot several dozen stars brighter than 12th magnitude, with its brightest suns spread throughout the cluster.

Sunrise: 6:42 A.M. Sunset: 4:46 P.M. Moonrise: 10:08 A.M. Moonset: 6:57 P.M. Moon Phase: Waxing crescent (14%)

Friday, November 13The Moon reaches apogee, the farthest point from Earth in its orbit, at 12:50 P.M. EST. At that time, our satellite will be 252,040 miles (405,619 kilometers) from Earth.

Celebrate Friday the 13th with something spooky: a ghost in the constellation Andromeda. This evening, point your telescope toward 2nd-magnitude Mirach (Beta [β] Andromedae), already nearly 60° high in the east by 7 P.M. local time. One of the Princess’ brightest stars, Mirach is a cool, reddish M-type giant. It lies some 200 light-years away and shines nearly 2,000 times as brightly as our Sun.

But Mirach is not quite our target — we’re looking for its so-called ghost, just 6.8’ northwest of the star. You’ll need a big scope to see it, but look carefully: Can you spot a faint smudge of light, about 4’ across, close to the star? This is the Ghost of Mirach, a far more distant elliptical galaxy glowing at 10th magnitude and cataloged as NGC 404. It lies some 8 million to 10 million light-years away, just beyond the gravitational bounds of our Local Group of galaxies. It’s called a ghost because it appears almost like a ghostly image of the bright star Mirach, which dominates the view.

Sunrise: 6:43 A.M. Sunset: 4:45 P.M. Moonrise: 10:54 A.M. Moonset: 7:55 P.M. Moon Phase: Waxing crescent (21%)

Alison Klesman is senior editor of Astronomy magazine. She holds a Ph.D. in astronomy and has studied a variety of topics, from minor planets to supermassive black holes.

#6386. Where children live may influence how well they focus

Children in greener neighborhoods scored slightly higher on attention tests, suggesting nearby trees and parks may play a role in focus.

Children often do better on attention tasks after a walk in the park or time in a school garden.

But researchers have had mixed answers about whether living near trees and parks is also linked to better focus.

A large study of American children now finds a small connection between neighborhood greenery and attention.

Links with reading and vocabulary were less clear after researchers accounted for family income.

Carina Fowler led the study at Washington University in St. Louis. She is a postdoctoral researcher in the lab of Deanna Barch, a professor in the Department of Psychological and Brain Sciences.

“If a child lives closer to green space, and has more access to green space, does this help them pay attention on demand when it’s required, and do they do better at school on achievement tests?” Fowler said.

The researchers explored an idea called attention restoration theory. It suggests that nature gives the mind a break from the effort of staying focused.

The theory describes two kinds of attention: one we use to concentrate on a task, and another that responds automatically to things around us.

Phones, TVs and traffic can grab that automatic attention completely, while trees and parks may hold it gently enough to let the mind wander.

This may give our ability to concentrate a chance to recover.

Fowler said earlier research suggests people dislike having nothing to see or hear, or sitting alone with their thoughts in a quiet room.

“It seems people need something to be occupying them a little bit – but not too much – and that nature can provide that really well,” Fowler said.

The team used data from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development Study, which recruited children near 21 sites across the continental United States.

The analysis included 11,868 children who joined between 2016 and 2018, aged nine or 10.

For each child’s home, the team studied the surrounding census tract, an area used in the national census that is roughly the size of a neighborhood.

Satellite images showed how much land trees covered.

Records checked by the Trust for Public Land showed how much land was parkland. The researchers averaged the tree and park percentages to give each child a green space score.

Across the group, the combined score averaged about 11%.

The children took five short tests that involved remembering things, switching between rules, ignoring distractions and processing information quickly.

The team combined the results into an attention score.

The score used a scale similar to an IQ test, with 100 in the middle and a typical spread of about 15 points.

Reading and vocabulary tests produced a second score that gave a rough picture of school skills.

The team looked at each child at one point in time. That means the results can show a connection, but cannot prove that greenery caused higher scores.

Children’s focus depends on many things. The researchers considered sex and how well off each neighborhood was.

They also included ADHD, stimulant medicines, sleep problems, weekly screen time and tobacco exposure before birth.

Other checks covered air pollution, physical activity and whether children felt safe from crime in their neighborhood.

According to the authors, no earlier study of green space and attention had included children’s own sense of safety.

“You have to feel safe in the green space to have an effect,” Fowler said.

After those checks, a 10-percentage-point increase in green space was linked to an attention score 0.76 points higher. Reading and vocabulary scores were 0.83 points higher.

A 10-percentage-point rise would mean going from 10% to 20%, for example.

The score differences were small: less than one point on a scale with a typical spread of 15 points.

Many children had little greenery nearby. About half lived in areas with a green space score below 10%, and about one in 10 had a score below 1%.

The authors suggested that even a small increase in greenery might matter in those places. Attention and school skills at this age can help predict later health, earnings and education.

Greener neighborhoods tend to have cleaner air, and studies have linked air pollution to attention problems. The team checked whether tiny pollution particles could explain some of the results.

These particles measure no more than about one ten-thousandth of an inch across, or 2.5 micrometers.

Lower particle pollution explained a small part of the link with both scores, which surprised the authors because they had expected it to explain none.

“There is something to the idea that air quality is partially explaining why green space is helping our attention,” Fowler said.

Exercise did not explain the link. Children in greener areas did not report more days with at least an hour of activity, although more active children scored higher on both measures.

The team then added family income to the analysis, which already included how well off the neighborhood was.

The link between greenery and attention became about half as large, but it remained.

The link with reading and vocabulary was no longer statistically significant. This makes it harder to tell how much greenery itself might matter for those skills.

The authors offered two possible explanations. Green space may have a weaker link with school skills, or it may help focus sooner while any effect on learning takes years to build.

The attention score combined several skills, so it was not a test of attention alone.

The school skills score covered reading and vocabulary, leaving out math, science and writing.

The study also included relatively few rural children because most of its brain-imaging centers are in cities.

And the team measured greenery at only one point in each child’s life, so it could not show what happens after a move to a greener area.

The authors suggested testing whether greener school grounds help children learn.

They also raised the possibility that keeping children inside during recess as punishment for poor focus or grades could make those problems worse.

Both ideas need testing, as does whether planting trees near homes or schools improves attention.

Experiments and studies that follow children over many years could help answer those questions.

The study is published in the journal Environment International.

Using machine learning, astronomers developed a new way of looking at James Webb telescope data that allows far-off planets to emerge from their star's glare.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

When it comes to spotting planets orbiting distant stars, the biggest hurdle is often separating the signal from the noise — specifically, trying to distinguish a planet from the stellar glare around it. That's true even for the most sophisticated telescopes, including the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST).

Now, astronomers have developed a new way to spot planets that were formerly drowned out in a sea of light. Using a combination of modeling and machine learning techniques, they picked out a previously hidden giant exoplanet in data from JWST. The results were published Nov. 4 in the journal Nature.

"Planets are a million times fainter than their stars," study first author Rodrigo Ferrer-Chavez, an astronomer at Northwestern University, said in a statement. "So, to image exoplanets, we need to remove that glare."

Telescopes like JWST use instruments called coronagraphs to block out some of this excess light, similar to the way the moon and a pinhole camera operate during a total solar eclipse. But even the best coronagraphs have limitations — for example, they can't block all the glare, and the telescopes themselves move.

Even the most stable telescopes vibrate almost imperceptibly as they collect light, so the images a telescope produces contain ever-so-slight mismatches compared with what the instrument actually sees. These slight shifts can be enough to obscure even very large exoplanets.

To address this, Ferrer-Chavez and his team developed a "digital twin" of JWST that virtually recreates how light travels through the telescope's detectors, minus any movement-based imperfections. To fine-tune this digital replica, the researchers used computational models based in real-world physics alongside machine learning techniques similar to those used to train AI. But the authors stressed that this is not an AI model.

"Because we already know the physics, we don't need AI to understand what's happening," study co-author Jason Wang, also an astrophysicist at Northwestern, said in a statement.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The researchers named their approach Physics-based Learning for Imaging Planets, or FLIP.

Using FLIP, the team analyzed data from three stars, including 51 Eridani, which is located around 97 light-years from Earth and was already suspected to have a giant exoplanet orbiting it. Although the planet, called 51 Eridani b, had been detected by ground-based telescopes, it was drowned out by light in previous JWST observations. With FLIP, however, 51 Eridani b popped out from the dataset.

The scientists hope this approach will help astronomers pick out even more hard-to-spot exoplanets, especially ones that look like the planets in our own backyard. In the nearly 35-year history of exoplanet hunting, the vast majority of planets we've found have been radically different from those in our own solar system, partially because larger and more reflective worlds are easier to spot with current telescopes.

"It's not that [solar-system-like planets] don't exist," Ferrer-Chavez said. "It's that we can't see them."

Ferrer-Chavez, R., Wang, J. J., Bouman, K. L., Freeman, W. T., Pueyo, L., Feng, B. Y., & Perrin, M. D. (2026). Imaging exoplanets below the telescope stability limit. Nature, 659(8139), 58–62. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-026-11213-z

Joanna Thompson is a science journalist and runner based in New York. #6383. Time between pregnancies may shape how fast mothers age

Each pregnancy adds biological age that takes months to come off, and birth spacing may decide how much a mother recovers before the next one.

Tests suggest that biological age rises during pregnancy and falls again in the months after birth. Researchers are now asking whether the time between pregnancies affects how fully those changes reverse.

Two Harvard researchers propose that the time a woman gets between pregnancies, not only how many she has, may shape how fast she ages for decades.

If the next pregnancy begins before that recovery is finished, the extra age may not be fully reversed, the authors wrote. The effect could then build with each closely spaced birth.

Stephen Albright and Jesse Poganik of Harvard Medical School and Brigham and Women’s Hospital laid out the idea in a review article. It pulls together studies from Europe, the United States, Israel and the Philippines.

The result is a hypothesis with testable predictions attached, not a new trial, and Poganik said the changes it describes don’t necessarily amount to damage.

“Our previous research has found that biological age transiently rises during pregnancy, peaking around the third trimester or at the time of delivery,” said Poganik, the corresponding author.

“If we accept the idea that these short-term changes in biological age occur, the question is how we can relate those changes to the overall trajectory of aging over the course of a lifetime.”

Biological age is an estimate of how much age-related change a body’s cells and tissues have accumulated, separate from the years on a birth certificate.

One way to estimate it is to read chemical tags on DNA that shift in a predictable pattern as people get older. Researchers call those readouts epigenetic clocks.

Run those clocks on blood drawn through a pregnancy and the number climbs as the pregnancy goes on, then partly falls after the birth.

Women on three continents show the same pattern, and so do mice. The authors wrote that this level of agreement is uncommon in their field.

The changes behind the number are physical. Blood volume rises by about half.

Cortisol, a stress hormone, climbs through pregnancy, and estrogen runs at roughly 100 times its usual level. The body also builds a new organ, the placenta, from nothing.

A detailed picture of the recovery comes from Israel, where researchers analyzed 76 routine lab tests from more than 300,000 pregnancies.

About half of those markers needed anywhere from three months to a year to return to where they had been before the pregnancy.

An aging clock built from those same lab results showed a dip before a large rise. In the first trimester a woman’s results looked about five years younger than her age.

From there they rose by about 20 years toward delivery, and it took roughly a year for them to recover.

Not every system recovers on the same schedule. Among more than 200,000 people, the reading from a clock built from wearable pulse sensors rose by about 3.5 years during pregnancy, then declined only slowly after birth.

Brain scans of first-time mothers showed gray matter volume falling across nearly all of the cortex during pregnancy and only partly recovering afterward.

The most direct evidence comes from a 2026 study that followed 130 women from pregnancy through nearly four years after the birth.

Among women who became pregnant again, the decline in their measured pace of aging was interrupted, and two other aging measures moved in the same direction.

Albright and Poganik call the time between a birth and the next conception the recovery window, and their hypothesis is simple to state.

Each pregnancy adds some biological age, and given enough time the body can undo at least part of it.

Under their hypothesis, another pregnancy could add to any biological-age increase that has not yet reversed.

Two women with the same number of children could therefore end up aging at different rates, depending on how far apart the births were.

The authors wrote that this is their central prediction, and it hasn’t been directly tested. No study has yet measured the spacing of pregnancies alongside biological age tracked for decades afterward.

Mothers of many children tend to die earlier in some populations and not in others, and the reasons remain unclear.

In the Finnish Twin Cohort, the risk of dying was highest among women with no births and women with five or more, and lowest among women with two or three.

Among adoptive parents, death rates declined as the number of adopted children increased.

A study of 2,356 women aged 35 to 74 linked more births to small increases in epigenetic age, measured well after their last pregnancy.

In 1,735 young women in the Philippines, with an average age of about 22, each additional pregnancy was linked to roughly two to three months of extra aging.

Spacing could explain why the count alone gives such mixed results, the authors wrote. Where women with many children tend to space them well, the count would carry little cost.

“It’s possible that this could change the overall trajectory of aging,” Poganik said.

“We know that some level of parity, or carrying a pregnancy to term, is actually beneficial to a person’s lifespan.”

The World Health Organization has recommended since 2005 that women wait at least 24 months after a live birth before conceiving again.

The advice rests on evidence linking short gaps to more preterm and low-weight births.

One review of 129 studies and nearly 47 million pregnancies linked gaps of 18 to 23 months to the best outcomes for babies. Gaps under six months were most consistently linked to harm for both baby and mother.

When a new pregnancy began six months after a birth, instead of 18 months, only women 35 and older faced a substantially higher chance of dying or becoming severely ill.

The age pattern fits their idea, Albright and Poganik wrote, because an older mother starts the recovery period biologically older, with less reserve.

Some factors were associated with differences in recovery.

Among about 120 women in one cohort, those who breastfed exclusively had a lower biological age three months after birth, whatever their body mass index.

A higher body mass index before pregnancy predicted a higher biological age afterward.

Sleep loss and chronic stress are suspected of slowing recovery too, though the authors found little or no research on either after birth.

Not every population fits. Tsimane women, who farm and forage for a living, have many children and little spare food.

Over a 10-year study their nutrition and immune markers largely held up however many children they had.

But those measures weren’t combined into a biological age, the authors wrote, so the cost they propose can’t be ruled out there.

Whether the extra age is wear, or the body remodeling itself for a demanding job, isn’t settled either. Clocks designed to tell the two apart are one way to find out.

Poganik said the work has a nearer-term purpose as well.

“What motivates me on a more near-term basis is addressing current clinical challenges, including the huge maternal mortality crisis in the United States compared with other industrialized countries,” he said.

“Any insights we can gain that can improve the health of mothers makes this a worthwhile research endeavor.”

The question underneath all of it is whether an incomplete recovery leaves a mother permanently older on the clocks, or whether the deficit fades given enough time.

Answering it means measuring biological age through several pregnancies, then following those women for 10 to 20 years, and no cohort has done that.

Until then, the 24-month guidance rests on pregnancy outcomes. Poganik said any advice based on a mother’s biological age would have to wait for that longer follow-up.

The review was published in the journal Trends in Endocrinology & Metabolism.

#6382. Little Ice Age cooling in Europe may have raised the risk of rickets

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Skeletal remains with signs of vitamin D deficiencies hint at how climate change impacted health

A volcano-fueled chilly climate during the 18th and 19th centuries may have made winter in England so bad, as depicted in this 19th century painting of a man collecting wood, that it raised the risk of kids getting rickets, a condition caused by vitamin D deficiency.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

England isn’t renowned for its weather. But just a few centuries ago, climate change–fueled conditions may have been so bad that they put children’s health at risk.

Calcium mineralization in the teeth and skeletons of people who lived in rural northern England suggests that children growing up during the height of the Little Ice Age routinely developed vitamin D deficiencies, researchers report November 5 in Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology. In the worst cases, these deficiencies developed into rickets, a bone disorder that can occur when people don’t get enough ultraviolet light.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Previous skeletal studies suggest that rickets became more common among Europeans during the 18th and 19th centuries. One culprit may have been the Industrial Revolution, when many Europeans lived in UV-poor polluted cities and often worked indoors. The unusually cold climate may have added “an extra layer of difficulty” to getting enough sunlight, says Ellen Kendall, a bioarcheologist at Durham University in England

The Little Ice Age was a period of global cooling from the 13th to 19th centuries caused by extreme solar cycles and a series of volcanic eruptions, which can cool the planet by ejecting aerosols into the atmosphere that block sunlight. In the last 200 years of the era, 18 major eruptions helped spur a temperature drop of 2 to 3 degrees Celsius over northern Europe.

Kendall and colleagues wondered how this cold climate affected health. They examined calcium deposition — how the essential mineral is incorporated into bones — in the remains of 21 people buried from 1711 to 1829 in the town of North Shields. Calcium often doesn’t fully mineralize in people with vitamin D delicacies, leaving voids in teeth as they grow.

The team found bands of failed calcium mineralization in the teeth, suggesting seasonal spates of vitamin D deficiencies. Some skeletons also showed signs of rickets. North Shields was a small rural town that hadn’t yet undergone industrialization, so these deficiencies probably weren’t due to bad air conditions.

The unusually cold weather may have changed people’s behavior during the winter, Kendall says. Residents may have kept their kids indoors or bundled them up so that little skin was exposed when they did go outside, preventing them from getting enough UV light, she says.

However, climate was still just one factor among many — including gender roles, diet and pollution — that shaped vitamin D deficiencies at the time, says Kendall. “Humans are very messy to study,” she says. “That’s one of the things that makes them so very fascinating.”

Questions or comments on this article? E-mail us at feedback@sciencenews.org | Reprints FAQ

E. Kendall. ‘The bright sun was extiguish’d’: metabolic health and vitamin D status in a Little Ice Age population (18-19th c.) in North East England. Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology. 2026. Doi: 10.3389/fearc.2026.1909791

#6380. A tiny plant’s unusual sex life depends on water flowing uphill

Common liverworts carry water up their stalks without a pump, helping sperm reach elevated eggs and revealing how the plants evolved.

Water runs downhill, and that’s a problem for liverworts, small plants whose sperm can reach an egg only by swimming.

In the common liverwort, a flat green species, the female holds her eggs up on a short stalk, away from the damp ground.

A new study found that the outside of that stalk carries water upward, against gravity, to the eggs at the top.

The upward flow helps resolve a conflict between fertilization and spore dispersal.

Height makes fertilization harder. But height also helps the plant spread its spores, and the study traces how the stalk came to handle both jobs.

Bo Xu, a professor at the Institute of Botany of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, led the work, and Xiaotong Qi is the study’s first author.

The team studied Marchantia polymorpha, the best-studied liverwort in biology labs.

Liverworts, mosses and hornworts belong to a group called bryophytes. They make no flowers or seeds, and they don’t have true roots.

They also lack the complex network of water-carrying tissue that larger plants rely on.

In bryophytes, a sperm cell has to travel through water to reach an egg.

Once an egg is fertilized, it grows into an embryo. The embryo then becomes a structure that makes spores, and those spores spread out and grow into new plants.

Every bryophyte has to meet both needs at once. Fertilization depends on water, while spores spread better from a higher, drier spot.

How small plants managed that is part of the larger story of how plants colonized land.

On a female common liverwort, a stalk lifts the egg-holding organs above the ground.

Xu’s team found that the stalk and the head on top of it carry water upward along their outer surface.

The flow depends on several kinds of tiny structures, each placed in a precise position relative to the others.

The researchers used three-dimensional X-ray imaging to map how those structures fit together on the stalk.

Water moving up that surface helps sperm reach eggs held well above the wet ground.

Keeping those surface structures intact helped water-based fertilization succeed, the team found.

One protein, called MpLAS, controls how all of those surface structures develop. It belongs to a family of proteins called GRAS, which switch other genes on and off.

MpLAS works by guiding how cells divide as they grow.

A second GRAS protein, MpGRAS10, helps build the stalk itself. It boosts the activity of two genes, MpKAOL1 and MpKAOL2, which help the plant make compounds related to gibberellin.

In many plants, gibberellin is the hormone that makes stems grow longer.

So one protein helps raise the eggs, and another builds the surface that gets water up to them.

Xu’s team also compared the common liverwort with its relatives and worked backward through their family tree.

The female stalk appears to have evolved only once in this group of liverworts, and several later lineages lost it.

The stalk turned up before the surface structures that carry water.

The researchers read that order as two separate steps. The elevated stalk helped the spores produced after fertilization spread farther.

The surface network came later and dealt with that problem.

In their account, later traits may have arisen to make earlier ones work better, by fixing what those earlier traits couldn’t do.

They said competing demands like these can push a complex structure to evolve one piece at a time.

Comparisons among living liverworts suggest that the stalk evolved before its water-carrying surface structures.

That sequence supports the team’s proposed explanation, although it does not prove how those traits evolved.

The findings could also inspire engineers.

By carrying water upward without a pump, the liverwort offers a model for surfaces designed to move liquid on their own.

The full study was published in the journal Nature Plants.

#6378. Major study argues we need immediate rules to protect young people from the harms of digital media

Lancet experts say digital media harms to young people come from app design and weak rules, not lack of willpower. They urge governments to act now.

When teenagers can’t stop scrolling on their mobile devices, the easiest explanation is to label them as having weak self-control.

A group of public health experts has a different answer. The feed was built to keep that thumb moving, and the responsibility belongs to the companies that built it and the governments that let them.

In a three-paper Series in The Lancet, the experts said the harm that digital media does to young people comes from business models, design choices and weak rules. They want governments to act now, before anyone has proof of cause and effect.

If they’re right, the question is no longer how many hours a child spends on a screen. It is what the apps on that screen were designed to do.

Professor Ilona Kickbusch of the Digital Transformations for Health Lab in Switzerland chaired the Series. Dr. Jay Shaw of the University of Toronto led its first paper.

The caveat arrives early. Heavy, addiction-like use is linked to poorer mental health, sleep and physical activity, Kickbusch said, but the evidence isn’t conclusive. A link isn’t proof of cause, and the authors rate the evidence low in certainty.

In an interview with Earth.com, she said the size of the effects is only half the question. “If you consider how many children are now using digital media, even small adverse effects might have significant public health consequences,” she said.

“That is why we are calling for a precautionary approach to policy rather than reacting only after harm has occurred.”

Open almost any social app and the feed never ends. Designers built that bottomless scroll deliberately, Shaw and his co-authors wrote, and it has encouraged amounts of screen time already known to be harmful.

The companies behind those features have lobbied to hold off regulation while knowing about the harms, the authors wrote.

“Most digital platforms are designed by companies to capture attention and collect data, not to protect health,” Shaw said. He added that infinite scroll, autoplay and personalized recommendation feeds are deliberate design choices that draw attention.

Scale turns a design detail into a public health question. By one estimate the authors cite, people who were online in 2025 spent an average of 141 minutes a day on social media apps, about two hours and 20 minutes.

In a 2025 survey of more than 10,000 adults in the United States, the average was more than 6 hours a day on phone apps, which is most of a school day.

Shaw’s paper compares the technology industry with tobacco and ultra-processed food. Both of those industries worked to weaken regulation while their products harmed health.

Governments have allowed digital companies to regulate themselves for decades, the Series reports, and commercial growth has come before health.

“Technology companies are borrowing a playbook well known from tobacco and fossil fuels: manufacture doubt, discredit critics, frame regulation as a threat to freedom,” said Professor Barbara Prainsack of the University of Vienna, a co-author on the Series.

Missing regulation doesn’t mean a technology goes ungoverned, she added. It means the companies set the rules instead of public policy.

Shaw and his co-authors called today’s approaches to governing that system deeply insufficient to protect public health.

They also describe adolescence and early adulthood as periods when the brain and social life are especially sensitive. The idealized selves people build online are linked to body shaming and poorer mental health, especially in young people.

Asked by Earth.com what surprised her most in the evidence, Kickbusch named the gaps. “What was most surprising about the evidence on the health impacts of children’s digital media use was what it doesn’t tell us,” she said.

Most studies measure individual behavior, such as screen time, she explained. Researchers have paid very little attention to the bigger structures, such as content created by algorithms and targeted advertising.

Young people also care about the benefits of going online and about AI, she said, and researchers have studied both of these areas less.

Access to data is another problem. “The most valuable data on how these platforms actually affect users are hidden within technology companies, limiting independent scrutiny and slowing scientific progress,” said Louise Holly, a Series author at DTH-Lab.

Shaw’s paper lists eight recommendations for researchers. One is to audit and publish the practices of technology companies that harm health, using insider accounts from former employees and investigative reporting.

Another is to keep industry money out of the research itself, a lesson the authors take from tobacco and pharmaceuticals.

Single measures such as age limits aren’t enough on their own, so the Series calls for action at the company, national and global levels at once.

Companies would have to test new products and features for harm before releasing them. They would also share data on how those features affect users’ health with vetted public-interest researchers.

A global treaty through the World Health Organization would set baseline standards, so weak rules in one country can’t undo progress elsewhere. A dedicated international body would monitor AI harms to children and young people.

Kickbusch told Earth.com that governments must work on several fronts in parallel: reduce access, regulate individual technologies and address the commercial models and algorithms behind social media. They also need to cooperate across borders, she said. “They must accept this is a major public health issue!”

Lawsuits are part of the picture too. Courts can compel companies to disclose internal documents in a way regulators often can’t, Kickbusch said. She sees litigation as one route to accountability among several, not a substitute for regulation.

The authors also worked with a youth advisory group of six adults aged 23 to 30, who talked with them about the lived experience the research can’t capture.

The steps governments and companies need to take will take time, Kickbusch said, because they are politically contested. Families don’t have to wait.

“Meanwhile, parents must help children mitigate risks by significantly reducing their use of digital media and the access to smartphones. They must explain to children how digital platforms and algorithms work,” she said.

Families who understand the design features and the commercial motives behind the platforms can protect themselves better, she explained, even when cutting back leads to difficult conversations at home.

“And parents themselves must change their social media use and be an example for their children,” she added.

No one has proved that the design features cause the harms linked to them, or measured how large those harms are, and the authors say so plainly. The links are modest in size and rest on evidence they rate as low in certainty.

The scope is also wider than the kids with phones. The same industries shape the health of people who don’t use the technology themselves, Shaw’s team wrote.

By the International Telecommunication Union‘s count, 2.2 billion people had no internet access in 2025. Africa was the least connected region.

Shaw said the field needs much more research into how specific design choices change the way people use digital media, instead of only measuring how long they spend online. That research depends on data the companies now keep to themselves.

Until that data is shared, the most important measurements of how these platforms affect adolescent health stay inside the companies that built them.

The full study was published in the journal The Lancet.

About half of people with long COVID see meaningful improvement in their symptoms after three years, a new study found.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Symptoms of long COVID ease in half of patients within three years of the infection that kicked off their illness.

That's the primary conclusion of a new study that tracked over 1,000 patients with long COVID, a chronic condition that can emerge after an infection with the SARS-CoV-2 virus. Among the patients, the chance of improvement varied sharply depending on how the condition affected their bodily systems.

In the study, published Tuesday (Nov. 3) in the journal Annals of Internal Medicine, roughly 60% of patients whose predominant symptoms were changes to their ability to taste or smell had significantly improved three years after their first positive test. But less than 20% of those with a multisystem presentation had improved in that time frame.

This latter group had symptoms that affected their cardiac, nervous and gastrointestinal systems, among others. An expert told Live Science that the condition resembled myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome (ME/CFS), which often arises after an infection and similarly impacts a wide range of bodily systems.

The new study's findings could help direct the structure of future clinical trials of treatments for long COVID, experts said.

The patients in the study were enrolled in the long-term RECOVER Adult Study. Funded by the National Institutes of Health, the project has recruited thousands of adults across the United States who previously tested positive for COVID-19.

Researchers scored patients based on how they were affected by a range of symptoms, including fatigue, brain fog, shortness of breath and heart palpitations. The study included patients who scored more than 10 points on a 30-point scale — called the 2024 LC Research Index (LCRI) — which attempted to capture these different symptom combinations.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Nearly 1,020 patients met this requirement and were tracked over time; they had in-person appointments and filled out symptom surveys every three months. Scientists marked patients as "improved" once they recorded LCRI scores of 10 or less at two consecutive visits. They found that 36% of the participants had improved two years after their inciting COVID-19 infection, and that figure rose to 50% after three years.

LCRIs hit zero for 26% of the participants after three years, meaning all of their symptoms were gone at the time of the survey.

Reeder said he was careful to avoid describing the participants as "recovered." This decision was influenced by input from the long COVID community to the RECOVER Adult Study, he said. They highlighted that their symptoms can wax and wane, whereas "recovery" implies a permanent resolution. The new study didn't capture, for example, whether individual patients who recorded meaningful improvement later relapsed.

The researchers analyzed which SARS-CoV-2 strain was associated with the most long COVID cases, controlling for patient vaccination status.

Some patients' journeys were far less straightforward than the top-line data might suggest. Although men and women improved at similar rates, adults under 46 were more likely to improve than older participants were. Patients affected by the Omicron variants of SARS-CoV-2, which emerged in 2021 and quickly became the dominant strain of the virus, were more likely to improve than those infected with earlier strains.

Some of the starkest differences in improvement rates were seen between patients with different symptoms.

In a previous study, RECOVER researchers had grouped participants into five subtypes, using an algorithm to connect patients with similar predominant symptoms:

In the new study, patients in the last three groups were less likely to get better within three years. The final group's rate was particularly low, at just 19%.

Dr. Carmen Scheibenbogen, an immunologist at Charité University Medicine Berlin, said these patients' progress resembles that of people with ME/CFS.

"It looks as if at least a major subgroup is suffering from ME-CFS," Scheibenbogen said, noting that COVID-19 may have triggered their condition. "This is a disease which is triggered by different infections, but in the end, the disease [itself] is very similar," she said.

Like long COVID, ME/CFS can affect a wide array of bodily systems, and it remains poorly understood despite recent advances in research.

The team's new findings highlight the need for clinical trials to test possible treatments for long COVID. Both Scheibenbogen and study co-author Harrison Reeder, a biostatistician at Massachusetts General Hospital, said these subtypes would be important to consider in the design of these potential trials.

The multisystem subgroup, Reeder said, "might be a group where an effective intervention can make a bigger difference than people who stand to potentially have a higher chance of improvement regardless."

Future work would need to further scientists' understanding of people affected by long COVID at the level of their genes and proteins, both scientists said.

"There's a lot of work to do in RECOVER and in the world of long COVID research," Harrison said. "There's a lot of opportunity."

This article is for informational purposes only and is not meant to offer medical advice.

#6376. The Sky Today on Friday, November 6: Nab the North America Nebula

Looking for a sky event this week? Check out our full Sky This Week column.

As fall gets into full swing, we are seeing less of the summertime stars. By 6 P.M. local time, the Summer Triangle — which flies high overhead on short summer nights — is now starting to set in the west. Lowest of its three points is Vega in Lyra; to Vega’s upper left is Altair in Aquila, while Deneb in Cygnus is almost directly above Vega and the highest of the three.

With no Moon in the sky, let’s use Deneb to find a favorite deep-sky object: NGC 7000, the North America Nebula. It’s a great small scope target, and its location just 3° east of Deneb makes it easy to center in the eyepiece. However, this huge emission nebula stretches about 2° across, so note that it requires a larger field of view to capture all in one go. It definitely benefits from a nebula filter if you have one.

On the sky, the nebula’s western side looks like the eastern coast of the continent for which it is named, and vice versa. The curve that mimics the Gulf of Mexico is particularly prominent, so start there if you’re having trouble seeing the shape. Look also to NGC 7000’s west — across a dark gulf, you’ll see a fainter, more compact patch of nebulosity. This is IC 5067/5070, also known as the Pelican Nebula.

#6375. Record-low temperature created on China’s space station

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

A Bose-Einstein condensate reached about 10 trillionths of a kelvin

An experiment on China's Tiangong space station (rendering shown) reached a record-low temperature in a state of matter called a Bose-Einstein condensate.

Shujianyang/Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Science has reached a new low. Temperature, that is.

Scientists cooled a collection of atoms to about 10 picokelvins, or 10 trillionths of a kelvin. That’s barely a smidge above absolute zero (−273.15° Celsius). The atoms formed a Bose-Einstein condensate, a quantum state of matter, colder than any before, researchers report November 5 in Science.

To achieve that record-low chill, scientists took their work to space. The atoms orbited Earth aboard China’s Tiangong space station. There, researchers used laser-based traps to contain 20,000 rubidium atoms and reduce their motion, thereby cooling them. At an atomic level, temperature is tied to motion: Atoms and molecules in the air around us move more slowly when it’s colder. Similarly, in systems of cold atoms, scientists can define an effective temperature based on how slowly the atoms spread apart when they are allowed to expand.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

On Earth, gravitational forces cause clouds of atoms to sag, reducing the effectiveness of cooling. But on the space station, the atoms experienced microgravity, the apparent weightlessness of an object in free fall.

To make a Bose-Einstein condensate, a disorderly gaggle of atoms is cooled until the atoms all take on the same quantum state, acting as one entity. By experimenting with ultracold atoms, researchers can study exotic states of matter and other mysterious physics. And they can test fundamental concepts, such as the equivalence principle — the idea that explains why objects of different masses fall at the same rate in a vacuum.

Spacefaring Bose-Einstein condensates were previously made on the International Space Station, at effective temperatures as low as 52 picokelvins. And an experiment on Earth, in which atoms were dropped down a tower to induce weightlessness, reached 38 picokelvins. But drop tower experiments are limited by the time their free fall lasts. That’s not an issue for experiments in Earth’s orbit. So cold atoms in space are really taking off.
