Madi Allen was 12 years old when she almost died from flu. Now 28, she shared her story with Live Science.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

In February 2011, Madi Allen, a healthy 12-year-old in Central Illinois, who loved playing sports, almost died from the flu. The influenza B virus resulted in her developing necrotizing pneumonia, where the infection triggers inflammation that destroys the tissue of the lungs, methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA), and her kidneys shut down. She was put on life support and dialysis, and was intubated for five weeks. She spent another two months in hospital and a decade recovering from the damage caused.

Allen, now 28, shared her experience with Live Science.

I was 12 years old when it all started. I was just a normal seventh grader, I played soccer and basketball. I didn't really have any health issues beforehand — just sports-induced asthma.

That weekend, I started to feel a little sick, but nothing too bad. My mom kept giving me over-the-counter medicine and it would work for a bit, then once it wore off, it would get really bad. I'd planned to go to one of my friend's birthday parties then spend the night with my best friend. I went to the party, but I texted my mom saying I should come home because I really wasn't feeling well, which was not usual for me at all. That night I asked my mom to sleep with me because I just felt terrible.

That was Saturday. By Sunday night, the only position that I could get comfortable in was my mom holding me like a baby. My mom just held me all weekend. My whole body just hurt and I started feeling like I couldn't breathe properly. That got way worse Monday morning.

We were waiting for my pediatrician to open up and my mom suggested taking a shower, saying, "Maybe that will help you feel a bit better before we go to the doctor." She had to help me take a shower because I was so weak, I couldn't stand by myself. She stepped away for a second just to grab a towel and said that when she came back, my lips were turning gray and my eyes were starting to look sunken in. She knew that something was not right so she called my dad, who was at the grocery store, and told him to just leave everything, that we need to get to the hospital.

Allen was put on life support and had to be intubated for five weeks after getting sick with flu.

Our local hospital is just a small rural hospital — everybody gets transferred out. They diagnosed me with double pneumonia and then sent me to a different hospital 30 minutes away that specialized more in kids.

My dad rode with me in the ambulance while my mom went home and grabbed a few things — she thought we'd just be there for a few days. By the time we got to the second hospital, I was in respiratory distress. They wanted to intubate me straight away but were waiting until my mom got there so she could talk to me — my dad did the best he could, but my dad didn't know how to calm me down.

I don't think the doctors even told me that they were putting me to sleep. My mom had to be the one to tell me. I remember being very scared. They put this mask on my face for the BiPAP [bilevel positive airway pressure machine, which delivers pressurized air to a patient] and I felt like that was suffocating me. It didn't feel like it was helping at all, which, I guess, at that point, it wasn't. They were just trying everything they could. I was begging them to take it off of me, crying and just saying, "one minute, just take it off for one minute."

Finally my mom tried to calm me down and she's like, "They're gonna have to put you to sleep now." I remember her telling me, "You're just gonna go to sleep for like a couple of hours and then you're gonna wake up and you're gonna feel a lot better."

My mom had to leave the room while they were doing that. As she was walking out the door, the last thing I said was "Mom" and then I put my hands in a heart shape. That was the last thing I did and the last time my mom heard my voice for five weeks.

After I was intubated, things got worse. I had to be put on life support so needed to be moved to a bigger hospital in St. Louis, Missouri. The flight team came to evaluate me and they later told me they didn't think they were ever going to get me to Saint Louis. They thought I wasn't going to make the trip. But they said my mom was begging them to help me, everyone in my family was begging them, so they did everything they could to get me on the helicopter. They worked on me for several hours — every time they tried to move me something would go wrong — but eventually they got me there.

The doctors had to call my parents to get permission to do surgery and put me on life support. My mom said that every time she heard my dad's phone ring, she thought they were calling to tell them that I didn't make it. They were told twice that it was more than likely I was going to pass than make it. They were trying to prepare my parents that I wasn't going to make it.

After getting out of hospital, it took years for Allen to recover, eventually having part of her lung removed that had been badly damaged by the virus.

I woke up five weeks later, and it was very confusing. Everybody was told if I asked what day it was, just to tell me the day of the week. When someone accidentally told me the date, I started crying because my aunt was supposed to be getting married a few weeks later and I was worried about being at her wedding. My mom wasn't there, so my dad had to calm me down and then he told me the wedding had been pushed to October so I could be there.

The second thing I was worried about was that I was supposed to take a test on the Constitution and that I'd missed it. I ended up taking it in the hospital. I was there for 93 days. I got out the very last week of school, so I got to go in on the last day of school and surprise my classmates and my teachers.

That summer, I didn't really do anything besides go to doctor's appointments. I was doing physical therapy, occupational therapy and speech therapy — literally all my time was spent at the hospital in therapy. I'd missed three months of school, but I got to start eighth grade with all my friends, and I ended up playing basketball again. But the next several years was a lot of hard work of trying to get back to my normal.

It probably took the rest of junior high and high school to get back to how I would have been before. It was a very long process and during that time I got sick a lot, so I ended up back in the hospital several times. And it was hard going through that as a teenager — I felt like everybody else is living their normal life, and I felt like I missed out on a lot. Looking back now, I still feel like I did miss out a lot. But I think we made the best of the circumstances.

During COVID, when I was 22, I kept getting sick, and the doctors finally told me that part of my lung was so damaged from the flu it was causing infections, so they gave me an option of getting part of my lung removed. It was a major surgery, but I did it and that was probably the best decision I ever made, because it's been five years and I have not been in the hospital once.

I moved to Florida about three years ago, and I started working as a medical assistant in a pulmonary clinic. This semester I got accepted into respiratory therapy school, so for the next two years, I'm going to be in school for respiratory therapy. It's kind of a full circle moment, to come back into the medical field, because there was a point in my life where everybody was asking me, "Oh, do you want to be a doctor? Do you want to be a nurse?" And I'm like, "Absolutely not." I was still so sick that I was there all the time. I never wanted to be there.

I went to college and I got a degree in criminal justice, but I never really knew what I wanted to do. I ended up getting a job at our local hospital — that first hospital that I went to. Every time they put me in the ER I just loved being there. That job made me realize that this is what I wanted to do.

When people hear my story, they don't realize that if I don't tell the end — after the hospital until now — they don't realize that my life didn't go back to normal after. It's taken 10 years. And it's hard. Some of the other family members that we've gotten to know through Families Fighting Flu, it's difficult listening to their stories. Sometimes I feel like I have this survivor's guilt. Their stories sound exactly like mine — but their kids didn't make it.

Before I got sick I got the flu shot every year, but that year we just got busy and it got put on the back burner. Since getting sick I have always made it a priority to get the flu shot every year. I know it is not a guarantee that I will never get the flu again — but hopefully it will reduce the chances of it ever getting that bad again.

With thanks to Families Fighting Flu, a non-profit organization that promotes flu vaccination and raises awareness of the severity of the infectious disease through families that have been affected.

#6353. The 6 Best Metal Detectors for Treasure Hunters and Experts Alike

Find treasure on the beach (or at least a bunch of beer cans) with these top-of-the-line devices.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

You've probably seen a metal detectorist hard at work at a beach or park with their funky-looking gadget and thought, "I wish I had one of those." It's easy to fantasize about stumbling upon a hoard of buried pirate gold or, more realistically, a lost piece of jewelry, but the reality of metal detecting is this: It's more about the process of searching than the actual find itself.

That said, metal detecting can be a fun and relaxing hobby for anyone to try, especially with friends, and the barrier to entry is low. It’s an activity that gives you an excuse to spend a few hours outside, scouring the sand or dirt for coins or who-knows-what, and you might even find something that really makes it worth your while, though it's best if you don't expect to.

To determine the best metal detectors for newbies and experts alike, I tested a number of different models on the beaches and in the parks of South Florida, rating their performance, handling, and overall usability across several different terrains. I also consulted with an expert detectorist who helped me understand what factors to consider when making my choices. No matter which of these machines works best for your use case, all of them are great gets.

I selected the best metal detectors after trying a handful of options that came recommended to me by Jeff Lubbert, an expert detectorist who has been tracking down treasures and finding lost rings since the mid-1980s, and a handful of other expert detectorists.

Lubbert has used his metal detector in 28 states, one United States territory, five foreign countries, and three foreign territories, where he has recovered items adding up to approximately $980,000. He is president of the Eureka Treasure Hunters Club in Denver, Colorado, and has written articles about metal detectors for outlets like American Diggers. He's also appeared on the TV show Forensic Files.

To test accuracy, I buried an old spoon and two different coins—a quarter and a penny—8 inches underground to check their level of discrimination and pinpointing. I also used each detector for several hours in a variety of conditions, including in a grassy park and at the beach, in both dry sand and wet sand, and under several inches of surf.

The Minelab Vanquish 560 is a dynamic metal detector that works well on every terrain, including wet sand, and is incredibly intuitive to use. Unlike the slightly cheaper Vanquish 440, my previous top recommendation, the 560 is waterproof to 16 feet, which makes it suitable for wading and underwater use. It also includes a rechargeable battery, a flashlight, and Bluetooth headphone support, making it one of the most fully-featured detectors in this guide, and especially for this price.

While it only has four find modes (including an adjustable “custom” option). That’s are far fewer than you will find on professional-grade detectors like the Minelab Equinox 900, but it's still much more than enough for most amateur metal detectorists.

The Vanquish 560 punches well above its weight, and value-wise, it's the best detector we tested on a per-dollar basis. It may feel like a splurge for first-timers, but you’re getting what you pay for. And it’s an incredibly handsome upgrade for folks looking strong accuracy and some quality-of-life improvements.

Since I primarily spoke with experts and enthusiasts, the Nokta FindX Pro was not remotely on my radar when I first began my research. But it may just be the best option for new detectorists looking to dip a toe into the hobbyist pool. It’s an all-in-one kit, complete with an effective digging tool, a nice duffel bag, and decent headphones—all for less than $200.

While it is not as accurate as my other recommendations, it’s a more than capable VLF detector. I was able to find items at both parks and beaches, though I noticed that its performance really suffered on wet sand and underwater. Its compact frame and adjustable handle make it accommodating to a wider-than-average range of newcomers, including kids and adults.

If you’re interested in the hobby and don’t want to spend too much to try it, the FindX Pro is a great fit for beginners.

While I wasn’t able to get this detector in for my current round of tests, Lubbert recommended the Minelab Manticore for expert detectorists who want the ultimate metal detector experience. He says it can visualize the ground beneath it in a 2D map, directing you to finds with depths and ID targets. It should work well in any terrain, including underwater, and has the most advanced backlight of any Minelab machine. Plus, with 10 search modes, there are many options for veteran detectorists looking to optimize for a specific type of search.

The price is substantial, but if you’re willing to spend this much money on a detector, I’m confident that it will be worth it.

The Simplex line is often recommended by experts as a good entry point for new detectorists. Nokta is one of the two biggest brands in the metal detecting game—the other is Minelab—and the Simplex Lite is a strong, basic VLF detector. I found it had top-notch discrimination, plenty of find modes, and a good coil size that easily found my testing materials and led me to beer cans, aluminum foil, and plenty of other objects on the beach.

Because this is a single-frequency VLF detector, it doesn’t perform as well as the Vanquish 440, especially on the mineralized sand at saltwater beaches. It’s still a very capable machine, though—even more so if you’re searching for a specific type of item, particularly coins and jewelry. Though it offers fewer customization options than its more expensive multi-frequency counterparts, it’s also much easier to pick up and use as a newcomer.

For those who are looking to spend a bit more, you can upgrade to the Simplex Ultra, which adds Bluetooth support and gives you precision detector tools like target ID scale and depth.

Underwater metal detecting is typically the domain of serious enthusiasts, especially if it’s in seawater. If this sounds intriguing, two different experts for metal detector recommendations (including Lubbert) suggest the XP Deus II, a high-end machine that specializes in just that. Expert Stanley Ross, known as the Metal Detector Man, who we spoke with for this article previously, says that he uses his Deus II to search for lost rings and other jewelry on the beach all the time.

The Deus II has something called "fast multi-frequency" technology, which allows for superior multi-frequency detection in a variety of conditions, and it's rated for up to 20 meters of water, a massive upgrade compared to our other picks that top out at 5 meters of water resistance. Our other multi-frequency picks use similar technology, but the Deus II offers better and faster response in saltwater conditions, making it easier to pinpoint buried targets without having to pass over the same spot multiple times, especially underwater.In order to use the Deus II underwater, however, you'll need a few accessories, including its waterproof wireless headphones and an underwater remote control. While these upgrades are technically “optional” in the sense that you can easily use the Deus II on land without them, they are virtually required for anything beyond getting your ankles wet.

Both of these additions will increase the price of the overall package considerably, depending on which exact model of headphones you choose. Both the $280 WS6 headphones (which can control the detector, but are not recommended for underwater use) and the $749 remote control have slightly different interfaces, but the remote control is generally recommended for both ease of use and underwater functionality. Because of its high customizability and 12 preset modes, the Deus II isn't quite as beginner-friendly as some of our other picks.

While I haven't yet tested the Deus II for myself, it’s highly regarded among enthusiasts. If you're interested in underwater detecting—whether that's wading around or even diving down—this choice will not disappoint.

The Minelab Equinox 900 is the most feature-rich metal detector I tested. From the second I picked it up, I could tell that it would be a cut above the rest. The build quality is noticeably better than that of other, less expensive models I tested—it just feels more substantial.

Its features and performance back up that first impression. The Equinox 900 consistently performed better than its less expensive counterparts as well, pinpointing targets precisely and identifying both their depth and target ID. Though I was able to find my planted targets with every detector, the Equinox 900 directed me precisely to all three, making the process quicker and easier in both dry and wet sand.

It also features a number of settings and tools that improve the detecting experience, including six customizable frequency settings, an easy-adjust handle, and Bluetooth support so you can use wireless headphones. All that customization is incredible if you’re an expert. I personally had more success using the premade settings, but I can see detectorists like Lubbert fine-tuning searches to great effect.

I was especially taken with its handgrip vibration feature, which gives you a rumbling haptic response when the Equinox picks up a target. It’s a great way to get your attention in a loud area, if you’re hearing-impaired, or if you’re just on a long walk and not paying close attention. Personally, I found it very helpful while roaming some very popular stretches of Miami’s beaches.

It’s worth noting that Minelab lists the Equinox 900 as a bit heavier than the other models we tested, though I personally didn’t notice a difference, even after several hours of sweeping. At more than triple the price of my best overall pick, it’s fair to say that the Equinox 900 is an investment for serious hobbyists. But it is far and away the most effective choice I tested and a worthy upgrade.

In addition to a decent pair of headphones, it helps to carry a pinpointer when using your metal detector. These precise, short-range auxiliary detectors assist you with determining the exact location of a find after picking something up with your detector’s large coil.

This one, from Minelab, is relatively expensive, but fully waterproof with five sensitivity levels, and it works very well. It also features ferrous discrimination, which allows it to tell if a target is made of ferrous metals like iron or non-ferrous metals like gold, silver, or copper. It isn’t strictly necessary but is an extra feature you’ll enjoy using in trash-filled parks.

We tested and loved the Minelab Vanquish 440, a slightly cheaper version of our current best overall pick, the Vanquish 560. It was recently replaced with a new and improved model, the Minelab Vanquish 460, which is also a strong choice. We ultimately chose to recommend the 560 because it offers a more robust set of features and works well over more types of terrain.

While shopping for a metal detector, you need to take into account a number of key factors, particularly the type, coil size, weight, and extra features like backlight and frequency customization. Weight and build quality also make a big difference, especially when you use these devices for hours at a time. It was initially hard to weigh these distinct traits, but after testing these machines myself, the features worth springing for became clear.

If you’re going to shop for a hobby-grade metal detector, it’s important to understand how they work. This is fairly technical equipment, so manufacturers will cater their products primarily to veterans who already have a bit of knowledge, which may be intimidating to new people.

Most metal detectors have a round head called the “search coil,” which is the actual detector itself. It has two parts, the transmitter coil and the receiver coil, which work in tandem to produce an electromagnetic field that shoots down into the ground wherever you wave it. When the field hits metal, it triggers another magnetic effect in response, which the coil picks up. Depending on the device, that signal may be able to tell you how deep an object is buried, based on the strength of the response.

Most of the detectors I recommend can determine what kind of metal they’re reading by measuring the object’s “phase shift,” or the time it takes for the object to react when the coil changes its magnetic current. This function, called “discrimination,” can sometimes help you figure out if your quarry is worth digging up before you go to the trouble of getting your digging tools out. However, as Lubbert notes, discrimination is not always reliable, and it’s generally best to err on the side of digging if you think you’ve found something worthwhile.

The first thing to look at before buying a metal detector is where you plan to use it, as some detectors are better equipped to scan specific types of terrain. For example, if you live near the coast and plan to sweep your local beach, you may want a different model than someone looking under hard soil in local parks. Though there are many kinds of detectors, I focused on the two most frequently used by novices and veteran hobbyists.

The physical size of the metal detector coil is important, too. If you don’t sweep the coil over an object, you aren’t going to get a ping, so bigger is better. Under most conditions, Lubbert recommends looking for a coil that’s at least 11 inches in diameter.

That said, Lubbert advises that smaller coils have their uses, especially in wooded areas, since it’s easier to get between twigs, grass, and weeds with a more compact head. Larger coils can theoretically detect objects that are deeper underground, but they’re also more susceptible to electromagnetic interference from the environment. He recommends having both a compact coil and a large coil option if you plan to scan a wide range of environments.

In general, all of my recommendations here seem relatively light on paper—the heaviest weighs only a few pounds. Keep in mind, though, that you could be waving this device around with one arm for hours at a time. Even a few ounces can greatly impact how quickly you tire out.

Mid-range and high-end metal detectors tend to feature backlit displays, which come in handy when searching in low-light conditions. (Some high-end models even come with flashlight functions). Though not a universal feature, I consider this essential for all but the cheapest options.

High-end metal detectors grant you a degree of customization through advanced settings, allowing you to set a specific level of discrimination that, when properly used, can help you identify relics and coins in a variety of environments. You need to know what you’re doing to take full advantage of these do-it-yourself search modes, but there are guides online to help you learn as you go.

Lastly, most metal detectors I researched and/or tested feature built-in batteries that last for hours on a full charge. That said, some models—including one of my picks—use disposable batteries instead. There are advantages and disadvantages to both: Disposable batteries can be replaced quickly, but you need to keep spare cells on you. It comes down to your preference, so go with what feels right.

“Make each swing of the detector take about 2 seconds and overlap your swings so that the coil covers all of the ground,” Lubbert says. “Wear headphones, as it helps you hear those deep target whispers.”

Lubbert also said that detectorists should be happy with what they find, and that you should expect 95 percent of your digs to result in trash. When that happens, be cool, and make sure to dispose of it properly.

According to Lubbert, a dedicated detectorist should have a pinpointer, proper recovery tools like a shovel, and a pouch to store trash and treasure separately.

Based on my testing experience and to echo his point above, I found headphones to be a must-have when using a metal detector, as the built-in speakers are difficult to hear, especially on a crowded beach.

Finding a legal place to use your metal detector is not as easy as you might think. It’s illegal to use a detector in U.S. National Parks and historic battlefields. Many cities ban using them on public property or require you to apply for a permit beforehand. Make sure to check your local city and county laws to determine if and where you may be allowed to use a metal detector and if you’ll need a permit to do so.

And, of course, if you plan to use your detector on private property, you should obtain permission from the owner, or else you might dig up a lawsuit instead of treasure.

Steven T. Wright is a freelance writer based in Miami, FL. He has been a full-time writer of various things for around a decade, especially long-form features about tech and digital culture. He enjoys spending time with his wife and cat, hiking, and reading weird fiction. You can follow him on Twitter @MadCathedral.

Jeff Lubbert has been an avid metal detector since 1980 and joined The Ring Finders directory in 2010. He is an active officeholder in Denver's Eureka Treasure Hunters Club and the co-host of American Digger Magazine's Relic Roundup, a weekly metal detecting podcast.

She has written about, tested, and reviewed everything from turkey fryers to high-definition TVs. Her byline has appeared in TWICE, Sound & Vision, Consumer Reports, and many others. #6352. How to Sing Karaoke Every Night, in Every Borough of New York City

In 1968, Daisuke Inoue decided he was going to be in two places at once. A musician who played in a backup band working Kobe’s nightlife circuit, Inoue soundtracked the evenings of soulful salarymen whom he befriended. With drums as his instrument of choice because “all you have to do is hit them,” he turned those relationships into business, arranging entertainment for their other engagements. As the legend goes, he couldn’t make it out to a gig he had booked at an insurance company’s trade show, so he invented the next best thing. Combining a standard eight-track tape player used in car stereos, a microphone, an amplifier, and a 100-yen coin slot, he placed his ghost in the machine, which he fashioned into the Juke 8. Inoue’s device—the progenitor to the modern-day karaoke machine—was a success.

A more rigorous history might question whether Inoue really invented the first such machine or whether that credit belongs to electronics manufacturer Shigeichi Negishi’s Sparko Box a decade earlier. But the meteoric takeoff of karaoke has soared far past its humble—and slightly murky—origins. A portmanteau of the Japanese words kara, meaning empty, and oke, meaning orchestra, karaoke evokes both loneliness and collective belonging. Nearly 60 years on, we still root for the little machine that could—and all the brave singers who bare their heart through age-revealing ballads and club classics.

An impassioned rendition of Celine Dion’s “It's All Coming Back to Me Now” transpires at Beats Karaoke Cafe in Williamsburg

Perhaps nowhere is karaoke’s full breadth more on display than in New York City, where, on one side, you’ve got lounges complete with floor-to-ceiling video walls and speakers with built-in auto-tune capabilities and, on the other, decades-old dives whose performers are as much an institution as the establishment.

A karaoke spot is the one place where post-prom dates, wedding parties, and career performers alike gather to spend their time and money on gloriously subpar entertainment, entirely without irony. When you’re the one behind the mic, it becomes something mythic—a reprieve from the passive consumption dominating much of the city’s nightlife. Tally up the past year’s most recent headlines, and you’d get the impression that we’re becoming less fun—we’re having less sex, drinking less alcohol, going to fewer parties, and hosting fewer of our own. The karaoke bar might be one of the last, thriving places in New York where we wait half an hour to openly embarrass ourselves, and for that it’s well worth our nights out.

With the hundreds of sing-along nights and 30-plus specialized bars in New York City listed on trackers like Karaoke Crowd, there was no way we’d be able to cover them all. So we visited one place a day for a week, crisscrossing the boroughs for a taste of the city’s diversity. We commenced our week in Koreatown, where some-dozen private rooms are conveniently concentrated on a single street, and continued our spree at an Irish pub on the Upper East Side, where shouting for sport and song are one in the same. We hit up a Staten Island dive of devoted locals and a year-old Astoria restaurant where, once the Tagalog ballads have begun, you must push the plate away and join in. These watering holes, old and new, are living proof of the many shapes karaoke takes and the unifying joy of belting it out together, even when so much else threatens to divide us.

A singer takes the stage at Iggy’s on the Upper East Side to perform Billy Joel and Elton John’s “Piano Man”

We began the week where many end it, on the dense corridor of West 32nd Street between Sixth and Seventh Avenues. Along this stretch of Koreatown, karaoke bars, podiatrists, escape rooms, and coworking spaces stack atop one another. Our crawl started at Gagopa, whose BYOB policy is a favorite among the large-group partiers and Midtown corporate crowd for fast-tracking camaraderie. The bar eluded us at first, not for a lack of signage but for its location on the fourth story of its building, and the search more or less provided a template for our crawl: a ride up an elevator the size of an airplane lavatory and head-scratching decor. At Gagopa’s sister bar, 32 Karaoke, this last item consists of Polaroids of visiting groups on the walls—the very karaoke canon that, once you’ve stepped through its doors, you become part of.

Anticipatory staircases aside, no amount of symbolic literacy can prepare you for a K-town elevator panel. Despite its abundance of labeled buttons, deciphering them only makes things more confusing. To reach Space Karaoke Bar and Lounge, for instance, you have to avoid accidentally ending up at Space Ping Pong, one of two Space sports bars, or the Space golf simulator. Take it as a sign to stop trying to make sense of things and just embrace the ride.

Across the street, Chorus Karaoke Lounge has a clubbier feel, with a purple-and-blue-lit bar. To the left is a hallway of private rooms, lined with porthole window portraits of Madonna, Morrissey, Elvis, and all the other greats. On the evening we visited, only one karaoke room at the end of the white hallway was occupied—by a lone singer crooning to himself. It may well have been a strict weekly ritual, the first step in a vocal warm-up regimen. “I sing, therefore I am,” read a sign near its entrance as we left, a reminder that although thinking may be proof of existence, song is proof of life. —Skyli Alvarez & Kat Chen

Pianist Mark Benjamin, left, accompanies performers at Sid Gold's Request Room on 26th Street, which has additional locations in Detroit, Nashville, and Washington, DC

In the liminal space between Chelsea and Flatiron, Sid Gold’s Request Room is a bit of an outlier. Sandwiched between an empty office space and halal buffet, its old-timey façade simply reads “piano” and “karaoke.” Both await you in the spacious piano lounge, tucked behind a pair of velvet curtains at the back of the cocktail bar.

We arrived around 9 p.m. and slid into one of the alcoved booths closest to the stage, a small black platform beside the bar centerpiece: a Baldwin baby grand. As we settled in, a singer, backdropped by pianist Mark Benjamin’s harmonies, wrapped up his performance to a crowd of now four; he then came to take our order. Fortunately, others trickled in: tourists and their New Yorker friends; Tuesday-night regulars; a dog named Henry. Many, as we learn, were here for Benjamin's performance—and succor.

As we came to find out later on in the week, karaoke works better in numbers, but Sid Gold’s makes the case for a small yet mighty group. A particularly moody evocation of Chris Isaak’s “Wicked Game,” prefaced by the singer’s memories of angst-ridden high school years, drew out lower-than-low notes. In what could only be described as a shouty but otherwise cheery cover of “Back to Black,” each verse’s forceful delivery was more unpredictable than the last. At some point Benjamin called upon someone named Eric, who kicked off his flip-flops to sing “Part of Your World,” a method for getting into character (one can only assume) that would be frowned upon everywhere else but here.

If you think you can evade the stage, Benjamin will make sure you get on up there. He’ll harmonize and improvise riffs even if he’s never heard the song (or wants you to think this); pause to match your pace; and convince you that it was made for you to sing. —S.A.

I was immediately given the cousin treatment when I passed the threshold of Barkada Social Club. In case there was any ambiguity about the cultural identity of this Astoria restaurant and bar, let it be known I walked into Bruno Mars’s “Risk It All,” with plates of lumpia and kwek kwek covering the tables. It was a good night to come—Barkada NYC, a separate but similarly named LGBTQ+ Filipinx community group, hosts its monthly Kikay Konek karaoke event here. Joey, a queer-affirming physical therapist by day and programming coordinator with Barkada NYC, was my gregarious host for the night. When I asked them about encountering struggles with finding kindred souls, they gave me a considerate look before breaking out into a smile and saying, “I honestly can’t relate.” This came as no surprise as I watched them record the “Toxic” floor routine for BNYC’s Instagram before rushing off to plan next month’s programming, discuss bringing BYNC to the Bronx, finalize plans for a hike three weekends away, and introduce me to their boyfriend. It takes a social whirlwind like that to bring together a collective of members from across all five boroughs, plus exotic reaches like Tenafly, New Jersey. The crowd is in constant flux, peeling off and joining in depending on what the song queue has in store. The one exception to the rule is when someone requests Jesse Zaragoza’s “Bakit Pa,” a sweeping Tagalog ballad from the ’90s about unrequited love that brings everybody rushing to the fore. “It’s like our national anthem,” Joey says. —K.C.

Tim sings at Steiny's Pub in Staten Island

At Sid Gold's, patrons are more than ready to be called up for a harmonized performance

At the site of the former Mayfair Bar and Grill, a favorite among St. George’s queer patrons in the 1950s and ’60s, Steiny’s Pub was once a low-key gay bar turned sports joint that now exists somewhere between the two. It’s fitting for a borough that’s often the butt of the joke, cloaked in its perceived suburban isolation, though an eight-minute walk from the Staten Island Ferry makes it surprisingly less difficult to reach from Manhattan than one might assume. We passed a small group of local 30-somethings smoking near the entrance and, once inside the dive, encountered a lively emcee who goes by the DJ name Nazz Raidience. We’re quickly singled out for not being regulars and handed a Sharpie and clipboard to add to a queue that Nazz only loosely followed.

As co-owner John Michael works behind the bar, a few seated patrons watch tennis and baseball while others belt it out to their backs. The L-shaped booth seating next to the DJ setup operates as the stage. Most who perform adhere to genre: bar patron Dia’s heavy metal numbers by Kittie are complete with death growls, Connor does Eminem with breakdancing and triple-threat delivery, and others insist on 1980s ballads. Nazz shepherds the queue at an auctioneer’s pace, sometimes joining in and always poking fun, calling upon you to spin the prize wheel that could lead to a free drink or 10 push-ups. Although they host karaoke nights across the city, Steiny’s is their favorite for the many different worlds it attracts, and they'll convince you to stay for the ferry sailors who, post-shift, are said to come singing around 2 a.m. When it became clear to us this would not be the night, we left without sea chanteys in our hearts but with a better understanding of the appeal of the city’s least-populated borough. —S.A.

Performing karaoke cosplaying as Shadow the Hedgehog, hands full with impulse purchases from Comic Con’s artist alley, is my penance. I had postponed this visit for too long, leaving me with no option but to come as I was. Bronx Beer Hall is nestled within a larger food hall in the historic Italian neighborhood of Arthur Avenue (please, try the veal). By the time Friday karaoke night is in full swing, all of the surrounding businesses are fully closed. From the outside the telltale sign that anything is happening is the ambient trail of music. Channel an ’80s B-movie slasher victim, and follow the noise into the darkness. Upon emerging into the light, you’ll see a hallway lined with T-shirts printed with lines like “Call it gravy, not sauce!” or “I’m not a gynecologist, but I’ll take a look.” As for the music selection, it’s what you’d expect from a generationally eclectic crowd. There’s tender performances of Bon Jovi and Air Supply following the crowd-rousing momentum of “NUEVAYoL” by a man wearing a snapback with what was certainly a record-breaking number Yankees logos embroidered on the design. Every three songs the DJ would queue up 50 Cent’s “In Da Club” to announce yet another birthday, and BBH turned out to be just the kind of place where an unrelated 24-year-old and 40-year-old blow out their candles together. Being Shadow the Hedgehog did not go unnoticed either. Our millennial bartender who grew up playing the original Sonic games requested “Live and Learn,” the main theme song of Sonic Adventure 2. As I took in the lyrics for the first time on the TV screen, I lived and I learned. —K.C.

The karaoke room at Iggy’s becomes rowdier as the night progresses

This Irish karaoke bar was our first reporting excursion, and it established a curious precedent. Between its Upper East Side location, Gaelic rafters, and portraits of 27 Club musicians, the place seemed tailor-made for Xennial dads. We assumed butt rock was inevitable and hedged our bets on at least one rendition of Hinder’s “Lips of an Angel.”

My hunch came from Eve Kosofsky Sedgwick, specifically her theories of homosociality: the nonsexual bonds between people of the same sex. Spend enough time at karaoke, and you’ll notice that “Lips of an Angel” is almost always performed as a duet between two men. For the uninitiated, the song imagines a phone call between a singer and an ex he still quietly yearns for, wishing she were there instead of the “girl” in the next room. Sure enough, two friends took up the mantle. Maybe it was simply a fun song to sing; maybe karaoke offered a safe conduit for expressing something else. We encountered the song at every subsequent karaoke night, always sung by two people of the same sex.

While some bars use online queues for song requests, attendees go analog at Iggy’s

As a week of karaoke draws to a close, you will come to find specific crowds come in waves. First come those who learned to love performance in youth-theater productions, usually in duos or trios, and take their sing-alongs seriously. Then there are the harder-to-place groups: coworkers, reunited friends, or couples using karaoke as a social buffer. Next come the balladeers and lone yearners, eager to broadcast exactly how they’re feeling, followed by the humble soloists who know they’re good and have nothing to prove. Finally, the rowdy late-night crowd of after-partiers spills in, at worst hogging the mic and at best uniting an entire room.

In our five hours at Iggy’s, the former theater kids delivered truly spectacular covers of “Defying Gravity,” the Irishmen shouted Irish pub songs, and the soloists flirted by way of song choice. Three dollars grant you one song that you select from an impressively up-to-date binder and scrawl onto a piece of paper, then the waiting game begins. “We just met in the photo booth” is how one performer introduced a B-side from The Cure, an effort to woo over a stranger who he knew shared at least one common interest. Karaoke gives singers permission to say what they otherwise cannot or will not admit, though the message is rarely subtle. —S.A. & K.C.

Though Seventh Heaven's evenings often begin with film screenings, watch parties, and other community events, they always end in karaoke

During a week when we spent every other waking hour thinking about karaoke-ing, we sometimes looked past dives and private rooms for other ambitious reinventions, like on a boat; in a taxicab en route to the airport; or in an East Williamsburg apartment turned karaoke rental. Still, it’s ultimately the most obvious spots that draw the crowds. Take Williamsburg’s Beats Karaoke Cafe, an eight-minute walk from the Bedford Avenue station, with a rustic bar on the first floor, leading to a hall of private rooms that continue downstairs. We eventually wound our way into film production coordinator Natalie’s group of eight, who told us this was their go-to whenever they “want to add a little divorced dad rock to the night,” and we had caught them testing out new material. Still, they made their way through classics like The Cranberries’ “Zombie” and “Time of My Life,” while also executing many Dirty Dancing lifts.

Farther along the L train, it was only appropriate that we ended up at a bar named Seventh Heaven. We were among the youngest crowd by far, at least in taste. Karaoke-goers swarmed the stage and fluently rattled off the romaji lyrics of “A Cruel Angel’s Thesis,” the theme song to ’90s anime Neon Genesis Evangelion. This bar gets its crowd, with a cocktail menu filled with allusions to the fandom, like the Apothecary’s Negroni fashioned after popular light novel series The Apothecary Diaries, or my own drink, the Boy’s Love G&T, which is named after the popular fiction genre that focuses on the romance between male characters. Turns out, there are plenty of effusive ex–theater kids who understand the assignment.

The DJ cued up our request, “Viva la Vida.” From the vantage point of the stage, the outstretched hands of the crowd looked not unlike the Eugène Delacroix painting of the Revolution of 1848, which Coldplay used as cover art their 2008 album Viva la Vida or Death and All His Friends. A notably resigned wedding party lingered at the back of the audience, while city newcomers hailing from nearby venue House of Yes gleefully accepted our mic to unleash a few verses. The karaoke-goers had in the very least not given up on tonight. —S.A. & K.C.

#6351. In Some Ways, Bluetti’s Step-Down Apex 200 is a Step Up From the Apex 300

This power station is one of Bluetti’s most multifunctional yet and a boon to solar power lovers.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

When I reviewed the Bluetti Apex 300 power station earlier this year, I was impressed with how powerful it was and how easy it was to expand into a robust home backup system. But there were a few notable trade-offs, mostly in portability and a lower variety of outlets. With Bluetti’s Apex 200 power station, those drawbacks are answered with a powerful model that’s much better suited to life on the road.

Physically, it’s not hard to notice the difference between the two units. At 84 pounds, the Apex 300 is large and heavy to tote around. The 200 is 59 pounds and roughly 28 percent smaller. It’s not as powerful as its larger sibling, but the 200 is still definitely built for use in the home, while being more adaptable for long road trips or cross-country treks in an RV.

The Apex 200 outputs up to 3,200 watts of continuous power (it says 3,600 on the front, but that’s only if it’s connected to an expansion battery). That’s enough to run several appliances or even a few circuits in your home electrical system if you connect it to a manual transfer switch using the 120-volt, 30-amp port. It also has a 2,560-watt-hour capacity, which can provide several hours of power—I ran my refrigerator for a full 27 hours on a single charge, and when I ran the numbers, I estimated that it runs just over 90 percent efficiently, which is very good for a power station.

The 200 also brings direct DC power back, with a bank of USB outlets and both 10- and 30-amp 12-volt outputs. This is something the Apex 300 doesn’t have built-in (it requires an optional hub to add it), which makes it a bit less versatile as a portable station.

One niche feature I really liked was the ability to turn off each AC outlet individually using the mobile app. Doing this helps to cut down on the slight battery drain that an idle outlet can contribute, and it’s not commonly seen on power stations. It might seem like a small thing, but when you’re trying to get the most runtime out of your power station, every little bit helps. It’s also handy if you want to turn off power to one device, but not another.

What you don’t get with the Apex 200, however, is 240-volt output for higher-powered applications like powering high-voltage appliances or HVAC systems. That means it’s not suited for advanced whole-home backup like the Apex 300 is, but it's fine if you're only powering 120-volt appliances.

The Apex 200 does, however, mimic the modularity of the 300. You can add up to six additional batteries to expand your capacity to over 33 kilowatt-hours using the largest batteries Bluetti offers, the B500K. You can also pair it with the Apex 300 to combine and increase total power output to over 7,000 watts.

One of the most surprising features I found with the Apex 200 was a maximum solar input of up to 3,000 watts. That’s incredibly high for a power station in this size range. It achieves this by offering two sets of inputs: low-voltage XT60 input (up to 1,000 watts) and high-voltage MC4 input (up to 2,000 watts). If you had the rated panels to support both of these inputs, you could fully recharge this station in just a few hours on a perfectly sunny day.

This attention to detail on solar recharging makes the Apex 200 one of the most robust power stations I’ve seen targeted to the on-the-go end user who likes to tap into the sun's rays for energy while off-grid and on the road. Of course, it also features standard charging from AC power, including a Turbo mode that supports fast charging, an auto mode that allows you to set the rate you prefer, or a silent mode that limits the amount of input so that the cooling fan doesn’t need to turn on (which on this model can be a bit loud).

Another feature I like is passthrough charging, which allows you to run devices from the station while recharging the battery at the full rate. The inverters in lesser power stations will throttle the input if they need to power something at the same time, but not here. This is true of the Apex 300, too, and I’m glad they kept this feature in the Apex 300.

For my money, this power station is best suited to those who plan to use the Apex 200 for limited home backup during emergencies to power 120-volt devices or circuits, while also wanting to take it on trips. Overlanders, especially, will appreciate the lighter weight and portability, and they’ll also love the high solar input, which can come in handy when you’re on the road and out of range of AC power. I still like the Apex 300 a lot, but the Apex 200 shows that a bit more versatility can go a long way.

A new study points to testosterone and proteins in the skin as reasons why males and females experience temperatures differently.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

It's a common observation that women often prefer warmer temperatures and feel cold more easily than men do, and the same trend appears among females of other species. Now, a study offers new clues as to what drives this preference — and testosterone may play a part.

Skin carries sensors to detect heat and cold that influence each organism's decision to stay in or move out of an environment. The new study, published Oct. 28 in the Journal of Physiology, found that these sensors activate at higher temperatures in female mice, which appears to shift their preferred temperature roughly 7 degrees Fahrenheit (4 degrees Celsius) higher than that of male mice. Testosterone seems to influence this difference in activation.

"You could say it's just a cute observation of no particular importance," said study co-author Peter McNaughton, a pharmacologist at King's College London who studies pain, thermal sensation and thermoregulation. "[But] it's got practical ramifications," in that it might be important in designing buildings and spaces that accommodate people, he told Live Science.

Proteins in the skin's nerve endings activate in response to warmth or cold. "You can look at them like little electrical generators in the nerve endings," said Dr. Michael Caterina, a neuroscientist at Johns Hopkins University who was not involved in the research.

When activated, these proteins allow charged ions to enter sensory nerve cells, which, in turn, transmit electrical signals to the brain. The circuits a given nerve cell connects to determines our perception of heat or cold, Caterina told Live Science.

Beyond humans, it is known that many female animals, including mice and birds, prefer slightly warmer temperatures than their male counterparts do. So the researchers set up an experiment to investigate these differences.

They put 30 male and 27 female mice on two adjacent plates of different temperatures — one at 91.4 degrees Fahrenheit (33 degrees Celsius) and another that varied between lower and higher temperatures. A camera tracked the mice's movements and calculated how much time they spent on each plate.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Both male and female mice spent more time at the 91.4 F plate when the second plate was cooler. However, when put next to a plate measuring 100.4 F (38 C), female mice spent significantly more time on the warmer plate than male mice did. The average preferred surface temperature was approximately 89.6 F (32 C) for male mice and 96.8 F (36 C) for female mice.

"Since the top of the cage was completely open, there was no question of the air temperature affecting the mice," McNaughton said, so the preference was driven solely by the sensors in their skin. The researchers also measured the internal and skin temperatures of the mice and confirmed that there were no significant differences between the sexes on those fronts.

The scientists explored what would happen if they genetically deleted the warmth-detector protein. In male mice, this reduced their avoidance of the warmer plate, suggesting this protein normally sends a signal that discourages them from staying on warmer surfaces. The mice's preferred temperature also rose to about 95 F (35 C), closer to that of females.

The study suggests that testosterone somehow tweaks the function of heat-sensing nerves in the skin.

In female mice, deleting or blocking the protein did not have any significant effect.

The team then tried eliminating or blocking the coolness-detecting protein, finding that males and females didn't avoid the cool plates as strongly as they did before. Female mice also spent less time on the warmer plates, but males' preference for the warmer plates didn't change.

"Females are a little bit more responsive to activation of the cold receptor," Caterina said, "and a little bit less responsive to activation of the warmer receptor." That's despite the temperature-sensing neurons in both sets of mice working identically, the team found.

The researchers suspected that sex hormones might help to explain this difference.

They gave a group of male mice a drug that blocks the production of testosterone. Weeks after the treatment, these mice spent more time on the 38 C plate than males with normal testosterone. Meanwhile, female mice given testosterone lost their preference for warmer temperatures.

Interestingly, giving male mice female hormones, including forms of estrogen and progesterone, did not affect their temperature preferences. And blocking the hormones in female mice also had no effect. These hormones are known to influence other aspects of temperature regulation in the body, though, such as heat dissipation through the skin; but in this case, they didn't seem to affect animals' perception of temperature.

"So it really seems as though testosterone is the most important determinant," McNaughton said. But these changes were only partial; testosterone did not completely reverse the differences between the sexes. "So there is something else going on that we weren't able to identify," he added.

The exact mechanism for how testosterone impacts the sensor proteins is not clear. Because the effect happened over weeks, researchers suggested that it did not directly affect the temperature-sensing proteins. It might instead act indirectly by influencing the activity of genes, but further studies would be needed to confirm this idea.

Although the researchers did not conduct any tests in humans, McNaughton noted that the same sensor proteins are present in people and that studies with humans suggest that they behave in a similar way.

This research provides "valuable information" for understanding how the proteins responsible for sensing temperature work, Caterina said. Understanding these mechanisms could be useful for studying conditions like neuropathic pain, in which people's sensitivity to heat and cold is enhanced.

"What kinds of signals create our daily experiences around temperature is by itself very important," he told Live Science. "It's a big part of understanding ourselves as living beings."

This article is for informational purposes only and is not meant to offer medical advice.

#6349. 15 Best Arch Support Shoes for Long Travel Days

I grew up believing that sore and throbbing feet were a necessary evil of long travel days, until a physical therapist said three magic words: arch-support shoes. She’d noticed the inside forefoot and outside heels of my shoes’ soles were completely worn through—a sign of overpronation because I have no natural arch. With that kind of misalignment, it was no surprise that even a simple day of set-jetting through The Sound of Music sites in Austria or strolling through the compact center of Prague was wreaking havoc on my feet.

As it turns out, as much as 37% of the population is believed to have some degree of flat foot, according to a National Library of Medicine study. But how it affects everyday life can vary by person. Initially, I only noticed the pain on high step-count days, but when I started long-distance running 10 years ago, I knew it was time to invest in supportive shoes capable of going the distance.

So I visited my local Fleet Feet in Hoboken, New Jersey, where nowadays its complimentary Fit ID 3-D scan can get granular, most recently showing me that my two feet have different lengths, as well as varying ball and heel widths. Most blaringly, both my arch heights are on the lowest possible end of the scale.

What I’ve learned more than anything is that there is no one-size-fits-all supportive shoe that works for everyone, which is why individual fittings are so crucial. (In extreme cases, like when I got posterior tibial tendinitis after running a half marathon, be sure to consult a healthcare professional.) But for a dose of stability, here are 15 arch-support shoes that are primed for long days on your feet.

For the last decade, the Brooks Adrenaline GTS has been my go-to shoe—that’s what GTS stands for, after all. The shoe’s GuideRails technology works its magic not by trying to correct your stride, but by guiding it in the direction that feels natural. Not only did it get me through my first few races with New York Road Runners, and eventually NYC Marathon training, but it’s always the shoe I go back to when I crave stability with just a sprinkle of cushioning. Whenever I slip these on, I feel locked in. The new version, which launched on November 1, retains its trusted features, while refining the heel tab and tongue to be sleeker and more functional.

During the most wrenching times of my foot pain, when every step I took hurt, an orthopedic doctor encouraged me to get a pair of Hokas and start running again. The brand may have led the way with oversized cushioned soles, but one of its bestsellers is this stability shoe, with an H-frame to prevent arch-less feet from turning inward. The newest version features a tighter mesh upper on the inside portion of the shoe, adding support to its arch side while retaining that soft cushiony feel. It even bears an American Podiatric Medical Association (AMPA) seal certifying that it’s beneficial to foot health.

Oofos may be known for its slides and recovery footwear (I wore a pair for a week after the 2024 Boston Marathon), but the same lightweight support strategies are applied to this casual sneaker. Its trademark high-impact absorbing Oofoam soaks up 37% of impact compared to regular shoes. Best of all, it’s machine washable with a closed-cell foam that prevents odors.

Let’s face it: Hiking shoes can be a pain to pack—which is what makes this Columbia hiking boot that's disguised as a sneaker so brilliant. Without any breaking in, they were immediately comfortable yet firm, and have kept my feet dry through sudden downpours and even river crossings on a hike in Thailand. This fall, they doubled as a sporty shoe, as I ran and biked the 32-mile Moose Loop Trail around Anchorage over three days, including a drizzly four-mile run on the final day.

Most impressively, during my Intrepid Travel Kenya Safari Adventure earlier this month, rain started falling while we were planting trees in the Mt. Kenya region’s Intrepid-adopted forest until we were trudging through mud. But the Konos’s sophisticated underfoot system provided support with maximum cushioning and traction so that I never doubted my stability any step of the way.

During the worst of my foot issues, I thought I'd be confined to a life of bulky orthotics. That’s when Vionic saved me. Every shoe in its collection—from sandals to dress shoes—is powered by its podiatrist-approved Vio Motion technology with a deep heel cup for stability, shock-absorbing cushioning, flexible movement, and most noticeably, strong arch-support that realigns the body while improving balance. This casual sneaker merges all that into a lace-up design that’s as supportive as it is cute. Not only was there zero break-in period for instant comfort, but it also meets the One Planet sustainability standard.

As I learned during my most recent Fleet Feet fitting, arch support and heel stability are inherently linked—and Kuru’s own patented sole hones in precisely those two traits. Together, they turn these lightweight court shoes into a secret weapon, able to endure the miles without an inkling of fatigue. Plus the versatile style can be dressed up or down.

The 90-year-old brand from the Italian Dolomites is best known for its mountaineering gear—and it’s that kind of technical expertise that was used to develop its Pedrock hiking shoe. The visible 3F System ties together flexibility, fit, and support. The adjustable laces ensure that the shoe fits like a glove while an EVA plate provides stability, along with reinforced heel and toe caps. All together, the urban-to-mountain shoe transitions perfectly through every step of your travels.

When it comes to technical gear, there are so many bells and whistles to consider that it’s easy to overlook the basics—namely, support. Teva never goes wrong in that realm and uses its own Lite-Comf midsole for a cushiony step, along with a patented universal heel lock system and Vibram grip for traction on the outer, so there’s no reason to teeter, even on multiple-day hikes over varied terrain. Those looking for less bulkiness with the same support can also opt for the lightweight road-to-trail Aventrail R2T shoe, which launched earlier this year.

The dependability that comes with Merrell’s high-performing outdoor wear is merged with Gore-Tex’s gold standard of waterproofness in this simple yet powerful hiking boot. It's easy to see why it's become my go-to for the last few years. At 16.36-oz. per shoe, it’s a hearty design, which equals stability throughout. The Kinetic Fit–blend contoured footbed strengthens the heel and a molded nylon shank adds arch support, while Vibram traction on the soles prevents slipping on slick surfaces, eliminating any flat-footed hiker’s worries—and taking me on adventures I thought were out of my range.

Cold weather footwear has long been a struggle for me—until I met this travel-friendly ankle boot from my trusted Vionic. Its classic design is easy to pair with anything from dresses to jeans, and the full-length zipper makes it easy to slip on and off. But don’t underestimate its durability, equipped with a completely waterproof leather upper and sealed seams to ensure not a drop seeps in. Plus, it conquers my fear of slippery sidewalks with articulated pods that provide traction for steady steps while still feeling cushiony.

The Kizik brand may seem like a novelty, focused on the ability to step in and out of shoes hands-free—yes, even these boots with laces (that don’t actually need to be tied). But the Juno 2 goes beyond just speeding you through TSA checkpoints. It’s chock full of support, boasting a molded EVA foam midsole for comfort and an Arch Form insole that molds to your foot shape.

Here’s what Vionic does best—take the patented footbed it's known for with orthotic-grade arch support and apply it to styles that don’t disclose your foot problems. This everyday loafer, made with post-consumer recycled materials, combines that solid support with extreme flexibility and a grippy sole. But the best part for travelers is how packable these loafers are—the upper (which comes in either super soft leather or suede) squishes easily, yet retains its shape and support. I’ve worn these to conferences and events, and often get asked who makes them, as it’s rare to find business casual shoes that are so supportive. I stocked up with three pairs waiting in my closet for when my first ones wear out—though after more than a year, they’ve shown no signs of aging.

A ballet flat with actual arch support? Only Birkenstock can make that possible with its trademark cork-latex footbed known for its firm arch support, along with a natural leather insole and suede lining. All that support may sound stiff, but it’s evened out with EVA cushioning. All together, it’s that free-flowing feeling from its famous Big Buckle sandals wrapped in a cozy exterior.

This leather slip-on may look like an everyday flat, but its comfort features are where it shines, starting with sturdy arch-support designed for all-day wear. Unlike most shoes of this genre, it has a removable footbed to slide in custom orthotics (I’m used to having to tear them out of flats!), plus a lightweight rubber outsole to keep you on your feet. Available in regular and wide, the Larisa also proudly wears an APMA acceptance seal.

The first time I slipped on the Aetrex Collette loafers, I immediately stood up straighter. There’s something about its sloping arch-support that directed not just my feet but my entire posture into a more confident stance. It turns out the footbed is designed to follow the natural curvature of each person’s foot, alleviating issues from plantar facilities to heel pain. The brand puts an emphasis on personalized fit, with the strap across the shoe cleverly doubling as an adjustable Velcro and, making them feel more like snug sneakers than loafers.

While it may seem like only people with flat feet or low arches require arch support, that’s not the case. “Anyone with tired feet or discomfort may benefit from a more supportive shoe,” Jenny Simpson, three-time Olympian and Fleet Feet’s chief running officer, tells Traveler. She adds that the specifics of your foot will dictate the support that works best. Generally, those with low or flexible arches can benefit from stability shoes, while those with high and rigid arches might do better with more cushioned shoes.

What to look for in an arch-support shoe?

Simpson cautions not to choose a shoe based on arch height alone: “Support should feel like it is meeting your arch, while the heel should feel secure,” says Simpson. Only you can tell what feels right once it’s on your foot, as “how you move and what feels comfortable to you” are the ultimate factors.

No singular shoe will address soreness for everyone. “The right choice depends on what is causing the discomfort, how your foot moves, and whether you need more cushioning, more stability, or a combination of both,” says Simpson. Since no product photo or descriptions can replicate how shoes will feel on your feet, in-person fittings are the most valuable.

Are arch-support shoes good for heel pain?

Simpson says that insoles can definitely be “an excellent tool for anyone looking for more tailored solutions for their footwear.” In particular, for those dealing with plantar fasciitis-induced heel pain, the extra support can reduce strain. Alternatively, cushioned shoes—like Hoka is known for—can make standing and walking more comfortable.

What brands design the most supportive shoes?

Running and walking shoes are built to endure the long days that travel requires, as Simpson calls out Brooks, Hoka, Asics, New Balance, and Saucony as strong options. She suggests trying different models since two styles from the same brand can have totally different fits. Other lifestyle shoes aren’t necessarily designed for the same level of wear. “My strongest advice is not to shop by label alone,” Simpson says. “Many shoes are labeled ‘supportive,’ ‘stability,’ or ‘orthopedic.’ They can be useful descriptions, but your foot gets the final vote. The best shoe is the one that fits your anatomy, supports your activity and allows you to move comfortably.”
